0.title: The Magna Carta of Christian Liberty: Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
0.overview:
Paul wrote to the Galatians in a state of controlled fury. He was angry not for himself but for them — and for the gospel. Every other letter in his corpus opens with a thanksgiving to God for the recipients; Galatians has none. He moves immediately, in the very first verse, to defend his apostolic authority, and by verse 6 he is in open astonishment: “I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel.” The urgency that presses through every paragraph of this letter was born of Paul’s conviction that the gospel itself was at stake — not a peripheral issue but the very core of what he had preached and what they had received.

The crisis had been created by a group scholars call the Judaizers — Jewish Christians who insisted that faith in Christ was necessary but not sufficient. Gentile believers also needed to be circumcised and observe the Mosaic law in order to be fully accepted by God and fully included in God’s people. This seems, on the surface, like a minor addition: faith in Christ plus a few religious practices. But Paul saw it with total clarity for what it was: a fundamental contradiction of the gospel. If anything in addition to Christ is required for justification — even something God-given and ancient like circumcision — then Christ is no longer sufficient, grace is no longer free, and the cross is no longer enough. “If righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose” (2:21).

Galatians is structured in three movements. Chapters 1–2 are autobiographical: Paul defends the divine origin of his gospel (he received it not from men but from Jesus Christ directly) and recounts his confrontation with Peter at Antioch, where the gospel’s logic was at stake in a table-fellowship dispute. Chapters 3–4 are theological: Paul argues from Scripture (Abraham, the covenant, the law’s purpose, the allegory of Hagar and Sarah) that the gospel of grace by faith preceded the Mosaic law by 430 years and is not superseded by it. Chapters 5–6 are practical: the freedom of the gospel is not license for the flesh but the only true basis for life in the Spirit and love for the neighbor.

Martin Luther’s Commentary on Galatians (1531) is the most celebrated commentary in the history of the church. He called this letter his “Catherine von Bora” — his beloved, the one he was married to. He wrote: “I do not know whether I have written anything better about the gospel than my commentary on Galatians.” For Luther, Galatians was the text that articulated what the Reformation was about: the righteousness of God is not a demanding standard to be met but a free gift to be received. Justification is by faith alone, in Christ alone, by grace alone. Anything added to that formula is a subtraction from it.

Read Galatians as the most passionate defense of free grace in the entire canon. Every person who has ever felt that their standing before God depends on their performance needs to hear it. Every church that has drifted toward moralism — toward making the Christian life about spiritual self-improvement rather than trust in the finished work of Christ — needs to be dragged back to Galatians and made to sit with it until the gospel is clear again. Paul wrote it because the gospel is always under threat, and the threat almost always comes from the same direction: the desire to add something to Christ, to make grace a little less free, to make human effort a little more decisive. Galatians says: no. The cross is enough. Christ is enough. Grace is enough. “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (6:14).

1.title: No Other Gospel: The Divine Origin of Paul’s Message
1.overview:
The letter begins with a defense of apostolic authority and immediately escalates to a declaration that would have shocked its first hearers: the gospel Paul preached is not of human origin, and anyone — even an angel from heaven — who preaches a different gospel is under divine curse. The word translated “accursed” is anathema — the strongest possible language of divine condemnation. Paul uses it twice in two verses (vv. 8–9), the repetition signaling that this is not rhetorical heat but deliberate, settled conviction.

The reason for the severity is simple: if the gospel can be modified by human authority — by apostles, by tradition, by ecclesiastical consensus — then it is not the gospel of God but the gospel of men. And the gospel of men, however sincerely presented, however religiously decorated, cannot save. Only the gospel that comes from God can bring a person into right standing with God. The divine origin of the gospel is therefore not an abstract theological claim; it is the practical ground of the gospel’s saving power.

Paul then makes his case autobiographically. He was not taught the gospel by the Jerusalem apostles; he received it directly from Jesus Christ, by revelation. The account of his conversion and his minimal contact with the Jerusalem church in the years that followed is not self-congratulation but an argument: his gospel is independently and divinely authenticated. It is the same gospel the Jerusalem apostles preach — but its authority does not rest on their endorsement. It rests on the revelation of Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul’s greeting is already an argument. In v. 1 the credentials arrive in the first breath — an apostle, not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father — because someone in Galatia had been describing him as a second-hand apostle who got his message from Jerusalem and edited it on the road. Two prepositions close both doors: no human being is the source of what he preaches, and no human being was even the delivery route. The clause he attaches to the Father, who raised him from the dead, is not decoration. The Twelve were commissioned by a Jesus they had walked beside; Paul was commissioned by a Jesus he had never met, and only the resurrection makes that a commissioning rather than a hallucination.

Verse 2 adds two things easily passed over. All the brothers who are with me — he is furious, and he is not freelancing; a room of Christian men send this letter with him. And to the churches of Galatia, his own congregations in the inland high country of Asia Minor, planted on his first journey through Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, in one of which he was stoned and left for dead. He greets them with nothing at all: no saints, no beloved, no thanksgiving. Just the address.

Then vv. 3–5 compress the whole gospel into a blessing. Grace and peace, in that order and never reversed — peace is not the price of admission but what grace leaves behind it. In v. 4 the pronoun is reflexive: Christ gave himself, not was given and not taken; nobody prised the Son out of the Father’s hand. He gave himself for our sins — not for our wounds or our unrealised potential, but for the thing actually wrong — to deliver us from the present evil age, where the verb is the word for snatching a man out of a burning building rather than renovating it. And it was according to the will of our God and Father: no reluctant Father talked round by a loving Son, but one will in heaven towards sinners.

Which is why v. 5 cannot stay in prose. The greeting breaks off into worship — to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen — before a line of the argument has been written.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace as Eternal Initiative, Not Emergency Repair

The christological formula of vv. 3–5 is among the earliest in the New Testament, and it grounds the Reformed conviction that salvation originates wholly in God. The Son’s self-giving is voluntary; its object is our sins; its effect is rescue out of an age, not improvement within it; and its source is the Father’s own will. Two errors are shut out at once. The first makes the cross a late correction to a plan that went wrong — but Christ gave himself according to the will of our God and Father, and Peter preaches the same thing at Pentecost, that he was delivered up by the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23).

The second sets a stern Father against a merciful Son, as though mercy had to be extracted from heaven by the death of Jesus. Verse 4 forbids it. The Father willed the giving; the Son gave himself; there is no division of sentiment in the Trinity toward sinners. Grace is not reactive. It is eternal initiative, and it terminates in glory to God (v. 5), which is where the letter will end up as well.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians had received a complete gospel and were being told it was a foundation needing a second storey. Paul’s opening answers that before it is raised: the apostleship is unmediated (v. 1), the senders are a company and not a maverick (v. 2), and the gospel summarised in vv. 3–5 has no vacancy in it for a human contribution — Christ gave himself, and the Father willed it.

Now: The same instinct survives wherever the gospel is treated as the entry requirement and something else as the real content of the Christian life — a sacramental record, a moral achievement, an intensity of spiritual experience. The test is simple and can be run on a bad week: if approaching God after a week of failure feels materially different from approaching him after a good one, something has already been added, whatever is said out loud. And the phrase the present evil age is not a phrase from a hymn. It is the age of the bad scan, the marriage that ends with lawyers, the news that is the same news every year with different names — and it is what Christ gave himself to pull people out of while they are still walking around inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead— and all the brothers who are with me, To the churches of Galatia:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul normally eases into a letter. He names himself, names his readers, and then spends a warm paragraph thanking God for them before a single argument begins. Not here. The credentials arrive in the first breath, jammed into the opening line between two dashes, and they are not modest.

An apostolos — the Greek word simply means one who is sent, an envoy carrying the authority of the person who sent him. A king’s messenger does not improve the message or soften it to suit the room he is standing in; he delivers it, and he answers to the throne, not to the audience. That is the office Paul is claiming in his first four words, and everything in the next six chapters depends on whether the claim is true.

Then two small prepositions doing very large work. Not from men: no human being is the source of what he preaches. Not through man: no human being was even the delivery route. Paul closes both doors at once, and he closes them before he has told us why they need closing. Somebody in Galatia had evidently been describing him as a second-hand apostle — a man who got his gospel from Jerusalem, went out with it on his own, and quietly dropped the awkward parts along the way. Paul does not argue with the description yet. He simply refuses it in his opening sentence.

And notice what he hangs on the Father: who raised him from the dead. It reads like a devotional flourish. It is load-bearing. The Twelve were commissioned by a Jesus they had walked beside for three years, eaten with, watched. Paul was commissioned on a road outside Damascus by a Jesus he had never met — and the only thing that makes that a commissioning rather than a hallucination is that the man is alive. Take the resurrection out of the sentence and Paul is a zealot with a story. Leave it in and he is precisely what he says he is. (cf. Acts 9:3–6; 1 Cor. 9:1)

And all the brothers who are with me. He is angry, and he is not alone. Whatever is about to be said in this letter, a room full of Christian men are saying it with him. This is not one man’s grievance dressed up as doctrine, and he wants that understood before the first blow lands.

To the churches of Galatia. Galatia was the inland high country of Asia Minor, in what is now central Turkey, and these were Paul’s own congregations — planted on his first missionary journey through towns like Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe (Acts 13–14). In one of them he had been stoned and dragged out of the city and left for dead. And here he greets them with nothing at all. No to the saints. No beloved. No my joy and my crown. Just the address, written the way you would write it on the outside of an envelope.

It is worth asking where a reader’s own confidence in the gospel actually rests. If it rests on the preacher who first explained it, or the church that raised him, or the tradition he has always trusted, then it can be revised by that preacher, that church, that tradition — and sooner or later it will be, because all three are made of people. Paul is about to insist that his message has a different pedigree, and therefore a different durability.

The letter has not yet made an argument. It has already told the reader what is at stake. Everything Paul is about to say about grace stands or falls on whether the man saying it was sent.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father, to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is still in the address, and he has already preached the gospel.

Grace to you and peace. A Greek letter opened with chairein, greetings; a Jew said shalom, peace. Paul takes the first word, bends it one letter into charis — grace, undeserved favour — and sets the Hebrew blessing beside it. Two worlds greeted each other every day with these words and meant almost nothing by them, the way we say “how are you” without waiting for the answer. Paul empties them and fills them again. And the order never reverses in his letters. Grace first, then peace. Peace is not the price of admission; it is what grace leaves behind it.

Who gave himself for our sins. The pronoun is reflexive and it is deliberate. Not who was given. Not who was taken. In the garden there were twelve legions of angels within reach and a Roman detachment that fell over backwards at his voice, and he handed himself across. Nobody prised the Son of God out of the Father’s hand. He walked forward. (cf. John 10:18)

For our sins — not for our disadvantages, our wounds, our unrealised potential. For the thing that is actually wrong. And the little word for here carries the whole weight of the cross: in our place, on our behalf, the innocent standing where the guilty should have stood.

To deliver us from the present evil age. The verb is exaireō, to snatch out — the word for a rescue party pulling a man out of a burning building, not a renovation crew improving the building. Jewish teaching divided all of history into two: this present age, and the age to come when God would put everything right. Paul does something startling with that map. He says the age to come has already broken in, and believers have already been hauled out of the old one — while still walking around inside it.

Which is worth making concrete, because “the present evil age” sounds like a phrase from a hymn. It is the age in which a scan comes back with bad news. In which a marriage that began with vows ends with lawyers. In which children are trafficked and old men die alone in wards and the news is the same news every year with different names. It is also the age in which the reader’s own heart quietly prefers itself to God on a Tuesday morning. That is what Christ gave himself to pull people out of.

According to the will of our God and Father. Paul will not let anyone think the cross was a rescue plan improvised late, or that a reluctant Father had to be talked round by a loving Son. The Son’s self-giving was the Father’s will. There is no kinder person in heaven than the Father; there never was.

And so the greeting cannot finish itself. It breaks off into worship: to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen. Paul has not written a line of his argument, and already he cannot get through his own opening without stopping to adore.

Consider what has just been said about the Son of God. He was not conscripted. He was not outmanoeuvred by Rome or by Judas or by the devil. He looked at an age that had produced Golgotha, and at people who had produced their own sins, and he gave himself — and the Father who sent him wanted it as much as he did. There is no reluctance anywhere in the Trinity towards sinners. The glory belongs to him for ever, and the church says Amen because there is nothing left to add.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Every other letter Paul wrote opens with thanksgiving. The Corinthians, who were tolerating incest and getting drunk at the Lord’s Table, still got one. Galatia gets v. 6: I am astonished. It is the loudest silence in the New Testament letters. The word could mean wonder at something glorious or bewilderment at something absurd, and it was also a standing formula of rebuke in ancient letters, so the readers heard both at once. Two details in the verse carry the weight. So quickly — not years; the ink was barely dry on their conversion. And deserting is the word for changing sides, a soldier crossing to the enemy lines. Most sobering of all, what they are deserting is not a doctrine but a person: him who called you in the grace of Christ. Nobody keeps the God of grace while leaving the gospel of grace behind; he does not come apart from his message.

Verse 7 names the thing precisely. They are turning to a different gospel — not that there is another one. Greek has two words where English has one: heteros, another of a different kind, and allos, another of the same kind. What Galatia is moving to is a heteron gospel, and there is no allo — it is not a second version of the good news, it is not good news, and there was only ever one. The men behind it are usually called Judaizers: Jewish Christians who believed in Jesus, honoured the Scriptures, and taught that Gentile converts must also take on circumcision, the food rules and the sacred calendar before counting as full members of God’s people. Not Christ instead of Moses — Christ plus Moses. And distort means to turn a thing inside out. Adding law to grace does not top grace up; it inverts it.

So vv. 8–9 reach for the strongest word available. Accursed is anathema, which in the Old Testament meant something placed under the ban and devoted to destruction. The two examples are chosen to be impossible: even if we — Paul first in the line of fire — or an angel from heaven. The gospel does not derive authority from its messenger; it stands over its messengers, Paul included.

Verse 8 might be dismissed as temper, so v. 9 repeats it in cold blood and drops the hypothetical: not even if but if anyone is preaching. Someone is. And the curse falls on the one preaching, not on the troubled congregation being taught — the same Paul calls these readers my little children at 4:19. Then v. 10 answers the charge that lay behind the accusation, that Paul had trimmed his message to fill his meetings: a man seeking human approval does not curse angels in paragraph three, and if pleasing people had been the aim, keeping circumcision was the obvious move (5:11). He is a doulos, a slave, and no one can be owned twice.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel Stands Over the Church That Preaches It

The double anathema of vv. 8–9 establishes something the Reformers staked their lives on: the gospel is not the church’s property, to be developed by councils or refined by consensus. A message that human authority conferred can be amended by human authority, and would be. Paul therefore submits himself and heaven’s own courier to the same test he asks the Galatians to apply, which is not the prestige of the teacher but conformity to what was first delivered. Luther read these two verses and recognised the whole controversy of his century in them.

It should be added, because Paul’s own practice requires it, that the curse is not aimed at every disagreement among Christians: he allows real latitude on food and days and disputable matters (Rom. 14). What cannot be renegotiated is the ground of acceptance with God. And the reason nobody may edit this gospel is that it was bought, not drafted — there was an anathema in this story before Paul used the word, and it fell on the Son, who became a curse for us (3:13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers were very probably sincere, and would have described themselves as the conservative party taking the Old Testament seriously. Circumcision was God’s own ordinance; the law was divinely given. They were not conscious apostates but well-meaning teachers who had inverted the relationship of law and grace — which is exactly why v. 10 matters, since sincerity was never the test.

Now: A different gospel rarely announces itself as one. It presents as the fuller, more serious, more culturally credible version. Two questions from this passage sort it out. Does this teaching change the ground on which a sinner is accepted by God, or only a secondary matter Christians have long disagreed about? And for a reader with a mother or a brother in such a church, the pastoral answer is in the grammar of vv. 8–9: the anathema falls on the one preaching, not on the sheep being misled. Verse 10 supplies the other half. The Galatians were not argued out of grace so much as flattered and shamed out of it, told by impressive men that they were second-class Christians. Bad theology usually travels on the back of a longing to be approved of, and the cure is not a tougher personality but a verdict already handed down in Christ, which demotes every other opinion to an opinion.

verseByVerse.quote: I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel— not that there is another one, but there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every other letter Paul wrote begins with thanksgiving. Every one. The Corinthians were tolerating a man sleeping with his father’s wife and getting drunk at the Lord’s Table, and they still got a thanksgiving. The Galatians get this.

It is the loudest silence in the New Testament letters, and the first readers would have heard it instantly — the way you hear it when someone who always greets you by name simply starts talking.

I am astonished. The Greek thaumazō can mean wonder at something glorious or bewilderment at something absurd; here it is plainly the second. It was also a standing formula in ancient letters of rebuke — I am astonished that you have not written — so the readers heard both the shock and the reprimand folded into one word.

So quickly. Not years. Paul had been there. He had preached, they had believed, the Spirit had come, and by the time the ink was dry on this letter they were most of the way to something else. The gospel’s hold on a human heart is more fragile than we like to assume, and a church can be evangelical on paper and past the point of no return in practice inside a year.

Deserting. The verb metatithēmi is the word for changing sides — a soldier crossing to the enemy lines, a man transferring his loyalty from one commander to another. It is not the language of a slightly mistaken opinion. It is the language of defection.

And here is the sentence that should stop the reader. They are not deserting a doctrine. They are deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ. A person. You cannot leave the gospel of grace behind and keep the God of grace; he does not come apart from his message. Every step away from grace is a step away from the One whose grace it is, however religious the walk looks from outside.

The people doing this were not pagans. They are usually called Judaizers, and since the word appears in almost every book about this letter it is worth saying plainly what it means. They were Jewish Christians who believed in Jesus, honoured the Scriptures, and taught that Gentiles who came to Christ must also take on the marks of the Jewish law — circumcision above all, along with the food rules and the sacred calendar — before they could be counted as full members of the people of God. Faith in Christ, and then also this. Not Christ instead of Moses. Christ plus Moses. They would have described themselves as the conservative party, the ones taking the Old Testament seriously.

And Paul’s verdict on Christ-plus-anything is in the next phrase, and it is surgical. They are turning to a different gospel — not that there is another one. Two Greek words sit behind that, and English blurs them. Heteros means another of a different kind; allos means another of the same kind. Paul says: you are turning to a heteron gospel — and there is no allo. Put plainly, what they are moving to is not a second version of the good news. It is not good news at all, and it is not a rival gospel, because there is only ever one.

Distort is metastrephō, to turn a thing inside out, to reverse it. That is the point a reader must not miss. Adding law-keeping to grace does not top grace up. It inverts it. The moment my acceptance depends even one per cent on my performance, the whole structure has flipped: God is no longer the one who justifies the ungodly but the one who audits the diligent, and I am back keeping score.

Here is a way to test where a heart has actually settled. After a week of failure — short temper, prayerlessness, the same sin again on Thursday — does approaching God feel different from how it felt after a good week? If it does, something has already been added to the gospel, whatever is said out loud. That is how quietly this happens, and it is why Paul is astonished rather than merely disappointed.

verseByVerse.quote: But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the most severe sentence Paul ever wrote, and he wrote it twice.

Accursed is anathema. In the Old Testament an anathema was something placed under the ban, devoted to God for destruction and not to be salvaged — Jericho and everything in it, Achan and the silver under his tent (Lev. 27:28–29; Josh. 7). To be anathema is to be handed over to the judgment of God. There is no stronger word available to him. He does not reach for it about immorality in Corinth or cowardice in Rome. He reaches for it here.

And look at the two examples he chooses, because they are chosen to be impossible. Even if we. Paul puts himself first in the line of fire. If the man who planted these churches came back through Galatia next spring with a revised message, the Galatians are to consign him to the judgment of God rather than believe him. Or an angel from heaven — not a demon disguised, but heaven’s own courier, glory and all. The gospel does not derive its authority from its messenger. It stands over its messengers, and Paul is one of them.

Then verse 9, and the tone changes. Verse 8 could be dismissed as temper — a man saying something enormous in the heat of the moment. So he says it again in cold blood: as we have said before, so now I say again. He had told them this face to face before the trouble started. He is not losing control. He is repeating a settled verdict, and the second time he drops the hypothetical altogether: not even if, but if anyone is preaching. Someone is.

Two questions come off this passage for anyone reading it honestly, and both deserve a straight answer.

The first: does this mean every doctrinal disagreement is a matter of damnation? It does not, and Paul’s own practice proves it. He allowed real latitude on food, on holy days, on matters where believers see differently (Rom. 14). What he anathematises is a gospel contrary to the one received — and the whole letter tells us exactly which question he means: on what ground is a sinner accepted by God? Church government, the details of the last days, the mode of baptism — Christians have argued these for centuries without either side being outside the faith. Change the ground of acceptance from Christ’s finished work to anything a person contributes, and the argument is no longer inside Christianity.

The second is the one that actually keeps people awake. A reader has a mother in a church that teaches something like this, or a brother who has gone somewhere that adds requirements to Christ. Is Paul saying she is accursed?

Read the sentence again and see who is in it. Let him be accursed — the one preaching. The anathema falls on the teacher, not on the troubled congregation being taught. And we know what Paul calls the Galatians themselves, because he tells us four chapters later: my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth (4:19). Those are not the words of a man consigning them to destruction. They are the words of a mother in labour. The severity is aimed at the wolves precisely because he loves the sheep, and a shepherd who shouts at a wolf is not shouting at the flock.

Which leaves one more thing to see, and it is the sweetest thing in the passage. Why is Paul willing to place himself and an angel of God under a curse to keep this message intact? Because of what it cost to obtain. There was already an anathema in this story before Paul ever used the word, and it did not fall on a false teacher. It fell on the Son. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (3:13). He stood where the ban falls, under the wrath that Jericho met and Achan met, and he did it to buy this gospel for sinners at the price of himself. That is why nobody may edit it. It is not Paul’s to amend. It was paid for.

verseByVerse.quote: For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The question is almost certainly a quotation of what his critics were saying about him.

The charge behind verse 10 seems to have been that Paul was a crowd-pleaser — a travelling preacher who had noticed that circumcision was a hard sell in a Gentile town and had quietly dropped it to fill his meetings. A gospel-lite salesman. Cut the difficult bits, keep the numbers up.

His answer is the passage they have just read. A man trying to please people does not pronounce a curse on angels in paragraph three. The approval of man — the verb peithō means to win someone over, to talk them round. Am I, he says, canvassing for human votes or for God’s?

And he has a second answer, which he gives later in the letter and which settles the matter completely: if I still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? (5:11). If pleasing people had been the aim, keeping circumcision was the obvious move. It would have delighted the synagogue, defused the opposition, and kept him out of prison. The man-pleasing option was the one he refused. His scars are the argument.

I would not be a servant of Christ. The word is doulos, slave — owned, not employed. And that is the logic, quietly devastating: a slave has one master. To need the approval of the room is to have taken a second owner, and no one can be owned twice.

Here is where this stops being about Paul. Take a moment and name the person whose disapproval would be hardest to bear — not hypothetically; the actual face that comes to mind. A father. A colleague at the desk opposite. A grown child. The people at church whose opinion somehow weighs more than the rest. Now ask what has already been softened, delayed or left unsaid to keep that face from changing.

Everyone has such a face, and the Judaizers had found the Galatians’. That is how this whole crisis worked. It was not really an argument about theology that a Gentile believer lost; it was the ache of being told, by impressive religious men from the mother church, that he was a second-class Christian — and the enormous relief on offer if he would just submit to the knife and be counted properly. Bad theology usually travels on the back of a longing to be approved of.

Which is why Paul’s freedom here is not toughness of personality. It is the arithmetic of grace, and the comfort is on the reverse side of the warning. A man whose acceptance is still being decided must manage everybody’s opinion of him, because any one of them might be the verdict. A man already accepted in Christ has had the verdict handed down in advance, in his favour, at the cost of the cross — and every other opinion in the world has been demoted to an opinion.

The tyranny of what people think does not end when a person finally wins their approval. It ends when their approval stops being the court. (cf. 1 Cor. 4:3–4; Prov. 29:25)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now argues from his own biography, and the argument is chronological. In vv. 11–12 he states the thesis: the gospel he preached is not man’s gospel; he did not receive it from any man, nor was he taught it. Those two verbs are the exact vocabulary of rabbinic transmission, the machinery that had made him a Pharisee, and he is saying it had nothing to do with this. (When he tells Corinth that he received and delivered the resurrection facts, there is no contradiction: the facts came from the church, the meaning and the commission came by revelation of Jesus Christ.)

Then the evidence. Verses 13–14 are his own record of shame produced as an exhibit: he persecuted the church beyond measure and tried to destroy it, the verb an army uses of a city it means to leave uninhabitable — and he was advancing beyond his peers, the outstanding student of his generation, winning at the system he was in. Nobody defects from the top of a religion he is succeeding at into a message that gets him flogged. In vv. 15–16 the sentence turns and every verb becomes God’s: set me apart before I was born (before there was a person there to be good or bad), called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son — God’s delight, not his duty — and the commission to the Gentiles arrives in the same breath as the conversion.

The rest is a chronology of distance. Verse 17 has him going not to Jerusalem but to Arabia, the Nabatean kingdom, where he was evidently preaching hard enough to make an enemy of a king (2 Cor. 11:32–33). Verses 18–19 give the numbers that carry the argument: after three years, fifteen days, two men — and the verb translated visit means to get to know someone, not to be trained or certified by them.

Verse 20 breaks off into an oath, which tells us Paul was not merely disagreed with but called a liar. Verses 21–22 put him in Syria and Cilicia — home to Tarsus, and something near a decade with nothing recorded — still unknown in person, literally unknown by face, to the very Judean churches he had once hunted. And vv. 23–24 close with the one sentence those churches kept repeating: he who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy. Their response was not to check his credentials. They glorified God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, Effectual Calling, and Revelation: the Grammar of Grace

Verses 15–16 are among the most compact statements of sovereign grace in Paul. Three divine acts stand in order, and Paul initiates none of them: God set him apart before birth, called him by grace, and was pleased to reveal his Son in him. The setting apart echoes Jeremiah called before the womb and the Servant of Isaiah 49; there may also be a deliberate play on words, since aphorizō, to set apart, sounds against the name Pharisee, most likely from a root meaning the separated ones.

Paul had separated himself by rigorous effort and it made him dangerous; God had set him apart before he separated himself from anything, and set him apart for the Gentiles. The calling is effectual, not an invitation awaiting a reply — the last thing Saul intended on that road was conversion. And the revelation is in me, internal as well as external: he had known the facts about Jesus for years and hated them. Grace that reaches a man riding in the opposite direction with warrants in his bag is not a reward for seeking. (cf. Rom. 8:29–30; Eph. 1:4–5)
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul’s critics could point to his absence from Jesus’ earthly ministry and his late arrival among the apostles. His reply is the chronology of vv. 17–22: he went to Arabia rather than Jerusalem, waited three years, stayed a fortnight, met two men, then vanished into Cilicia for years, and the Judean churches would not have recognised him in the street. If his gospel came from that world, its members would at least have known his face.

Now: Three things in this section reach an ordinary reader directly. A history that feels disqualifying (vv. 13–14) is not erased in Paul but made into evidence — the worse the record, the better it proves the message did not come from him, which is just what he says at 1 Timothy 1:15–16. A believer anxious about whether he chose God or God chose him can settle it from v. 15 with a simpler question than the usual one: on the day it happened, was I looking for him?

And the hidden years of vv. 17 and 21–22 speak to anyone whose life feels like a waiting room — the gifts there and nothing asked of them, a decade gone with nothing to show. Moses had forty years in Midian, David was anointed and then hunted through caves, and the Son of God spent thirty years in a workshop and three in public. Most believers are unknown by face to almost everybody. Nobody has yet been forgotten in a waiting room.

verseByVerse.quote: For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man’s gospel. For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I would have you know is a formula — gnōrizō, I make it known to you — the phrase a writer uses to flag the thing he most wants remembered. And he calls them brothers. He has just spoken of angels under a curse, and the next word out of his mouth is a family word. He is fighting for them, not with them.

The claim itself is in three parts, and each closes a door.

Not man’s gospel — kata anthrōpon, literally not according to man: not measured by a human standard, not shaped to a human taste, not invented by a human mind. I did not receive it from any man — nobody handed it on to him. Nor was I taught it — he did not sit under anybody to learn it.

Those last two verbs are worth pausing on, because they are the exact vocabulary of the world Paul came from. Receiving and being taught were how a rabbi was made: tradition passed down hand to hand, master to pupil, Hillel to Gamaliel to Saul of Tarsus, every link named and verifiable. It was the most respectable pedigree a Jewish teacher could have, and Paul had it. He is saying that the machinery which made him a Pharisee had nothing whatever to do with this.

A careful reader will feel a problem here, and should. Writing to Corinth, Paul says the opposite in almost the same words: I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received — that Christ died, was buried, was raised, appeared (1 Cor. 15:3–4). Received from whom? Plainly from the church before him. So which is it?

Both, and they are not in conflict. What Paul received from others were the facts on the ground — the dates, the burial, the names of the witnesses, the sort of thing anyone in Jerusalem could have told him and which he certainly heard from Peter over those fifteen days. What no one gave him was the meaning of those facts and his commission to carry them. He knew perfectly well before Damascus that a man called Jesus had been crucified; he was persecuting people over it. What he did not have, and could not be taught, was that this crucified man is the Son of God, that his death is the end of the law as a way of acceptance, and that Paul himself was to take that news to the nations. That came the way he says it came.

Through a revelation of Jesus Christ. The Greek phrase can mean a revelation about Jesus or a revelation from Jesus, and Paul most likely intends both at once, because on the Damascus road they were the same event: the risen Christ pulled back the curtain and what was behind it was himself.

Which is the point that outlasts the argument about apostleship. A gospel that comes from human consensus can be amended by human consensus — and a committee that had the authority to adopt it has the authority to update it next century. A gospel that comes from the revelation of Jesus Christ cannot be amended by anyone, because nobody in the discussion outranks him. That is not a limitation on the church. It is the church’s security, and it is the reason a believer in Galatia in the first century and a believer reading this on a Monday in the twenty-first are standing on exactly the same ground. (cf. 2 Tim. 3:16; 2 Pet. 1:20–21)

verseByVerse.quote: For you have heard of my former life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it. And I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people, so extremely zealous was I for the traditions of my fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now produces his own past as evidence, and it is not the sort of evidence a man volunteers unless he has a reason.

You have heard of my former life in Judaism. They had. It was the first thing anyone in the Mediterranean world knew about him — the way certain names still arrive in a room before the person does.

He gives three details, and each is worse than the last. I persecuted the church of God violently. The phrase behind “violently” is kath’ hyperbolēn — our word hyperbole — and it means beyond all measure, past the point where anyone was keeping count. And tried to destroy it. The verb portheō is what an army does to a city it intends to leave uninhabitable. Not to intimidate the church. To finish it.

Luke supplies the pictures Paul is too brief to give. Saul going house to house, dragging off men and women and committing them to prison — the detail about women is not decoration, it tells you the thing had stopped having limits (Acts 8:3). Saul casting his vote for the death penalty. Saul going from synagogue to synagogue trying to force believers to blaspheme, and following them to foreign cities because Jerusalem was not enough — “in raging fury against them,” as he put it himself to Agrippa (Acts 26:10–11). There were widows in Judea when Paul wrote this letter who were widows because of him.

And the third detail is the one that makes the argument. I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age. The verb prokoptō means to cut a path forward, to hack through undergrowth — a pioneer’s word. He was not a failing religious man looking for something gentler. He was winning. He was the outstanding student of his generation, on the fastest track in Israel, so extremely zealous for the traditions of my fathers, and by every standard he recognised he was succeeding.

Which is exactly why he brings it up. The suggestion in Galatia was that Paul’s gospel was a softened Judaism — the religion trimmed down for people who could not manage the whole thing. His answer: look at who I was. Nobody drifts from the top of a system he is winning at, into a message that got him flogged, because he wanted an easier life. A man like that does not change his mind. Something has to happen to him.

There is a second thing in these two verses, and for some readers it is the only thing in the chapter that matters. Paul is not confessing here; he is citing. He puts the worst of his life on the table as an exhibit, calmly, in a letter he expects to be read aloud in the churches of four towns.

Some reader carries a history he has never said out loud — something done at twenty-two, something a family still lives with, something that surfaces at three in the morning and argues that whatever else grace is for, it is not for that. Notice what has happened to Paul’s history. It has not been erased, denied, or explained away; he names it in plain words and calls himself the man who did it. It has been made into evidence for the gospel. The worse the record, the better it proves the point he is making, which is that this message did not come from him.

He said the same thing later, and more simply, so that nobody could miss it: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost. But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him (1 Tim. 1:15–16). Foremost. Not a qualifier — a demonstration. The chief of sinners was kept alive on that road and made an apostle so that no one afterwards could ever say his own case was too far gone.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son to me, in order that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately consult with anyone;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sentence has been building since verse 13, and now it turns. Everything before this was Paul acting. Everything from here is God acting, and there are four verbs, and not one of them belongs to Paul.

He who had set me apart before I was born. Before. Before the zeal, before the persecution, before the promising young man in Gamaliel’s classroom, before there was a person there at all to be either good or bad. The language deliberately echoes the prophets: before I formed you in the womb I knew you (Jer. 1:5), and the Servant of Isaiah 49 who was called from his mother’s womb.

There may be a quiet play on words here that the first readers would have caught. The Greek is aphorizō, to set apart or separate — and the word Pharisee most likely comes from a root meaning the separated ones. Paul had spent his adult life separating himself: from Gentiles, from the unclean, from the careless, by rigorous effort, and it had made him the most dangerous man the church knew. God’s reply is that he had been set apart before he separated himself from anything at all — and set apart, of all things, to go to the Gentiles.

And who called me by his grace. Not who called me because of my zeal, or in spite of my record, or on account of anything visible at the time. By his grace: the call had no cause outside God. And this is a call that does what it says. God’s call in Paul’s letters is not an invitation left on the table awaiting a reply; it is the summons that raises the dead man who is being summoned. The last thing Saul intended, riding to Damascus with warrants in his bag, was to become a Christian.

Was pleased to reveal his Son to me.Eudokeō — it was God’s good pleasure, his delight. Not a duty discharged. Not a reluctant salvage of a wasted life. The Father took pleasure in showing this man his Son. Read that with Acts 9 in view: at the moment Paul is described as still breathing threats and murder, God is described as glad.

And the phrase is more intimate than most translations can carry: literally, to reveal his Son in me. Not merely a bright light on a road, an external event Paul witnessed and later reported. Something opened on the inside. He had known the facts about Jesus for years and hated them. Now the Son himself was unveiled within him, and everything he already knew rearranged itself around a living person.

In order that I might preach him among the Gentiles. The commission arrives in the same breath as the conversion. There is no gap, no probationary period, no question of what this is for. He was not saved and then, later, given something to do. He was set apart for it before he was born.

A believer troubled about whether he chose God or God chose him can settle it here without a word of philosophy. Ask a simpler question than the usual one: on the day it happened, was I looking for him? Paul was not merely uninterested; he was riding in the opposite direction with legal authority to arrest the people who loved the name. If grace reached him there, then grace is not a reward handed to the seekers, and no one need audit the sincerity of his own first steps to find out whether he is safe. The question is not who moved first. The answer to that is already in the verse. (cf. Rom. 8:29–30; Eph. 1:4–5; John 15:16)

And that is the thing to stand still in front of. Before the world had a Saul in it to hate the church, the Son of God had already been appointed to be revealed to him. The Father set him apart, and called him, and was pleased — delighted — to unveil his Son to a man on his way to do harm in the name of religion. Heaven was not scandalised by Saul of Tarsus. Heaven had made arrangements for him before his mother knew she was carrying him. This is what the grace of God is like, and it has never once been embarrassed by the material it was given to work with.

verseByVerse.quote: nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The argument is negative and it is precise: nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me. That is the accusation, answered. If his gospel had come from the Twelve, this is where he would have gone, immediately. Newly converted, freshly commissioned, with no Christian instruction behind him and a lifetime of persecution to explain — every instinct says go to headquarters. He did not. He went the other way.

But I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus.

Arabia here is not an empty desert of sand dunes, whatever the paintings suggest. It means the Nabatean kingdom, south and east of Damascus — a real state with towns, trade routes and a capital at Petra, ruled by King Aretas. And Paul lets slip elsewhere what he was doing there: the governor under Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize him, and he escaped over the wall in a basket (2 Cor. 11:32–33). Kings do not post guards for men who have been quietly meditating. He had been preaching, and he had been at it long enough to have made an enemy of a monarch.

Then the number, dropped in the next verse and covering all of this: after three years. Three years between the road to Damascus and the first conversation with Peter. Three years in which the most gifted man of his generation, freshly given the greatest news in the world and a commission to the nations, is somewhere off the map with nothing recorded about him at all.

Scripture does not say what happened in those years, and it is better to admit that than to fill it in. What is certain is that the Paul who wrote Romans did not have Romans in his head on the Damascus road. Somewhere between the light and the letters, the whole of the Old Testament was rebuilt around Christ in that mind — and the only teacher named anywhere in the account is the Lord himself.

This is where the chapter unexpectedly meets a reader who is not interested in first-century apostleship at all.

There are believers whose lives feel like a waiting room. The gifts are there and nothing is being asked of them. The training was done and the door never opened. Illness took the decade that was supposed to count. Someone is at fifty and cannot see what the twenty years since conversion were actually for, and the suspicion underneath is that God has mislaid him, or that the useful part of his life was somehow spent while he was looking the other way.

The pattern in Scripture runs so consistently the other way that it is almost the rule. Moses had forty years in Midian minding another man’s sheep after Egypt and before the burning bush. David was anointed king as a boy and spent the following years hunted through caves. Joseph went from the dream to the throne by way of a pit, a false accusation and a forgotten promise in a prison. And the Son of God himself spent thirty years in a workshop in a town of no consequence, and three in public.

Which suggests the hidden years are not the delay before the work. They are part of it, and generally the part that makes the rest possible. The apostle who could write I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content did not learn it in Arabia by accident.

Nobody has yet been forgotten in a waiting room. The God who set Paul apart before he was born was not less involved in the three silent years than in the light on the road; he was simply not narrating them. Much of what God does in a life is done without commentary, and it is finished long before anyone notices it has begun.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and remained with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three years. Fifteen days. Two men. Paul is counting, and every number in the sentence is doing work.

He does eventually go to Jerusalem — his case would collapse if he pretended otherwise, and he is not pretending. He is dating it. Three years after his conversion, not three weeks. And when he arrives, he sees two people.

The purpose is exact. The verb translated to visit is historeō, a rare word that Paul uses nowhere else. It means to go and see a person in order to get to know them — to make the acquaintance of someone worth meeting, to enquire. It does not mean to be examined, to be trained, or to be commissioned. He went to meet Peter, not to be certified by him.

(Paul calls him Cephas here and throughout the letter: it is simply Peter’s name in Aramaic, the everyday language he and Paul spoke. Both words mean “rock” — the name Jesus himself gave him, John 1:42.)

And fifteen days. It is a strange detail to include unless the length is the argument, which it is. Fifteen days is long enough for two men to talk themselves hoarse. It is nothing like long enough to train an apostle, and everyone in the ancient world knew what a rabbinic apprenticeship looked like: years, not a fortnight.

Still, one would like to have been in that house. Peter had denied the Lord three times over a charcoal fire and been restored over another one. Paul had hunted down the people Peter was pastoring. Neither man had a past he could be proud of, and both had been handled by the same mercy. Whatever else those fifteen days contained, they contained the eyewitness accounts — Peter describing what it was like in the boat, in the courtyard, on the shore — and a man who had never seen any of it listening to every word.

But I saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother. This is Jesus’ own brother, raised in the same house in Nazareth — and during the ministry he did not believe (John 7:5). Then his brother was killed, and then, we are told in a single line, he appeared to James (1 Cor. 15:7). Whatever passed between them, that meeting turned an unbelieving brother into the leader of the Jerusalem church and the author of a letter that calls him the Lord Jesus Christ. It takes something considerable to make a man worship the boy he grew up beside.

One honest difficulty should be faced here rather than stepped over. Luke’s account of the same visit says Barnabas brought him to the apostles — plural — and that Paul was going in and out among them at Jerusalem (Acts 9:27–28). Paul says he saw none of them except James. Is one of them wrong?

No, and the resolution is in ordinary speech rather than in special pleading. Luke is summarising a visit in two verses and uses “the apostles” the way anyone uses a collective term — Peter and James being, between them, the two most prominent figures of that circle and its recognised leadership. We do the same thing constantly: a man who met the Prime Minister and the Chancellor says he met the government. Paul, whose whole argument depends on the precise number, gives the precise number, because for him the point is that the list is short. The accounts are answering different questions, and both answers are true.

Which is where the argument lands. Fifteen days with Peter, one meeting with James, and then he was gone. If the Galatians want to believe that Paul’s gospel was issued to him in Jerusalem, they must believe it was issued in a fortnight, three years too late, by two men who never afterwards claimed to have given it to him.

verseByVerse.quote: (In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul stops the narrative, turns to the reader, and swears an oath.

It is startling, and it is meant to be. He is halfway through a plain account of his own movements — dates, places, names — and he breaks off to call God as his witness that he is not making it up. Nobody does that unless something is at stake.

What that tells us is worth sitting with, because it is easy to read this letter as though Paul were merely arguing with people who had different opinions. He was not. He was being called a liar. A rival account of his life was circulating in the Galatian churches, and it had enough detail and enough plausibility that a straightforward denial would not do. Somebody had told these congregations a different story about where their founder got his message, and the story was sticking.

There is a fair question here for any reader who knows the Gospels, and it deserves an answer rather than a shrug. Did the Lord not say do not take an oath at all, and let your yes be yes (Matt. 5:34–37)? Does James not repeat it (Jas. 5:12)? And here is an apostle swearing in writing.

Look at what Jesus was actually forbidding. The system in view was one where oaths had become a sliding scale of honesty — swear by the temple and you may wriggle out; swear by the gold of the temple and you are held to it (Matt. 23:16–22). The whole apparatus existed so that a man could indicate how much of what he was saying he intended to stand behind, which meant that his ordinary word was worth nothing. Christ abolishes the scale. A disciple’s plain yes is to carry the full weight of an oath, always.

That is not what Paul is doing. He is not grading his own truthfulness; he is under formal accusation, testifying to the truth of a matter on which men’s souls depend. Scripture is not embarrassed by that kind of solemn witness — the same Paul does it more than once (Rom. 1:9; 2 Cor. 1:23), and God himself, having no one greater to swear by, swore by himself to guarantee a promise (Heb. 6:13–17). The Lord who said let your yes be yes was himself put under oath at his trial and answered (Matt. 26:63–64).

And notice what Paul does not do with the parenthesis. He does not defend his character. There is no wounded paragraph about years of service, no list of what these churches owe him, no appeal to how hard he has worked. He swears to one thing only: the facts of where the gospel came from.

That restraint is the tell. A man defending his reputation protects his reputation. Paul lets his name take whatever damage it takes and puts the oath where the danger actually is, because he is not the thing under threat. If the Galatians conclude that Paul is unimpressive, nobody is lost. If they conclude that the gospel is a human product, everything is.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chronology continues, and the point continues to be the distance.

Syria and Cilicia — the region north and west, and Cilicia is where Tarsus is, which is to say Paul went home. Luke fills in why: the Greek-speaking Jews in Jerusalem were trying to kill him, so the brothers took him down to Caesarea and put him on a ship to Tarsus (Acts 9:29–30). And then Luke leaves him there, and the book of Acts simply carries on without him — until Barnabas, some years later, has an idea and goes to Tarsus to look for him (Acts 11:25).

Add up the years between and it is somewhere near a decade. A decade with no recorded sermon, no named convert, no letter, no church planted that we know the name of. Whatever Paul was doing in Cilicia, the New Testament does not consider it worth reporting, which is a striking thing to be true of the man who wrote a quarter of it.

And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ. Literally, unknown by face. The churches in Judea, the very congregations he had once hunted through, would not have recognised him if he had walked past them in the street.

That is the argument, and it is now airtight. These are the churches closest to Jerusalem, most saturated with apostolic teaching, most likely to have shaped a young convert’s theology. If Paul’s gospel had been absorbed from that world, its members would at least have known what he looked like. They did not. He was, to them, a name in a story.

There is something quietly steadying in that phrase for anyone whose Christian life has no audience. Most believers are unknown by face to almost everybody. The work is done in a house where nobody is watching, in a job nobody would write about, among two or three people who will never be famous either. The years in Cilicia produced no headline, and they produced the apostle to the Gentiles.

And a second thing, gentler. Paul is not simply hidden here; he is hidden from the people he had wronged. He had made those Judean churches widows and orphans, and now they were praying for a man they would not have recognised. There is a kind of restoration that God does at a distance, where the people harmed are not asked to manage the person who harmed them, and both sides are carried by the same grace without ever meeting.

verseByVerse.quote: They only were hearing it said, “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” And they glorified God because of me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul had not seen these churches. But something had reached them, and Paul preserves it — the actual sentence they kept repeating about him.

They only were hearing it said — the tense is continuous, the report going round and round the villages of Judea, told again at every gathering the way a church tells the story it cannot get over.

And here is the sentence: He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.

Notice us. This is not a report about a distant public figure. It is being passed between the very people he hunted — families who had lost someone, congregations that had scattered, men and women who had been dragged out of their homes by the man now being described. The word for “the faith” here means the body of truth Christians believe, the thing itself; he is not merely being polite about religion in general. The man who set out to make sure this message did not survive is now the one carrying it across the empire.

It is one line long, and it is the whole gospel. There is a before and an after, the change is total, the person did not manage it himself, and the evidence is not what he says about himself but what he is now doing with his life.

Then the last verse of the chapter, and it lands somewhere nobody would have predicted. And they glorified God because of me.

Not: and they were reassured about my credentials. Not: and they admired my transformation. The literal phrase is that they glorified God in me — they looked at what had become of Saul of Tarsus and they worshipped. He was, to them, a piece of evidence about God, and the evidence made them praise.

Which is the answer to the whole chapter, and it arrives without Paul having to say it. He has spent twenty-four verses arguing that his gospel did not come from men. The Judean churches settled the question years earlier, on the strength of one report, and they did not settle it by weighing his credentials. They looked at the impossibility of what had happened and knew whose work it was. No committee produces a man like that.

So consider how the chapter ends, and who it ends with. It opened with a curse pronounced on angels and closes with worship rising from villages that had buried their dead because of the man being spoken of. The persecutor is preaching. The widows he made are glorifying God. The church he meant to leave uninhabitable is on its knees giving thanks for him. This is what the risen Christ does with his enemies when he means to have them — he does not merely stop them; he turns them into the reason his people worship. And the last word of the chapter is glory, and it is not Paul’s.
