The proof is Deuteronomy 27:26, the last of the twelve curses Israel answered with its own Amen. Four words carry it: everyone, all things, abide by, and do them. The law is not a pass mark; it is a seamless garment, and it cannot be scored out of a hundred.

Verse 11 states the conclusion as something already plain — no one is justified before God by the law — and grounds it in Habakkuk 2:4, the verse that broke the medieval church open. Verse 12 sets the opposing principle beside it from Leviticus 18:5: the one who does them shall live by them. A thoughtful reader feels the difficulty, since Leviticus is God’s word too. The answer is that the law’s offer was never a bluff; the fault lies not in the law but in the material it works with.

Then v. 13, the summit of the chapter. Christ redeemed us — bought us out of the slave market — from the law’s curse by becoming a curse himself, and the text quoted is Deuteronomy 21:23, the very verse that made a crucified Messiah unthinkable to Saul the Pharisee. Verse 14 gives the purpose twice: so that the blessing of Abraham might reach the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, and so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith — which closes the circle opened by the question in v. 2.
verseByVerse.theology:
Penal Substitution: The Curse Exchanged

That Christ bore the penalty due to sinners in their place, exhausting the law’s sentence, is not a later development of doctrine but the explicit content of v. 13. The exchange is legally precise. The curse of vv. 10–12 fell on him, so that the blessing of v. 14 could fall on those who have no claim to it. This is not sympathetic solidarity — he suffered with us — but substitution: he suffered instead of us, bearing what was ours.

Two guards belong here. First, becoming a curse does not mean the Father ceased to love the Son or turned on him in temper; Jesus said the opposite (John 10:17). The sentence was real and the Father’s delight in the obedient Son was real at the same hour. Second, the Deuteronomy text is about the public display of an already-condemned man, so the tree did not make him cursed — it published the verdict. Saul had read that publication correctly and been wrong about only one thing: whose curse it was.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers offered the law as a supplement, a way of securing what faith had begun. Verses 10–12 show that the law has no supplementary setting. It accepts one condition only, and no one has ever met it, so those who take their stand there have entered a system whose only two verdicts are flawless obedience and curse. Verse 13 names the single exit, and vv. 13–14 together explain how a Gentile with no covenant and no ancestry ends up holding the Spirit of God.

Now: Some readers come to v. 10 with their stomach already tight, half expecting confirmation that God is disappointed with them. Read it exactly. Paul does not say that people who sin are cursed; he says that people who rely on law-keeping are, because they have chosen a standard that will convict them. The curse is aimed not at your failure but at the thing you were using to cover it. And v. 13 says what became of it: the sentence was carried out, and not on you. Verse 14 adds that the Spirit you already have is the receipt.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has proved his case from Abraham. Now he turns and proves it from the law itself — and the argument is devastating, because he lets the law do the talking.

All who rely on works of the law are under a curse. Read that slowly, because it is not what anyone expects. He does not say that those who break the law are under a curse. He says that those who rely on it are — the serious ones, the observant ones, the men who get up early to keep it. The very people who thought the law was their shelter are told they are standing under the one thing it actually guarantees.

And then the proof, quoted from the law’s own closing ceremony. In Deuteronomy 27, Israel is drawn up in two halves on two mountains, Ebal and Gerizim, with the covenant read aloud between them, and the last of twelve curses is the one Paul takes: Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them (Deut. 27:26). At the end of every curse the whole nation answered Amen. They said it. Out loud. They ratified the terms themselves.

Now weigh the four words Paul leans on. Everyone — no exemptions, no distinguished-service discount. All things — the whole code, not a representative selection. Abide by — continuously, not in a good season. And do them — performance, not agreement; you can admire a command all your life without once obeying it.

Put those together and the law turns out not to be a pass mark but a seamless garment. It cannot be scored out of a hundred. James says the same thing from the other end: whoever keeps the whole law and fails at one point has become guilty of all of it (Jas. 2:10). That sounds harsh until you see why it is true. The law is not a list of separate regulations; it is the expression of one Person’s will. To break any of it is to have said no to him, and you do not need to say no on every subject to have said no.

So the choice Paul lays out is not between an easier and a harder road to God. It is between a road and a cliff. Anyone who takes his stand on law-keeping has entered a system in which the only two possible verdicts are flawless obedience and curse — and he has already failed, and he knows it, which is why the religion of the law-keeper is so often anxious under its composure.

This is where a certain kind of reader needs to be met honestly, because he is reading with his stomach tight. He is not a Judaizer. He has simply never been able to shake the sense that God is disappointed with him, and this verse looks like proof. If you are that reader, notice exactly what Paul says and what he does not. He does not say that people who sin are cursed; if he did, there would be no hope for anyone in this letter or out of it. He says that people who rely on law-keeping are cursed, because they have chosen a standard that will certainly convict them. The curse is not aimed at your failure. It is aimed at the thing you were trying to use to cover your failure. And in three verses he will tell you what happened to it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.” But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two verses, two quotations from the Old Testament, and between them Paul settles the question of how anyone has ever been right with God.

First: it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law.Evident — dēlon, plain, obvious, in view. He is not about to prove something contested; he is pointing at something already established. And the proof is Habakkuk 2:4: The righteous shall live by faith.

Habakkuk had been watching the Babylonians come, and he could not square the horizon with the character of God. The answer he was given was not an explanation but a way to survive: the righteous man will live — keep breathing, keep standing, keep his footing when everything visible is against him — by faith. Paul takes that sentence as the shape of the whole Christian life, and Luther took it from Paul, and it broke the medieval church open. This is the verse that made the Reformation.

Then verse 12, and the contrast: the law is not of faith, rather ‘The one who does them shall live by them.’ That quotation is Leviticus 18:5, and here a thoughtful reader hits a genuine difficulty which the commentary should not skate over. If Leviticus 18:5 is God’s own word, how can Paul use it as the losing side of an argument? Is God quoted here against himself?

No — and the resolution matters. Leviticus 18:5 states the law’s operating principle truthfully. The law really does promise life to whoever keeps it. That offer was never a bluff, and there is nothing defective about the law: it is holy, righteous and good (Rom. 7:12). The defect is in the material it has to work with. As Paul puts it elsewhere, the law was weakened by the flesh (Rom. 8:3) — like a perfectly sound contract offered to a bankrupt. The terms are excellent. He cannot meet them.

So the two verses are not two rival ways to God, one strict and one generous. They are two different kinds of sentence. Do these things and live puts the weight on the doer. The righteous shall live by faith puts the weight on the one believed. And that is why they cannot be blended, however reasonable a blend sounds. Faith and works are not two ingredients that improve each other; they are two answers to the question who is responsible for my standing before God, and the second answer cancels the first.

And there is one more thing to say, because it turns a hard verse into good news. Leviticus 18:5 was never revoked. Someone had to do the things and live by them — and someone did. There has been exactly one man on this earth who could stand under the law’s own terms and claim its promise honestly. He kept all things written in the Book of the Law and did them. He earned the life. And then, having earned it, he went to a place where the law had nothing but a curse to give, and he took the curse instead, and left the life to us. That is the next verse, and it is the summit of the chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. If you had to choose one sentence in the New Testament to carry the whole doctrine of the atonement, this would be a strong candidate. Everything in the chapter has been climbing to it, and every word in it is load-bearing.

Redeemed is exēgorasen, a word from the slave market: to buy out, to purchase and remove. It assumes a real transaction with a real price paid to secure a real release. Nobody in a first-century town heard that word as a metaphor. They had watched it happen in the square.

And what were we bought out from? Not from the law — from the curse of the law, which is verse 10 come home. The sentence that stood over every human being who had ever taken his stand on his own obedience has been executed, and not on him.

Then the mechanism, and it is deliberately shocking: by becoming a curse for us. Not by pitying us, not by identifying with us, not by showing us how much God cares. He became the thing itself. And the proof text is one that no Jew could hear without flinching: Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Deut. 21:23).

That law is worth understanding precisely. In Deuteronomy 21 hanging is not the method of execution. A man convicted of a capital crime is put to death, and then his body is hung on a tree as a public sign of what he was — and it must be taken down by nightfall, because a hanged man is cursed by God and the land must not be defiled. The tree did not make him cursed. The tree announced it, so that everyone walking past the field could read the verdict of heaven on that man without being told.

Now put Saul of Tarsus in front of a crucifix. For a Pharisee, this text was not a difficulty about Jesus of Nazareth — it was the closing argument. Whatever that man had said, whatever the fishermen were now claiming, God had published his verdict on a beam outside the city wall for the whole province to read. A crucified Messiah was not merely improbable. It was blasphemy with a scriptural footnote.

Which is what makes this verse, written by that man, one of the great turnings in Scripture. On the Damascus road the argument did not go away; it went inside out. Saul had been right that the tree published a curse. He had been wrong about only one thing: whose. For us. The two smallest words in the sentence, and they are the whole gospel. He was cursed, and not for anything he had done.

Guard one thing here, because tender consciences trip on it. To say Christ became a curse is not to say the Father stopped loving the Son, or was privately disgusted with him, or turned on him in temper. Jesus himself said the opposite: For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life (John 10:17). The Son was never more precious to the Father than in the hour he was bearing our sentence, and the sentence was real, and both of those are true at once.

Stand back and look at the exchange. The law had one thing to say to every human being who came to it for a verdict, and it said it without pity, and it was right to say it. And the Son of God walked into the courtroom, took the sentence out of the judge’s mouth before it reached us, and carried it out of the city on his own back. The tree that was designed to publish the curse of God has become the place where the curse of God ran out. There is nothing in the universe like this. Every other religion tells a man what he must do; here is a God who went to the gallows in his place and did it himself. (cf. 2 Cor. 5:21; 1 Pet. 2:24)

verseByVerse.quote: so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the purpose clause, and Paul gives it twice: so that… so that… The cross was not simply a rescue from something; it was a rescue for something, and he names two results, both of which the Judaizers had been quietly denying.

First: so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles. Trace that line back and it goes to Genesis 12 — in you shall all the families of the earth be blessed — and it has been travelling for two thousand years, through Isaac and Jacob and a nation and a monarchy and an exile, and here it arrives, in a Galatian town, in the hands of people whose grandparents worshipped Zeus. That is what the cross did. It opened a promise made in Mesopotamia to the whole world.

And observe how it arrives: in Christ Jesus. Not around him, not because God relaxed the terms, not by God deciding after all these years that circumcision did not matter much. The blessing reaches the nations by way of one man’s cross. The Judaizers wanted Gentiles brought in through the door marked become a Jew; God brought them in through a door marked be in Christ, and it is the only door there has ever been.

Second: so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith. And with that Paul has closed the circle he opened in verse 2. He began the chapter by asking how they got the Spirit. He now says the cross is why they got him. Between the question and the answer he has laid out Abraham, the curse, and the exchange — and the whole argument lands back on the Spirit they already have.

It is worth pausing on the phrase the promised Spirit, because it tells the reader what he is holding. The Spirit is not a bonus for advanced believers or a second stage for the especially earnest. He is the promise — the thing God swore to Abraham, working out in the end as God himself coming to live in Gentile bodies. When Ezekiel said God would put his Spirit within his people and cause them to walk in his statutes (Ezek. 36:27), and Joel said he would pour him out on all flesh, this was the payment they were describing. The Galatians had it. They were being told they lacked something.

Which is where the verse presses on the reader. The most common form of Christian discouragement is not doubt about doctrine; it is the settled suspicion that you have somehow received a lesser version of the Christian faith than other people have — that there is a fuller thing, a deeper blessing, a level of God’s favour that others reached and you did not. Verse 14 forecloses it. The blessing of Abraham and the promised Spirit are not two prizes handed out at different levels of attainment. They are one gift, purchased at one cross, received by one faith, and if you are in Christ you have them.

Look at what it cost to get that gift to a Gentile. The curse had to be exhausted, and it was exhausted on the Son of God outside a city wall, in the dark, at the hands of the very people the promise was aimed at. Nothing was cheapened to let the nations in. The full weight of the law’s sentence fell, and it fell on him, so that a man in Iconium with no covenant, no ancestry and no merit could be handed the Spirit of the living God. He did not lower the terms. He met them, and then paid for everyone who never could.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The temperature drops and Paul takes the Galatians from Golgotha to a lawyer’s office, calling them brothers for the first time since the letter began. Verse 15 gives the principle from everyday life: once a covenant or will has been ratified, no one annuls it or adds a clause. If that holds for a document drawn up by men who forget things and change their minds, how much more for one God has sworn. The Judaizers were not proposing to tear up the promise; they were proposing an amendment, and an amendment is not a modest adjustment but a legal impossibility.

Verse 16 makes the exegetical observation that troubles modern readers: the promise was made to Abraham’s offspring, singular, who is Christ. Since the word is collective in both Hebrew and Greek, this looks like a trick — until you notice that Paul himself uses it collectively in v. 29. The argument is not about grammar in isolation but about the shape of the history. The promise narrowed at every fork: Isaac not Ishmael, Jacob not Esau, Judah, David. It was always funnelling toward one person.

Verse 17 dates it. The law came 430 years after the promise, and the later document cannot cancel the earlier one; the figure follows the Greek Old Testament Paul’s churches used, which counts from Abraham to the exodus. Verse 18 states the either-or underneath: if the inheritance comes by law it no longer comes by promise. These are not two ingredients that improve each other but two answers to the question of who is responsible for my standing, and the second cancels the first.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priority and Indestructibility of the Promise

The covenant of grace — God’s unconditional oath to bless all nations through Abraham’s seed — is prior to the Mosaic law and independent of it. This is a foundation of Reformed covenant theology, and vv. 15 and 17 are where Paul argues it. The Mosaic administration does not replace the Abrahamic covenant or amend its terms; it operates within it and serves it for a season, leaving its character as promise untouched.

Verse 16 supplies the reason the promise cannot fail, and it is more than a point of grammar. Had God covenanted with Abraham’s descendants as a body, the covenant would have rested in the hands of a nation that broke every arrangement it was given. He covenanted with one heir who would not break it, and everyone else inherits by being in him. Verse 18 draws the practical edge: God has given it, in the perfect tense, and it stands given. A promise whose security is the character of the one who swore it is a different kind of possession from anything conditioned on the one who receives it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers were arguing, in effect, that the later Mosaic legislation modified the conditions of the earlier Abrahamic promise. Verses 15 and 17 show why that is not a theological preference but a legal impossibility, and v. 18 shows what it would cost if it were allowed: not an improved promise but no promise at all. Verse 16 removes their last foothold by identifying the heir they were claiming to represent.

Now: The difference v. 18 describes is invisible from the outside. Two Christians can keep the same hours, give the same money and serve on the same rota, one obeying a Father who has already given him the house, the other trying to secure a house he is not sure of. You can tell them apart only when something goes wrong: one fails and runs to his Father, the other fails and hides, because for him the failure has moved the inheritance. Verses 15–18 exist to put every reader in the first category and keep him there.

verseByVerse.quote: To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified. Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To give a human example, brothers. The temperature drops. He has just been at Golgotha; now he takes them to a lawyer’s office. And he calls them brothers — the first time in the letter that the anger has let a warm word through.

The example is a diathēkē, a word that covers both a covenant and a last will and testament, and Paul is trading on the overlap. His point holds either way: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified. Once the seals are on and the witnesses have signed, an interested party cannot come along later and insert a clause. If that is true of a document drawn up by men, who forget things and change their minds, how much more of an agreement God has sworn to?

The relevance is exact. The Judaizers were not proposing to tear up the promise to Abraham. They were proposing an amendment — the promise, plus a condition. Paul says that is not a modest adjustment. It is a legal impossibility, and anyone attempting it is not adding to God’s covenant but writing a different one.

Then verse 16, and this is where readers stop and frown, so it must be dealt with properly. Paul observes that God said to your offspring, singular, not offsprings, plural, and concludes that the promise was made to one person, who is Christ. To a modern reader that looks like a trick. Offspring is a collective word in English — singular in form, plural in meaning — and the Hebrew zera’ and the Greek sperma behind it work the same way. Genesis 15:5 promised Abraham descendants as numerous as the stars, and it plainly does not mean one star. Is Paul playing games with grammar?

He is not, and the proof that he is not is thirteen verses later. In verse 29 Paul himself uses the same word collectively: you are Abraham’s offspring, of a whole church full of people. A man does not build an argument on a word’s singularity and then use it of a crowd unless he knows exactly what the word does.

So what is the argument? This: the promise to Abraham always narrowed. It was never handed to his descendants as a body. Ishmael was a son of Abraham and was excluded — through Isaac shall your offspring be named (Gen. 21:12). Esau was a son of Isaac and was passed over. The line runs to Judah, then to David, then to David’s house, and at every fork it gets narrower, never wider. Read the story forwards and it is obviously funnelling toward somebody. The singular form is what permits Paul to say what the shape of the history was always saying: this promise had one destination, and it was a person.

And Genesis itself hints at it. After the binding of Isaac God says that in Abraham’s offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, and the pronouns around it turn singular — his enemies (Gen. 22:17–18). Paul is not importing Christ into the Old Testament. He is reading it the way the risen Christ taught his disciples to read it on the Emmaus road (Lk. 24:27).

The pastoral force of this is easy to miss. If the promise was made to Christ, then the promise cannot fail, because its heir cannot fail. Had God made his covenant with Abraham’s descendants as a body, it would have been in the hands of a nation that broke every covenant it was ever given. He made it with one man who would not break it, and everyone else gets in by being in him.

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void. For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Paul puts a date on it. The law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God. The promise is the older document by four centuries, and in any court the later paper cannot cancel the earlier one.

A reader with a study Bible will stop at the number, and he is right to, so here is the arithmetic. Exodus 12:40 says the people of Israel lived in Egypt 430 years. But the Greek Old Testament that Paul and his readers used — and the Samaritan text — reads in Egypt and in Canaan, that is, 430 years from Abraham to the exodus in total. On that reckoning Abraham to Jacob’s descent into Egypt is about 215 years, and the stay in Egypt is the other 215. Paul is not being careless with chronology; he is counting from the promise to Sinai, using the text his churches had in their hands. And note that nothing in his argument depends on the exact figure. Four hundred and thirty years, or four hundred, or two hundred: the promise came first, and that is the whole point.

Then verse 18 states the principle underneath, and it is the cleanest either-or in the letter. If the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise.

Paul is not saying that law and promise are enemies. He is saying they are different species of thing, and that a single inheritance cannot be received on both terms at once. A promise is something one party swears and the other receives. A law is something one party demands and the other performs. Try to hold both and you have not enriched the promise, you have dissolved it, because the moment my performance is a condition, the swearing was never the ground.

Illustrate it and it becomes obvious. A father tells his son that the house is his when the father dies; it is written, signed, witnessed. Later the father says, and keep your room tidy. If tidiness is house-keeping in the ordinary sense — how a son who has been given a house behaves in it — nothing has changed. But if tidiness is now the condition of inheriting, then the son does not have a promise any more. He has a contract, and he will spend the rest of his life measuring the floor, and he will never once be sure.

That is precisely the difference between a Christian who obeys God and a Christian who is trying to secure God. The behaviour can look identical from the outside. Both are up early. Both give. Both serve. The difference is invisible until something goes wrong, and then it is unmistakable: one of them fails and runs to his Father, and the other fails and hides, because the failure has just moved his inheritance.

But God gave it to Abraham by a promise. The verb is a perfect — God has given, and it stands given. That is the tense the whole Christian life rests on. The deed was signed before Sinai, before Moses, before there was a law to keep or break, and it was signed by someone who does not revise. (cf. Rom. 4:13–16; Heb. 6:17–18)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–25 — The Purpose of the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If the law cannot justify, cannot give life and cannot amend the promise, the obvious objection has to be faced, and v. 19 faces it: why then the law? Paul answers with three phrases, each of which puts the law in its place without insulting it. It was added because of transgressions — drawing the line that turns vague wrongness into named counts. It was until the offspring should come, with an expiry written into it, not a failure but a term. And it was put in place through angels by an intermediary, which is the sharpest demotion of all.

Verse 20 is the most compressed sentence in the letter, and honest commentators admit that its details are disputed. But the direction is clear from the chain Paul has just counted. A mediator implies two parties; the presence of Moses on the mountain tells you Sinai was a two-sided arrangement that could fail, and it failed at the foot of the mountain. God is one: when he came to Abraham there was no second party, and in Genesis 15 he passed alone between the pieces while Abraham slept through his own covenant.

Verse 21 asks whether the law is therefore contrary to God’s promises and answers with Paul’s strongest negative. They are not rivals but a diagnosis and a cure. He grants freely that if any law could give life, righteousness would have come that way. Verse 22 gives the true verdict: Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, shut in like fish in a net, so that the promise might be given by faith. Verses 23–25 name the jailer’s office — the law was our paidagōgos, the household slave who walked the boy to school until he came of age. Verse 24 says he was doing it so we might be justified by faith, and v. 25 says the arrangement has ended.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Law as Guardian: Genuine, Severe, Temporary, Fulfilled

Reformed theology has always held to the unity of the covenant of grace across both Testaments while recognising the distinct function of the Mosaic administration within it. Verses 19 and 24 are the classic ground for that. The law was genuinely from God, genuinely binding in its time, and genuinely serving the covenant of grace — but it was designed for a phase and not for the end. Its close as a system of justification is not God changing his mind; it is God completing his plan.

Two guards belong with vv. 23–25. It does not follow that God’s moral will has been repealed: Paul will say in 5:14 that the whole law is fulfilled in loving your neighbour. What has ended is the law as the framework of the relationship, the guardianship under which the people of God lived as minors. Nor does it follow that Old Testament believers were second-class. They were children in the same family under the care their age required. And v. 22 shows the severity was mercy: the exits were closed so that the one open door would finally be taken.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers wanted the guardian reinstated after the child had come of age. Verse 19 answers that the guardian was appointed for a term that has expired, v. 20 that the promise never depended on two signatures anyway, and v. 25 that the arrangement is over. A man insisting on it now is not more faithful than everyone else; he is standing on the platform arguing about the timetable while the train he was waiting for pulls out.

Now: Verse 21 meets the reader who assumes his problem is information or willpower. A speed limit has never made a reckless man careful; it tells him what careful looks like and records that he is not. Verse 22 meets the reader who has found that the harder he tries the worse the accounting gets — that may be God closing the exits rather than God withdrawing. And vv. 23–25 meet the largest group of all: believers who are technically adults in Christ and emotionally still under supervision, still measuring the day’s performance and still surprised by kindness. The Father did not relax the rules. He ended the arrangement and brought the boy into the house.

verseByVerse.quote: Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has been so severe about the law that the obvious objection now has to be faced, and he faces it head on: Why then the law? If it cannot justify, cannot give life, and cannot amend the promise, why did God give it at all? Was Sinai a mistake?

The answer is three phrases, and each one puts the law in its place without insulting it.

It was added because of transgressions.Added is the first demotion: an addition is not the foundation. And because of transgressions means this: sin was in the world long before Sinai, but it was not yet transgression. A transgression is a stepping over — and you cannot step over a line that has not been drawn. The law drew the line. It took the vague human sense that something is wrong with us and turned it into ten specific counts with names on them. As Paul puts it elsewhere, he would not have known what it was to covet if the law had not said you shall not covet (Rom. 7:7).

That sounds like a strange gift, and it is the kindest thing God could have done. A man who feels vaguely unwell will put off the appointment for years; a man handed a diagnosis with a name on it goes that afternoon. The law is the diagnosis. It does not cause the disease and it cannot cure it, and anyone who mistakes the chart for the medicine will die holding it. But without it we would have gone on managing our symptoms and calling ourselves basically decent people, which is exactly what most of the human race is doing.

Until the offspring should come. The second demotion, and it is the one that ends the argument with the Judaizers. The law came with an expiry written into it. Not a failure — a term. It was doing a job for a period, and the period ran until the Offspring of verse 16 arrived. He has arrived. A man who insists on the arrangement after the date is not being more faithful than everyone else; he is standing on a platform arguing about timetables while the train he was waiting for is pulling out.

Put in place through angels by an intermediary. The third demotion, and it is the sharpest. Scripture elsewhere describes Sinai as attended by angelic hosts — the Lord coming with ten thousands of holy ones (Deut. 33:2), the chariots of God among them (Ps. 68:17) — and both Stephen and the writer to the Hebrews take it for granted that the law was delivered by angels (Acts 7:53; Heb. 2:2). Then Moses stood between the angels and the people, because the people had begged not to hear the voice themselves (Ex. 20:19).

Count the links in that chain: God, angels, Moses, Israel. Now count the links in the promise: God, Abraham. The law came down a staircase. The promise was handed over directly. If you want to know which of the two is the greater, do not ask which is louder or which has more smoke on the mountain. Ask how many people God needed between himself and the man he was speaking to.

verseByVerse.quote: Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one. This is famously the most compressed sentence in the letter, and commentators have counted hundreds of proposed readings of it. It is worth admitting that plainly rather than pretending to a certainty nobody has. But the direction of the thought is not really in doubt, because Paul has just spent verse 19 counting links in a chain.

A mediator, by definition, stands between parties. You do not need one where there is only one party involved. So the very presence of Moses on the mountain tells you what kind of arrangement Sinai was: a two-sided arrangement, God on one side, Israel on the other, with a man in the middle holding the terms — all that the LORD has spoken we will do (Ex. 19:8). Everything then depended on both parties keeping their word, and everyone knows how that went; the ink was barely dry before there was a golden calf at the foot of the mountain.

But God is one. When God came to Abraham there was no second party and no man in the middle. Abraham did not negotiate; he was asleep. In the strangest scene in Genesis, God put him into a deep sleep and then passed alone between the pieces of the sacrifice — a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch walking the aisle of blood by themselves (Gen. 15:12, 17). In that ceremony the two parties walked the path together and invoked the fate of the animals on whoever broke faith. God walked it alone. He took both halves of the oath on himself, and Abraham slept through his own covenant.

So the contrast is not between a harsh arrangement and a kind one. It is between an agreement that can fail because it has two signatures on it, and a promise that cannot fail because it has one — and the one who signed it is God, who does not have a bad year.

This is where a reader should stop and do the sum on his own life, because it is the difference between two entirely different experiences of being a Christian. If your standing with God is a two-party arrangement, then it is only ever as secure as your last fortnight, and every failure is a breach, and you will spend your life in the anxious accounting that looks so much like devotion from the outside. If it is a one-party promise, then your failures are real, and grievous, and to be repented of — and they are not renegotiations. There is nothing for them to renegotiate. Only one name is on the document.

And that is worth sitting with quietly. God put a man to sleep and swore the whole covenant by himself, knowing every century of unfaithfulness that was coming, and knowing exactly what it would cost him to keep his own oath when the other side had broken theirs. He walked between the pieces alone at Ur, and two thousand years later he walked out to a hill alone, and kept it. (cf. Heb. 6:13; 2 Tim. 2:13)

verseByVerse.quote: Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law. But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has demoted the law three times in two verses, and he knows how it sounds, so he asks the question his opponents would shout: Is the law then contrary to the promises of God?

Certainly not! — mē genoito, the strongest negative he owns, the one he reserves for conclusions that would be blasphemous if true. The law and the promise both came from the same God and both serve the same purpose. They are not rivals. They are a diagnosis and a cure, and only a fool sets those against each other.

Then the reason, and it is a careful sentence: if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law. Notice that Paul is entirely willing to say it. If any legal code could make a dead man live, God would have used it and gladly counted people righteous that way. The law is not being blamed for failing at a job it was given. It was never given that job, because no law can do it. A speed limit has never once made a reckless man careful. It tells him what careful looks like and records the fact that he is not.

What law cannot do is generate life. And that is the true measure of our condition. If we were merely misinformed, instruction would be enough; if we were merely weak, encouragement would be enough. Scripture says we are dead in trespasses (Eph. 2:1), and nothing you say to a corpse improves it.

Then verse 22, and the image is a prison. The Scripture imprisoned everything under sin. The verb is synekleisen — shut up together, locked in with no other door; it is the word for a shoal of fish enclosed in a net. And the object is not everyone but everything, the whole realm, the entire order of things. Nobody is standing outside the net commenting on the people inside it.

And note the jailer. It is Scripture that did the locking. God’s own word turned the key — which means our confinement is not an accident of history or a verdict we can appeal to a higher authority. It is published, and it is his.

Which is savage, until you read the purpose clause: so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe. The imprisonment is a mercy. As long as a man believes there is another way out, he will keep trying doors. He will try being respectable, and being useful, and being sincere, and being spiritual, and each door will hold just enough to keep him busy. God locked every one of them so that we would finally turn round and see the one door that stands open — and it has a person’s name on it.

So if you have come to a point where nothing you can do about yourself seems to work, and the harder you try the worse the accounting gets, do not read that as God’s absence. It may well be his kindness. He is not punishing you with failure. He is closing the exits so that you will stop trying to be your own way out and take the one he has provided.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed. So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before faith came — Paul is using the word in a bigger sense than the act of trusting. Abraham had faith, and so did Habakkuk. He means the era of faith: the age that opened when Christ came and the gospel went out to the nations, so that faith is now the open, public, announced way in. The Old Testament believer was looking down a corridor at a door he could not yet see. We are standing in the room.

And what was the interval like? We were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed. The same verb as verse 22 — shut in. But now comes the image that governs the whole passage, and it is worth getting right, because most readers have been given a sentimental version of it.

The law, Paul says, was our paidagōgos. English versions say guardian, and older ones said schoolmaster, which is exactly wrong. A paidagōgos was not the teacher. He was a household slave — usually an old one, often stern, sometimes harsh, and in the comic plays of the period a byword for being no fun at all. He was given charge of the boy from about six until he came of age. He walked him to the schoolroom and walked him home, kept him off the wrong streets, checked his manners, and had a stick and authority to use it. He was not there to educate the boy. He was there to get him to the one who would, and to keep him out of trouble on the way.

So three things follow, and they are the whole answer to the Judaizers. The paidagōgos was genuinely appointed — the father chose him, and the boy who resented him was resenting his father’s arrangement. He was genuinely strict, and strictness was the job. And he was genuinely temporary: nobody was under a paidagōgos at thirty. His whole office was defined by an end.

But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian. The Offspring has come. The son has come of age. And the Judaizers were going to the grown man in the courtyard and telling him that if he really wanted to please his father, he should send for the old slave again and ask to be walked to school.

Two things need guarding here, because the verse is misused in both directions. It does not mean God’s moral will has been repealed. Paul will spend the last two chapters of this letter telling these people how to live, and he will say the whole law is fulfilled in one word, love your neighbour as yourself (5:14). What has ended is the law as the framework of the relationship — the system of guardianship under which the people of God lived as minors. And on the other side, it does not mean the Old Testament era was a mistake or that those believers were second-class. They were children in the same family, in the care their age required, waiting for the day this letter says has now arrived.

Which raises the question the passage actually puts to a Christian: are you living like a son, or like a boy who has never been told the guardian was dismissed? A great many believers are technically adults in Christ and emotionally still under supervision — still measuring the day’s performance, still expecting the stick, still surprised by kindness. The father in this story did not merely relax the rules. He ended the arrangement and brought the boy into the house as an heir. That is the sentence Paul is about to write.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The guardian has been dismissed, and v. 26 says what the boy has become: in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. Every word is aimed at something the Judaizers were saying — you, the uncircumcised; all, with no tiers; sons, not wards; through faith, not through the knife. Paul writes sons rather than children deliberately, because in that world sons inherited. The word is about legal standing, so a woman reading it is being told she holds the inheritance rights of a firstborn son in the household of God.

Verse 27 supplies the clothing image: as many as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. In the Roman world a boy who came of age laid aside the child’s striped toga and put on the plain white toga of a man. Paul has just dismissed the guardian; now he hands out the adult garment, and the garment is Christ. He names baptism because in the New Testament nobody imagined an unbaptized believer, not because water performs what the whole chapter has credited to faith.

Verse 28 then levels the three load-bearing walls of the ancient world — Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female — and the third pair is quoted word for word from Genesis 1:27, as if to reach past the social order to creation itself. What is levelled is the ground on which a person stands before God: one Christ, one righteousness, one inheritance. Verse 29 draws the line home. The promise was made to the Offspring; the Offspring is Christ; therefore if you are Christ’s, you are Abraham’s offspring and an heir according to promise.
verseByVerse.theology:
Union with Christ, and the Unity It Creates

Verses 26–27 give the ground of everything Paul has argued: the believer’s standing is not a quality in himself but a location. He is in Christ, clothed in Christ, and therefore holds the status of the Son. This is why assurance is possible for people who know themselves well; the clothing does not fluctuate with the wearer.

Verse 28 is the theological ground of the New Testament’s social revolution. The gospel does not merely change individuals, it creates a community in which the stratifications of the old age no longer determine worth or access. Sincere believers who honour this book read the verse differently when it comes to office and order, some hearing the end of every distinction of role, others holding that Paul speaks of standing here and of roles elsewhere; this commentary stands in the second tradition and says so openly. What neither side qualifies is what the verse indisputably says, and it is the larger thing: at the cross there is no hierarchy of worth, and in the inheritance of v. 29 there is no smaller share.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jew and Greek was a divide so absolute that a Jew would not enter a Gentile house; slave and free described perhaps a third of a city’s population as property; male and female determined whose testimony counted in court. There was even a prayer in circulation thanking God for not having been made a Gentile, a slave, or a woman. Verse 28 takes those three walls and says they do not run through the room. Verses 26–27 explain why: everyone in it is wearing the same garment. Verse 29 tells Gentile believers they are not associate members of a Jewish covenant but full heirs.

Now: Every congregation holds people who have quietly concluded they are second rank — the woman talked past in every church she has attended, the man whose job or record marks him out, the convert whose parents are not believers. Verse 28 does not offer them a role; it says something better and harder to believe, that Christ has no larger portion for anyone in the building. And v. 29 refuses to leave the inheritance vague: God himself as your portion, a body raised imperishable, a world put right, a face to see, and real work in a real kingdom. You are an heir now, while it is all still unseen.

verseByVerse.quote: for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. The guardian has been dismissed in the verse before; now we are told what the boy has become. Not a graduate. A son.

Take the words one at a time, because every one of them is aimed at something the Judaizers were saying. You — the Galatians, the uncircumcised, the ones being told they were not yet full members. All — no tiers. Sons — not wards, not apprentices. Through faith — not through the knife. And in front of it all, governing everything, in Christ Jesus: the sonship is not something we possess in ourselves; it is ours because we are in the Son.

A word about sons, since a modern reader may hear it as a door closing. Paul writes huioi and not children, and he does it deliberately, because in that world sons inherited and daughters generally did not. The word is not about gender; it is about legal status — the standing of the heir. So when a woman reads verse 26 she is not listening in on something addressed to the men. She is being told that she holds the inheritance rights of a firstborn son in the household of God. Two verses later Paul will say so explicitly. Far from excluding her, this is the most generous word in the sentence.

Then verse 27, and the clothing image: as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.Put on is enedysasthe, the ordinary word for dressing — and in the Roman world it carried a particular resonance that fits this passage exactly. When a boy came of age, the family held a ceremony in which he laid aside the child’s striped toga and put on the plain white toga virilis, the garment of a man, and from that day he was treated as one. Paul has just dismissed the guardian. Now he hands out the adult garment — and the garment is Christ himself.

So what the Father sees when he looks at a believer is not a person making progress. It is his Son’s own righteousness worn as clothing, covering everything the man is ashamed of and everything he has not yet dealt with. That is why assurance is possible for people who know themselves well. The clothing does not fluctuate with the wearer.

One guard, because the verse is used to prove more than it says. Paul is not teaching that the water does the work — that would flatly contradict the argument of the whole chapter, which has just insisted that everything comes by faith and nothing by an outward rite performed on the body. He names baptism because in the New Testament nobody imagined a believer who had not been baptized; it is the God-appointed sign and public putting-on of what faith has received, so the two are spoken of in one breath. Sincere Christians differ on when that sign is rightly given, and this verse settles neither side of that question. What it settles is the thing both sides confess: what clothes a sinner before God is Christ, and it is received by faith.

Look at what that means for the ordinary Sunday. There is no better-dressed Christian in your congregation than you. The most disciplined believer you know is wearing exactly what you are wearing, and neither of you made it, and neither of you paid for it. (cf. Rom. 13:14; Isa. 61:10)

verseByVerse.quote: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now says the thing that has echoed for two thousand years: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.

Feel the size of it in its own century. Those three pairs were not opinions about society; they were the load-bearing walls of the ancient world. Jew and Greek was the religious and ethnic divide, so absolute that a Jew would not enter a Gentile house. Slave and free was the economic order, and something like a third of the population of a city like Corinth was property. Male and female determined whose testimony counted in court. There was even a morning prayer in circulation among Jewish men thanking God that they had not been made a Gentile, a slave, or a woman. Paul takes the three walls of that prayer and says that in Christ they do not run through the room.

And notice a detail in the Greek. The first two pairs are neither… nor. The third changes: no male and female — which is not clumsiness but a quotation. It is word for word the Greek of Genesis 1:27, male and female he created them. Paul has reached past the social order all the way back to the creation account, as if to say: the deepest distinction God ever made in humanity does not determine your standing in Christ.

So what exactly is being levelled? The context answers it, because Paul has not changed the subject: he is talking about who is a son of Abraham, who is justified, who is clothed in Christ, who inherits. On that ground — the ground where a person stands before God — the three walls are gone entirely. There is not a Jewish justification and a Gentile one, a free man’s adoption and a slave’s, a fuller portion for a husband and a lesser one for his wife. One Christ, one righteousness, one inheritance, and every believer holds all of it.

Is it then the abolition of the differences themselves? Plainly not in every sense, and the same letter proves it: Paul goes on being a Jew, Onesimus goes on being a slave in the eyes of Roman law while Paul works on Philemon to change it, and men and women go on being men and women. Difference remains. What has gone is difference as a measure of worth and as a condition of access.

Beyond that, sincere Christians who love this book and honour its authority read verse 28 differently when it comes to office and order in the church and the home — some hearing in it the end of every distinction of role, others holding that Paul addresses standing here and speaks about roles elsewhere and that both are his settled mind. This commentary stands in the second tradition, and says so plainly rather than hiding it. But it is worth naming what both sides confess without reservation, because it is what the verse indisputably says and it is bigger than what divides them: at the foot of the cross there is no hierarchy of worth, and in the inheritance there is no smaller share.

Which is where it stops being a debating point and starts being pastoral. Every congregation contains people who have quietly concluded that they are the second rank — the woman who has been talked past in every church she has attended, the man whose accent or job or prison record marks him out, the family that will never be asked to host anything, the convert whose parents are not believers and who feels the room close slightly when testimonies are given. Verse 28 does not offer them a role. It says something better and harder to believe: you are not on the edge of this. Christ has no larger portion for anyone in the building than the one he has already given you.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise. The whole chapter comes to rest here, and the logic is one clean line. The promise was made to the Offspring, and the Offspring is Christ (v. 16). Therefore everything depends on one question only: are you his? If you are, then you are inside the one to whom everything was promised, and it is all yours.

Notice the route the argument does not take. Paul does not say you have become a good enough Jew, or you have qualified, or God has decided to be generous with the entry requirements. The requirements were never lowered. Every one of them was met by one man, and you are in him.

And weigh the word heirs. An heir is not someone who has been given a gift; he is someone who has been given a standing, and the estate follows from the standing. He does not earn it, cannot be dismissed from it, and does not receive it because he has been useful. He receives it because of who he is in the family. This is why nobody in the New Testament is told to work at becoming an heir. You cannot work your way into a family tree. (cf. Rom. 8:16–17; Eph. 1:11)

So what is actually inherited? Scripture does not leave it vague, and the vagueness of most Christian talk about the future is a loss, not a piety. The inheritance is: God himself as your portion, which is the substance of every promise (Gen. 15:1); a body that does not fail, raised imperishable (1 Cor. 15:42–44); a world put right and handed over, the meek inheriting the earth (Matt. 5:5; Rom. 8:17–21); a face to see, which is the thing Moses asked for and was not given (1 Jn. 3:2; Rev. 22:4); and real work in a real kingdom with genuine authority attached (Lk. 19:17). That is what stands to the account of the Galatian farmer who believed a travelling preacher, and it is what stands to yours.

And hold the tense the way Paul holds it. He does not say you may one day become an heir if things go well. He says you are — now, while the estate is entirely unseen and you are still in a life that mostly contradicts it. Everything else a person owns can be taken away by a diagnosis, a market, a war, or simply by time. An inheritance held in Christ has none of those exposures, because its security is not your grip on it but his.

Stand back and look at what God has done. He made a promise to one man under a night sky and swore it by himself. He kept it through four hundred and thirty years of silence and fifteen hundred more of a people who broke every term they were given. He narrowed it through Isaac and Jacob and Judah and David until it came down to one, and that one carried the curse of the broken law out of the city on his own back so that the promise could be paid to everyone who had no claim on it. Nothing was cheapened, nothing was waived, and nothing failed. The oath he swore alone in Genesis 15 he kept alone on Calvary, and it is finished, and the nations are coming in.
