4.title: Sons and Heirs: From Slavery to Sonship
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the emotional and theological apex of the letter’s central argument. Paul has shown that the law functions as a guardian for children; now he shows what the alternative is: full sonship, the Spirit of the Son, and the cry of “Abba! Father!” from the depths of the adopted heart. The contrast is not merely between two systems but between two existences — the existence of the slave who must perform, and the existence of the son who simply belongs.

The chapter’s opening argument (vv. 1–7) draws on the legal reality of an heir who is underage: he possesses everything but controls nothing, lives under guardians and managers until the time set by the father. Israel under the law was in this condition — heirs of the promise but living under the law’s custody until “the fullness of time.” Then God acted: he sent his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. And confirmation: he sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, the Spirit who cries “Abba! Father!” — the most intimate address to God in all of Scripture, the word Jesus used in Gethsemane, now placed on the lips of every adopted child of God.

The chapter then turns to a personal appeal (vv. 12–20) of remarkable emotional intensity — Paul reminding the Galatians of how they received him when he first came to them, sick and in need, and how they would have plucked out their eyes for him. His anguish over their drift is the anguish of a parent whose children are being led away: “I am in the anguish of childbirth again until Christ is formed in you.” Finally, the allegory of Hagar and Sarah (vv. 21–31) makes the theological point in narrative form: the two covenants produce two kinds of children, and only the children of the free woman — the children of promise, of grace, of the Spirit — are the true heirs of the heavenly Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul takes the guardian of chapter 3 and runs the picture from inside the household. In v. 1 the heir, while still a child, is no different from a slave — and Paul concedes in the same breath that he is the legal owner of everything. Ownership and enjoyment are two different things, which is why Old Testament believers could be genuinely saved and still described as in bondage. Verse 2 names the arrangement: guardians over his person and managers over his property, and both hold office only until the date set by his father. The boy does not choose the day, and neither do the guardians.

Verse 3 puts the whole race inside that picture — Jew and Gentile alike enslaved to the stoicheia, the elementary principles. The phrase is genuinely disputed: the ABCs of religion, or the spiritual powers behind the nations, or both. Paul’s argument does not depend on settling it, because whatever they are, the Gentiles were under them and the Judaizing programme would put the Galatians back under them. The Mosaic law and the pagan calendar end up in the same drawer, not because they are morally equivalent but because of what they do when made the ground of standing.

Then vv. 4–5 turn everything. At the fullness of time — the Father’s appointed date from v. 2 — God sent his Son, born of woman and born under the law, into the exact conditions of the problem, to redeem those under the law and to bring them to adoption. Verse 6 gives the second sending: because they are sons, God sends the Spirit of his Son into their hearts crying Abba! Father! — the status first, the experience following from it. And v. 7 narrows from plural to singular for one reader: you are no longer a slave but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adoption, and the Double Sending of Son and Spirit

Verses 4–6 are among the most trinitarian sentences Paul ever wrote. The Father sends the Son; the Father sends the Spirit of the Son. The two missions are distinct and inseparable: the Son accomplishes redemption and adoption as objective legal realities outside us, and the Spirit applies them within, so that the adopted child knows the Father and calls him by name.

Adoption (huiothesia) is the doctrine this chapter states most clearly, and it goes beyond forgiveness. In Roman practice the adopted son took the father’s name, inherited on the same footing as any natural son, and had his former debts cancelled; the act was witnessed and irreversible, because what had changed was not his conduct but his family. Verse 7 draws the conclusion in three words — no longer, son, heir — and adds through God, so that nobody imagines an inheritance of this size arriving any other way. John Stott called adoption the highest privilege the gospel offers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians already had everything vv. 4–7 describe. They had the Spirit, they had cried Abba, they were heirs. The Judaizers were offering them a route to a standing they already held, and Paul’s answer in vv. 1–3 is to show them what they would be going back to: the nursery, the guardians, the managers, and a calendar. A son does not earn his way into a family he is already in.

Now: The test that v. 3 suggests catches good practices rather than bad ones. Take the religious habit you value most and imagine losing it for a fortnight through illness. If what rises is disappointment, that is a son missing his Father’s company. If what rises is dread, that is a slave who has missed a quota, and the habit has quietly become a stoicheion. And v. 6 answers the reader who does not feel like a son: the Spirit is sent because you are one, so the feeling is the consequence of the status and never the cause of it. Verse 2 speaks to a different ache — the prayer unanswered for years. There is a date, it is not arbitrary, and it was set by a Father, not by the guardians who seem to be running your life.

verseByVerse.quote: I mean that the heir, as long as he is a child, is no different from a slave, though he is the owner of everything, but he is under guardians and managers until the date set by his father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 3 ended with the guardian dismissed and the son given the adult garment. Now Paul takes the same picture and runs it from the other end, from inside the household, and the first thing he says about the heir is shocking: as long as he is a child, he is no different from a slave.

Not different in law — in law he is the owner. Paul says it in the same breath: though he is the owner of everything. The deeds are in his name. The land, the house, the animals, the servants, all of it is legally his. And it makes no practical difference whatever, because he is seven. He cannot sell a field or sign a contract or give an order that anyone has to obey. He eats what he is given and goes where he is taken. Watch him through the day and you could not tell him from the boy who carries the water.

That is the situation Paul is describing, and it explains something that puzzles readers of the Old Testament. Were the believers before Christ saved? Yes — genuinely, by faith, on the same ground we are. Then why does the New Testament speak of their condition as bondage? Because ownership and enjoyment are two different things. They held the title deeds to promises they could not yet handle. Abraham owned the world (Rom. 4:13) and died having buried his wife in the only field he ever bought.

Then verse 2 names the arrangement: guardians and managers — epitropoi, the men with authority over the boy’s person, and oikonomoi, the stewards who ran the property. Both were servants. Both had more practical power over the estate than its owner did. And both held it only until the date set by his father.

That last phrase is the one to hold on to. In the ancient world the arrangements varied — Roman law fixed some ages, provincial custom left more to the father, and a man could set the term in his will. Paul is not writing a legal treatise; he is fastening on the one feature every version had in common. The boy did not choose the day. The guardians did not choose the day. The father named it, and when it came, it came.

Which is worth taking personally, because a great deal of Christian frustration is about timing. Not doubt — timing. The prayer that has gone unanswered for eleven years. The change in yourself you keep asking for and keep not receiving. The season that has gone on so long you have stopped expecting it to lift. Verse 2 does not promise that the date is soon. It says there is one, that it is not arbitrary, and that it was fixed by a Father, not by the guardians who currently seem to be running your life. The child in this story has no say in the calendar and no reason to be afraid of it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way we also, when we were children, were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same way we also, when we were children, were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world. Paul takes the picture and puts the whole human race inside it. That we is broad: he is speaking to a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles, and he includes himself, the Pharisee, in the same sentence as men who grew up sacrificing to Cybele.

The phrase behind elementary principles is ta stoicheia tou kosmou, and it is one of the genuinely disputed phrases in Paul. It is worth being honest about that rather than pretending to a certainty that does not exist. Stoicheia means things in a row — the letters of the alphabet, and by extension the ABCs, the basic building blocks of anything.

Some take it that way here: the elementary stage of religion, the primer, the rudiments God gave the world to work through before the Son came — and to go back to them now is to be an adult sounding out letters. Others hear something darker, since Paul says enslaved, and the word was also used of the spiritual powers thought to stand behind the nations and their calendars. On that reading, going back to law-keeping is not merely childish, it is a return to territory that has an occupant. An older view took the word for the physical elements — earth, air, fire and water — and few now hold it.

Most readers today combine the first two, and the good news is that Paul’s argument does not depend on which you choose. Whatever the stoicheia are precisely, two things about them are certain in this letter: the Gentiles were under them before they knew God, and the Judaizing programme would put the Galatians back under them. That is what makes verse 3 so devastating. Paul has just filed the Mosaic law and the pagan festival calendar in the same drawer.

He is not saying that Moses and Cybele are morally equivalent; nothing in his writing would allow that, and he will say in Romans that the law is holy. He is saying something about function. Take any good and God-given thing — the Sabbath, the law, the sacraments, a doctrinal system, a discipline of prayer — and make it the thing that secures your standing with God, and it will do to you exactly what an idol does. It will demand, and it will never say enough, and you will serve it.

Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable because it catches good practices rather than bad ones. Take the most valued religious habit in your life — the daily reading, the giving, the fasting, the service. Now imagine dropping it for a fortnight, not through rebellion but through illness. Is what rises in you disappointment, or is it dread? Disappointment is a son who has missed his father’s company. Dread is a slave who has missed a quota. The habit is identical. The relationship is not.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the fullness of time had come. Two words turn the letter. Everything before has been minority, guardians, waiting, bondage; and then God moves.

The phrase is to plērōma tou chronou — the moment when the vessel was full to the brim, not a minute early and not a minute late. It answers a question honest readers ask: why then? Why leave the world in the dark for so long, and then act in an obscure province in the reign of Augustus?

Some of the answer is visible even from here. There were Roman roads for the first time running the length of the world, and a Roman peace that made it possible to walk them. There was one language a Galatian, a Roman and an Alexandrian could all read. There were Jewish synagogues scattered through every major city with Gentile God-fearers already attached to them, so that Paul had a hearing prepared in each town he entered. And there was a civilisation whose confidence in its own gods had quietly drained away. Take one of those away and the gospel travels differently.

But the deeper answer is in the sentence itself: it was the date set by his father from verse 2. History was not waiting for conditions to be right. It was waiting for a Father to say now.

Then the sending, and every clause is precise. God sent forth his Son — sent forth one who was already his Son, already there to be sent. Born of woman: the only place Paul mentions the birth of Christ, and the phrase is a Hebrew way of saying human, mortal, of our stock (Job 14:1). He did not appear in the world; he was carried in it, and delivered from it, and fed at a human breast. Born under the law: he took his place inside the very jurisdiction that had every one of us condemned — circumcised on the eighth day, redeemed with two pigeons, up to Jerusalem at twelve, keeping every clause of the code that was killing us.

A question is often raised about that phrase, and it should be answered rather than left hanging, because a reader who has met it will wonder why nobody addressed it. Paul says born of woman, not born of a virgin, and it is sometimes argued from this that he knew nothing of the virgin birth. But that is more weight than the sentence will carry. Paul is not writing about how Jesus was conceived; he is writing about which side of the counter he stood on, and every clause in the verse is chosen to press him further into our situation, not out of it.

Born of woman is the standard Hebrew way of saying a human being, and it is the last thing you would expect from a man who thought the Son had merely appeared to be one. If anything, the phrase is evidence on the other side of the argument, and Luke, who travelled with Paul, records the annunciation in detail.

And now the purpose, in two halves. To redeem those who were under the law — exagorasē, the slave-market word again from 3:13, to buy out and take away. And then something more than release: so that we might receive adoption as sons.

Huiothesia is a Roman legal term, and the Roman practice is the picture. A man without a suitable heir would take a young man, often an adult, out of one family and into his own by a formal legal act before witnesses. From that day the adopted son bore the new father’s name, inherited his estate on the same footing as any natural son, and — this is the part that stops you — his old debts were cancelled. Legally he was a new person. The transaction could not be reversed, and no later misbehaviour could undo it, because what had been altered was not his conduct but his family.

It is worth distinguishing two things the New Testament says about believers and their Father, because holding them together is a great strengthener of assurance. The new birth makes a person a child of God by an inward act — a nature given, a heart made alive, so that he begins to want what he never wanted (Jn. 1:12–13). Adoption is an outward, legal act: a standing conferred, a name given, an inheritance settled, done before witnesses and entered in the record. One is a change in you; the other is a change in your position, and it is done by somebody else entirely. That is why assurance is not finally a matter of examining your feelings. On a day when the inward evidence is hard to find, the outward act stands exactly where it stood, because it was never yours to perform.

So notice how much more the gospel gives than most Christians expect from it. Redemption alone would have been extraordinary: the slave bought out of the market and set at liberty at the gate. A freed slave owes his liberator everything and has nowhere to go. God did not stop at the gate. He bought the slave, cancelled the debt, gave him his own name, and walked him into the house as a son with the same inheritance as the firstborn. That is not a rescue. That is a family.

verseByVerse.quote: And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the first four words slowly, because the order of them settles more anxious questions than almost any sentence in Paul. And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts.

Not: cry Abba hard enough and you will become a son. Not: work up the feeling and God will respond to it. The sonship comes first, established by the Son’s redemption in verse 5; the Spirit is sent because of it. The felt experience is the consequence of the status, never the cause. Which means that when the feeling is absent — and for many believers it is absent for long stretches, in illness, in depression, in grief, in plain tiredness — nothing has happened to the sonship. A son asleep in his bed is as much his father’s son as a son laughing at his table.

The Spirit of his Son. Paul does not say the Spirit of God, though he is; here he is named as the Son’s own Spirit, because what he brings into the believer’s heart is the Son’s relationship to the Father. You are not given a new arrangement of your own. You are brought inside his.

Crying, Abba! Father! A word about that, because most readers have been told something about it that is not quite true. It is often said that Abba is baby-talk, a toddler’s Daddy. It is not, and grown men in Jesus’ day used it of their fathers all their lives. But the truth is not less moving for being accurate. Abba is the ordinary, intimate, domestic word a family used inside the house — not the formal word for the deity, not the reverent circumlocution of the synagogue, but the word a son would use turning round in the doorway. It is the word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mk. 14:36), and it is the word the Spirit puts in your mouth.

Notice also who is doing the crying. Paul says the Spirit cries, and in Romans he says we cry (Rom. 8:15). Both are true, and together they are enormous comfort: the prayer of a Christian is the Spirit of God praying in him. So the man who says he cannot pray — who gets three words in and dries up, who feels nothing, who is ashamed of how thin it sounds — is describing the outside of something. The cry that reaches the Father is the Son’s Spirit, and he is not thin.

Then verse 7, and watch the pronoun change. All through the letter Paul has said you plural, to churches. Here, at the point of the conclusion, he narrows to the singular: you are no longer a slave, but a son. He wants one person to hear it.

Three words in that verse are worth carrying about all week. No longer — a door has shut behind you, and slavery is now your history rather than your condition. Son — the status, given. Heir — and Paul adds through God, lest anyone suppose an inheritance of this size could be got any other way. (cf. Rom. 8:15–17; Eph. 1:5)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The register changes from argument to appeal. Verse 8 recalls what the Galatians were: not irreligious but enslaved, serving beings that by nature are not gods. Verse 9 begins to say they now know God and Paul corrects himself mid-sentence — or rather to be known by God — refusing to let their discovery stand where God’s election belongs; and then asks how they can turn back to principles that are weak and beggarly, adding the phrase he will not soften, whose slaves you want to be. Verse 10 reports what they are doing with no verb of judgement at all, only an exclamation mark: days and months and seasons and years. Verse 11 admits fear rather than pronouncing sentence.

Then the personal appeal. In v. 12 Paul begs them to become as he is, since he became as they are — a Jew who laid down every marker the Judaizers are selling — and clears his own grievance off the table: you did me no wrong. Verse 13 discloses that the gospel reached Galatia because Paul was ill; the illness was not the obstacle to the mission but the mechanism of it. Verse 14 says they did not spit at him, the customary gesture before a diseased stranger, but received him as an angel of God. Verse 15 asks what has become of their blessedness, recalling that they would have given him their own eyes, and v. 16 asks the loneliest question in the letter: have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?

Verses 17–18 name the technique being used on them — courting followed by shutting out, so that the Galatians will keep working for an approval always just withheld — and set beside it the two marks of healthy zeal: a good purpose, and constancy when the teacher is absent. Verses 19–20 close the section with Paul as a mother in labour until Christ is formed in them, wishing he could change his tone, and admitting he is perplexed.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Symmetry of Bondage, and the Goal of Ministry

Paul’s equation in vv. 8–10 of Judaizing observance with the pagan calendar the Galatians had left is one of the most startling moves in the letter. He is not saying Moses and Cybele are morally equivalent; he says in Romans that the law is holy. He is speaking about function. Any good and God-given thing — law, Sabbath, sacrament, doctrine, discipline — will behave like an idol the moment it is made the ground of acceptance: it will demand, it will never say enough, and it will be served. Reformed theology has always held that moralism is not a minor error but a rival gospel that produces its own bondage.

Verse 9 also contains one of Paul’s clearest incidental statements of election, dropped in as a pastoral correction rather than a seminar topic. To be known by God is not for God to learn facts but for God to set his love on a person and claim him (Jer. 1:5). And v. 19 supplies the only metric for ministry the New Testament finally accepts: not attendance, giving or doctrinal precision, but Christ formed — morphōthē, taking shape from within, the word used of a child forming in the womb.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians had loved Paul extravagantly in vv. 14–15 and had cooled by v. 16, and vv. 17–18 explain the mechanism. The Judaizers courted them, flattered them, and held the door a few inches short of open. Verse 20 shows what Paul wanted instead: not their allegiance to him but Christ formed in them, which is why he would rather have been in the room than winning on paper.

Now: Verse 10 raises the question every honest reader asks — may a Christian keep Christmas, or Easter, or Sunday? Paul answers it himself in Romans 14:5–6, where one esteems a day and another esteems all days alike and neither is to despise the other. What he attacks here is not the observance but the ground. The test is what you feel when you miss it: the fellowship lost, or the credit. Verses 17–18 describe spiritual manipulation with uncomfortable accuracy — unusual attention early, a group with an inside, a standard always nearly reached, and leaving framed as betrayal. And v. 13 belongs to the reader whose life has been rerouted by his body. Paul did not plan to be in Galatia; he was ill, and the churches are still being written to.

verseByVerse.quote: Formerly, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to those that by nature are not gods. But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now turns the argument on the Galatians’ own past, and it is a hard turn to watch. Formerly, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to those that by nature are not gods.

Be clear what that describes. These were not philosophical atheists. Galatia was crowded with religion — the mother goddess with her ecstatic priests, the imperial cult with its temples in every colony town, the household shrines, the local shrines at the springs. The Galatians had been intensely religious and enslaved at the same time, which is a combination most people assume is impossible. By nature are not gods: there was nothing behind the statues. The whole apparatus of fear and appeasement had been built around beings who did not exist, and it had still owned them.

Then verse 9, and Paul begins a sentence and corrects himself in the middle of it, and the correction is one of the great small moments in his letters. Now that you have come to know God — and he stops. Or rather to be known by God.

Why the change? Because the first way of saying it puts the Galatians in the active seat and God in the passive one, as though the decisive event were their discovery. Paul cannot let that stand even for the length of a clause. Yes, they know God now; that is real, and it is the sweetest thing about them. But if you ask what actually happened, the verb belongs to God. They were known — sought, chosen, and drawn, before they had turned a single thought toward him.

And known here does not mean God learned some facts about them. In Scripture, for God to know a person is for God to set his love on him and claim him: before I formed you in the womb I knew you (Jer. 1:5). This is election, and Paul introduces it not as a seminar topic but as a pastoral correction on the way past.

Which is where it earns its keep. If your Christian life began with you, it can be ended by you, and every wobble is a threat to it. If it began with God knowing you, then the thing underneath your faith is not your grip. Ask the assurance question the right way round: not do I know God well enough — nobody does — but does God know me? And the evidence that he does is that you are asking at all. Nobody who has not been sought goes looking.

Then the wound in the sentence: how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more? Weak — they cannot deliver what they demand. Worthless — literally beggarly, poor, with nothing in the account. And whose slaves you want to be: Paul will not let them describe this as being pressured. Somewhere in them, they wanted it. That is worth sitting with, because it is the strangest fact about religious bondage — a system that tells you exactly what to do and exactly where you stand is restful in a way that grace, at first, is not. Grace gives you nothing to hold. Slavery hands you a list.

verseByVerse.quote: You observe days and months and seasons and years! I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You observe days and months and seasons and years! There is no verb of judgement in the sentence. Paul simply reports what they are doing, and the exclamation mark carries the whole weight. He is a Jew, raised on that calendar, and he is looking at Gentile converts keeping it and he can hardly speak.

Four terms, and they map onto the Jewish year as a whole: the Sabbath, the new moons, the festivals — Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles — and the sabbatical years. Not a stray superstition. The God-given calendar of the Old Testament, in the book Paul believed to be the word of God, being kept by people who wanted to please him.

Which raises a question every honest reader of this verse asks, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a pious swerve: does this mean Christians should not keep Christmas, or Easter, or Sunday? Is a church calendar a return to bondage?

No — and Paul is the one who settles it. Writing to Rome about exactly this, he says that one person esteems one day above another and another esteems all days alike, and each one should be fully convinced in his own mind, and neither is to despise the other, because both are doing it to the Lord (Rom. 14:5–6). That is not the language of a man abolishing calendars. He allows both practices in the same congregation.

So what is he attacking here? Not the observance. The ground. The Galatians were not marking Passover in gratitude; they were taking on the calendar as the thing that would complete their standing with God, on the advice of men who told them their faith was insufficient without it. The same act can be worship or slavery depending entirely on what it is being asked to do.

Which makes this verse far more searching than an argument about holy days, because everybody has a calendar. Sunday attendance, the daily reading before work, the annual conference, the fast in Lent, the family devotions after supper. All good. All potentially either. The test is simple enough to run this week: when you keep it, is it gratitude, and when you miss it, is the loss the fellowship you missed — or the credit? A Christian who has missed church through flu and feels sorrow is worshipping. A Christian who has missed church through flu and feels exposed is observing days.

Then verse 11, and the mood drops. I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain. No thunder now. The man who has been issuing anathemas admits to being frightened. He does not say they are lost — he never does in this letter, and the restraint is deliberate. He says he is afraid, and he says it to their faces, which is a different and far more disarming thing than a warning. He has years in these towns: the stoning at Lystra, the nights teaching, the walking. He is telling them he can see all of it going.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, I entreat you, become as I am, for I also have become as you are. You did me no wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, I entreat you, become as I am, for I also have become as you are. The tone changes completely, and the first word is the tell: brothers. Then entreat — deomai, the verb for begging, the word a man uses when he has run out of arguments and is simply asking.

The sentence is compressed to the point of obscurity, and it is often misread as a general appeal to imitate Paul’s character. It is much more specific than that, and once you see it, it is very moving.

I have become as you are. Paul was a Jew of impeccable pedigree — circumcised the eighth day, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee (Phil. 3:5). He had every marker the Judaizers were selling and he had them by birth. And he had laid them down. He lived among Gentiles as a Gentile lived, ate at their tables, sat loose to the calendar, refused to make his heritage the ground of anything. He had walked away from the whole apparatus of privilege and become, in the eyes of his own people, a man with no standing at all.

Become as I am. So the appeal is: I gave up my law-keeping to stand where you stand, on Christ alone. Do not now take up the law-keeping I put down. Do not walk into the room I walked out of.

It is worth weighing what that cost him, because the appeal is only as strong as the price behind it. Writing to Philippi he made a list of everything he had laid down — the pedigree, the tribe, the blamelessness under the law — and said he counted it all loss, rubbish, for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ (Phil. 3:7–8). The word he used is not delicate; it is what you throw out. This was not a man with nothing to lose recommending detachment to people who had everything. He had held the whole hand the Judaizers were dealing, and he had thrown it in the fire, and he was asking the Galatians not to go scrabbling for it.

Which puts a question to anyone reading who has never had to give anything up for Christ. Not a guilty question — some believers are simply spared it. But most of us are carrying something we have never once considered laying down: a family standing, a competence we are known for, a record of respectability, a theological rigour that has become an identity. None of those is wrong to have. Every one of them is fatal to hold on to as the thing that makes you acceptable, and the way to find out which you are doing is to ask what it would take from you if it were gone.

Then a short sentence that would be easy to skip: You did me no wrong. He is answering something. Nobody says that unless the other party might think he is nursing a grievance. And the Galatians could be forgiven for wondering — he is furious in this letter, and people who are furious usually have a personal injury somewhere in it. Paul forecloses it. This is not about him. They have not slighted him, offended him, or failed him personally, and he wants that off the table so it cannot be used to explain away what he is saying.

That is worth a moment for anyone who has to say a hard thing to someone they love. The temptation, always, is to let the personal hurt do the work — to let it be understood that you are wounded, because a wound wins arguments. Paul refuses the advantage. He wants them to have nothing to react to except the truth of the case, so he clears his own grievance out of the way first. It is one of the most self-disciplined sentences in the letter, and it costs him the easiest weapon he had.

verseByVerse.quote: You know it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first, and though my condition was a trial to you, you did not scorn or despise me, but received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Paul does something that changes the temperature of the whole chapter: he takes them back to the day he arrived. You know it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first.

Read that again, because it is easy to slide past. The gospel came to Galatia because Paul was ill. He had not planned to preach there. Something happened to his body that stopped him or diverted him, and while he was in that condition he preached, and churches were born that are still being written to.

What was the ailment? We do not know, and the honest answer is better than a confident one. Some have suggested malaria caught in the coastal lowlands, which would drive a man up onto the Anatolian plateau where these towns are. Some suggest a disease of the eyes, on the strength of the gouged-out eyes in verse 15 and the large letters of 6:11. Others have thought of the thorn in the flesh of 2 Corinthians 12. Paul does not say, and every generation of sick Christians has been the richer for his silence, because it means no one can be told that their particular affliction is not the kind God uses.

What he does say is that the illness was the occasion. Not the obstacle to the mission — the mechanism of it. That is a hard providence to receive while it is happening. Nobody lying in a fever in a foreign town composing his losses is thinking about the churches that will come of it. Paul only saw it afterwards, which is how this almost always works. The pattern is everywhere in Scripture and it is worth naming plainly for the reader whose life has been rerouted by his body: Joseph in the pit, Jeremiah in the cistern, John on Patmos, Paul in chains writing the prison letters. God’s habit of building his church out of interrupted plans is not an occasional exception. It is nearly the rule.

Then verse 14, and a detail that most translations soften. My condition was a trial to you — whatever it was, it was hard to look at, and it made him hard to receive. And Paul says: you did not scorn or despise me. The second verb is exeptysate, and it means literally you did not spit. In that world, when you met a person visibly diseased, you spat — to ward off the contagion, and to ward off the evil eye that was assumed to be behind it.

Hold that beside 3:1, where Paul asked who had bewitched them with an evil eye. The Galatians had once refused to treat a sick preacher as a man under a curse. Now someone has looked at them and they are enchanted. They would not spit at Paul when it would have been the normal thing to do; they will not look at his gospel now that it is the popular thing not to. Paul is not making a debating point. He is reminding them what they used to be like.

But received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus. That is the height of it. They took a sick, unimpressive, possibly repellent stranger and treated him as though the Lord himself had come to town — which, in the only sense that matters, he had.

verseByVerse.quote: What then has become of your blessedness? For I testify to you that, if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me. Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then has become of your blessedness? The word is makarismos, the noun behind the Beatitudes — the state of being congratulated, the happiness of people who know they have been given everything. Paul is not asking where their doctrine went. He is asking where their joy went, and he asks it as a man who remembers what they were like.

That is diagnostic, and it is worth pausing on. Legalism does not usually announce itself by error first. It announces itself by a change of atmosphere. The doctrine is still broadly right, the meetings still happen, the language is still Christian — and the gladness has gone out of the room, and been replaced by an earnest, watchful, slightly anxious carefulness that everyone mistakes for seriousness. If you want to know whether a church has drifted, do not start with its confession. Start with whether anyone in it looks relieved.

You would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me. It may be a proverb for giving away what you value most, and it may be pointing at what was actually wrong with him. Either way the shape is the same: there was nothing they would not have given him.

And then verse 16, one of the loneliest sentences in the New Testament: Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?

The word for telling the truth is alētheuōn — truthing, dealing truthfully. It is the same root Paul uses in Ephesians when he tells the church to speak the truth in love (Eph. 4:15). And notice the position he is now in. He has not changed. He has said the same thing he always said. What has changed is what they are willing to hear, and the effect is that the man who loves them most is now filed as the opposition.

Every pastor eventually arrives at this verse, and so does every Christian who has told a friend something true. There is a particular grief in it that is different from being disliked by strangers: it is being reclassified by people you helped. Yesterday you were the one who brought them the best news they ever had; today the same voice saying the same thing is a threat, and you can watch it happening in their faces.

Two things must be held together here, and the passage holds them. First, the possibility that you have become the enemy is not proof that you were wrong — the whole letter assumes Paul is right and unwelcome at the same time. Second, it is not proof that you were right either. Some men are treated as enemies because they told the truth, and some because they enjoyed telling it. The test is what Paul does next: he does not withdraw, and he does not harden. He goes on writing, and within three verses he is calling them my little children and speaking of labour pains. Truth-telling that has stopped hurting the one who does it has usually stopped being love. (cf. Prov. 27:6; 2 Cor. 2:4)

verseByVerse.quote: They make much of you, but for no good purpose. They want to shut you out, that you may make much of them. It is always good to be made much of for a good purpose, and not only when I am present with you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now names the technique, and it is worth naming plainly, because it has never gone out of use. They make much of you, but for no good purpose.

The verb is zēloō — to be zealous for, to court, to pay ardent attention to. It is the word for a suitor. The Judaizers were not bullying the Galatians; they were paying court to them. Flattering them. Singling them out. Making them feel that they, particularly, were worth the trouble of a long journey and a personal interest.

And then the second move, which is the whole point of the first: They want to shut you out, that you may make much of them. The courting is bait; the shutting out is the hook. Draw a person close enough to feel the warmth of belonging, then hold the door a few inches short of open, so that the belonging is always nearly his and never quite. A man treated that way will work harder and harder for the approval that is always about to be granted, and he will end up defining himself by the people withholding it.

That is the anatomy of spiritual manipulation, and it does not require a heretic. It happens wherever a leader’s significance depends on being needed, and it can be entirely sincere. The signs are consistent: unusual attention early; a suggestion that you have been seen more clearly here than anywhere else; a group with an inside; a standard you are always approaching; and a quiet impression that leaving would be a betrayal rather than a departure. If a reader recognises the pattern in a room he is currently sitting in, this verse is written for him.

Paul then does something careful in verse 18. He does not conclude that all such attention is wrong. It is always good to be made much of for a good purpose, and not only when I am present with you. He is not sour about affection; he has just spent four verses saying how much he enjoyed theirs. There is a zeal that is entirely healthy, and he names its two marks.

The first is purpose: for a good purpose. So the question is never whether someone is courting you. It is what they want you for. A teacher who wants Christ formed in you will be delighted when you grow past needing him, because that was the object. A teacher who wants you to make much of him will find your independence threatening, and will say so in spiritual language.

The second mark is durability: not only when I am present. Attention that is switched on in the room and off outside it was never about you. The love that is worth having is the kind that keeps working when the person is three hundred miles away and cannot see whether it lands — which is precisely what Paul is doing as he writes this. He is absent, unpopular, and still labouring over them. The letter in the reader’s hand is the demonstration of the standard it is setting.

verseByVerse.quote: my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you! I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, for I am perplexed about you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My little children. The anger drops out of the letter completely, and what is left is a parent. It is the only time Paul uses this particular tender address anywhere in his writings, and it comes at the point where he has the least reason to be tender.

Then the image, and it is startling from a man: for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you. Elsewhere he calls himself the churches’ father (1 Cor. 4:15). Here he is their mother, and specifically a mother in labour — ōdinō, the word for birth pangs. He had gone through this once already to bring them to birth. Now he is going through it a second time, and anyone who has watched a birth knows that this is not a picturesque way of saying he is concerned. It is a way of saying he is being torn.

Notice, too, what he is in labour for. Not until they come back to him. Not until they see he was right, or repudiate his opponents, or apologise. Until Christ is formed in you.

The verb is morphōthē, from the root that gives us transformed in Romans 12:2 and conformed to the image of his Son in Romans 8:29. It is not a word for imitation or improvement. It is the word for something taking its proper shape from the inside — and the image sits inside the birth metaphor exactly, since it was used of the foetus taking form in the womb. Paul is saying: I am in labour, and the child in the womb is Christ taking shape in you.

That is the goal of all Christian ministry, and it is worth measuring things by it, because almost everything else that gets measured is easier. Attendance can be measured, giving can be measured, doctrinal precision can be examined, and a congregation can be strong in every one of them while Christ is no more formed in them than he was a decade ago. Paul’s metric is brutal in its simplicity: do these people look more like Jesus than they did? A ministry that produces admirers, or partisans, or well-informed critics of other churches, has produced something — but not this.

Then verse 20, and it is one of the most human lines Paul ever wrote. I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, for I am perplexed about you.

He knows how the letter sounds. He has written anathemas into it and he is not withdrawing them — but he would give a great deal to be in the room, because a letter cannot modulate and a voice can. He wants to say the same words with his face visible.

And then the admission: I am perplexed about you.Aporoumai — at a loss, without a way through. The apostle who has just settled the doctrine of justification for the whole church does not know what to do about this particular set of people. It is worth letting that stand, because it is a mercy to anyone praying for someone who has drifted. Certainty about the truth and bewilderment about a person are not incompatible. Paul had both.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — Hagar and Sarah: Two Covenants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 21 turns the tables with exact sarcasm: you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? He means the Pentateuch, and he is about to answer the Judaizers from the story of the man they claim as their father. Verse 22 states the fact they had never weighed — Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman — which by itself disposes of physical descent as the qualification, since Ishmael had it and was circumcised by Abraham’s own hand. Verse 23 gives the real distinction: one son was born according to the flesh, the other through promise. Ishmael was produced by a plan that was legal, customary and effective; Isaac was produced by nothing at all, when Sarah was ninety and had laughed.

Verse 24 makes the interpretive move that has troubled careful readers — this may be interpreted allegorically — and then identifies the first covenant: from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery, and she is Hagar. Verse 25 extends the line to the present Jerusalem, putting the whole visible establishment of the religion the Judaizers were selling on Hagar’s side of the family. Verse 26 gives the Galatians another address: the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. Verse 27 quotes Isaiah 54:1, the verse immediately following the suffering servant, telling the barren woman to sing before anything has visibly changed.

Verse 28 names the Galatians as Isaac, children of promise. Verse 29 explains the opposition they are suffering by the pattern of Genesis 21:9, where Ishmael mocked the weaning feast by turning Isaac’s name into a joke — and says it is happening again. Verse 30 lets Scripture pronounce: cast out the slave woman and her son. Verse 31 lands the chapter on an identity rather than a warning, and changes the pronoun to we.
verseByVerse.theology:
Typology, and Why the Two Covenants Cannot Share a House

Verse 24 is not allegory in the Alexandrian sense that dissolves history. Paul’s premise is that it is written that Abraham had two sons; he treats the mothers, the statuses and the manner of each birth as facts. He is saying the history happened and was designed to carry a meaning the coming of Christ has made visible — which is what the risen Christ himself did on the Emmaus road (Lk. 24:27). If God governs history, a pattern in a true story is not imposed by the reader; it is put there by the author.

Verses 24–25 supply the test that governs the whole section: what a covenant produces tells you what kind of covenant it is. Sinai was genuinely from God and still bore children for slavery, because that was its office. And v. 30 states the reason a mixture is impossible. Add merit to grace and the result is not a moderate position but merit, since the moment performance is part of the ground the whole weight has moved onto it. Two guards belong with v. 30: Paul casts out a system, not persons — he is in labour pains for the people who hold it — and Genesis itself has God hearing Ishmael in the desert and being with him as he grew (Gen. 21:17–20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers presented themselves as the true heirs of Abraham. Verse 22 shows that blood was never the mechanism, v. 23 that the difference lay in how each son came to exist, and vv. 24–25 place the Jerusalem establishment on the slave woman’s side. Verse 29 then explains why religious men were persecuting a Gentile church: a man who has spent his life earning his standing cannot hear that a farmer who believed last month is equally accepted, because it writes off the investment. The elder brother of Luke 15:29–30 says nothing untrue about himself and is furious.

Now: Verse 23 finds most readers before the Judaizers do. The situation you have decided you must arrange yourself because God is taking too long is Hagar’s tent — not usually wickedness, but Sarah with a calendar, right about the arithmetic and wrong about God. Verses 24–25 give a test for any church: never mind the pedigree of the teaching, look at the children, and ask whether they are free to admit failure and free to be glad. Verse 27 will find the reader who is literally barren and has been told to rejoice by people who meant well; Isaiah’s command to sing is addressed to a woman whose grief is real and whose situation has not yet changed. And v. 29 is a warning before it is a comfort: watch what rises in you when someone is blessed without having earned it.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the son of the slave was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? The sarcasm is exact and it is the hinge of the passage. You want the law? Then let us read it. And he is about to demonstrate that the Judaizers have been quoting a book they have not understood.

Note the second use of the word: the law here means the Pentateuch, the five books of Moses as a whole, not the commandments as a code. Paul is going to Genesis. The people demanding law-keeping are about to be answered from the story of the man they claim as their father.

Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. The whole argument rests on a fact so obvious that the Judaizers had evidently never thought about it: physical descent from Abraham cannot be the qualification, because Ishmael had it. He was Abraham’s son, circumcised at thirteen by Abraham’s own hand (Gen. 17:23), and outside the covenant line. Blood was never the mechanism, and the family tree proves it before you have left Genesis.

Then verse 23 gives the real distinction, and it is not about the mothers’ status but about how each son came to exist. The son of the slave was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through promise.

Put the two births side by side. Ishmael was produced by a plan. God had promised Abraham a son; ten years passed; Sarah did the arithmetic on her own body and concluded that God needed help, and offered her slave. It was legal, it was customary, and it worked — a healthy boy was born, exactly as intended. That is what according to the flesh means here: not immorality, but competence. Human capability doing what it can, on God’s behalf, because waiting had become unbearable.

Isaac was produced by nothing at all. By the time he was conceived Sarah was ninety and past every natural possibility, and she had laughed at the announcement (Gen. 18:12). There was no mechanism. There was a promise, and then there was a baby, and nothing in between that anyone could take credit for.

So the two sons are two ways of getting a result: what a capable person can arrange, and what only God can give. And that is the question the whole letter is asking. Everyone believes God can save; the live question is whether he needs the help. The Galatians were not planning to abandon Christ any more than Abraham was planning to abandon the promise. They were proposing to assist it.

Which is worth turning on the reader before Paul turns it on the Judaizers, because the instinct is universal and it usually looks like responsibility. The thing you have decided you must arrange yourself because God is taking too long — the situation you are managing, the outcome you are engineering, the good end you are pursuing by means you would rather not examine — that is Hagar’s tent. It is not usually wickedness. It is Sarah with a calendar, doing the sum, and being right about the arithmetic and wrong about God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this may be interpreted allegorically: these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar. Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia; she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now this may be interpreted allegorically: these women are two covenants. This sentence has caused more anxiety among careful readers than anything else in the letter, and it deserves a straight answer.

The worry is legitimate. In Paul’s century, Alexandrian interpreters — Philo above all — read the Old Testament allegorically in a way that dissolved the history: Abraham became the soul, Sarah became virtue, and whether any of it happened ceased to matter. If that is what Paul is doing here, then the door is open for anyone to make any text mean anything, and readers who prize a plain reading of Scripture are right to be uneasy.

But it is not what he is doing, and the evidence is in his own sentences. He has just insisted that it is written that Abraham had two sons — the history is his premise, not his raw material. He names the son’s mother, her status, and the manner of each birth as facts. He is not saying the story stands for something instead of having happened. He is saying that it happened, and that God so arranged it that it carries a meaning the coming of Christ has now made visible.

That is typology rather than allegory in the Philonic sense, and it is what the risen Christ himself did on the Emmaus road when, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Lk. 24:27). The history is real, and it was designed. If God governs history and knows the end from the beginning, then the pattern in a true story is not something a reader imposes; it is something the author put there.

Then the identification, and this is where the passage becomes explosive. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar. Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia; she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.

Follow the line and feel what a first-century Jew would have felt. Hagar — the Egyptian slave, the outsider, the one who was sent away — is Sinai. Sinai, where the law was given in fire, is the mother of slaves. And Sinai corresponds to the present Jerusalem: the actual city, the temple, the priesthood, the whole visible centre of the religion the Judaizers were selling. In four clauses Paul has put the Jerusalem establishment on Hagar’s side of the family, and the Galatians on Sarah’s.

This is the most audacious thing in the letter, and it is not Paul being clever. It follows from everything he has argued: what a covenant produces tells you what kind of covenant it is. A system that demands performance can only ever produce people in bondage, however holy the mountain it came from and however ancient the city that keeps it. You do not judge the tree by its address.

And that is a test worth running on any religion, including your own. Never mind the pedigree of the teaching or the seriousness of the people. Look at the children. Does this produce men and women who are free — free to admit failure, free to be glad, free to stop performing — or does it produce a household of anxious servants who cannot rest? Sinai was genuinely from God, and it still bore children for slavery, because that is what it was for.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written, “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than those of the one who has a husband.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. After the severity of the Hagar line, Paul gives the Galatians an address.

They had been made to feel provincial — latecomers on the edge of the empire, whose membership depended on satisfying a committee eight hundred miles away in the real Jerusalem. Paul does not tell them to stop caring about that city. He tells them their mother lives somewhere else. There is a Jerusalem above, free, and she is not an idea; the writer to the Hebrews says the same congregation has already come to it — to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, to innumerable angels in festal gathering (Heb. 12:22). The believer’s citizenship is not pending. It is filed.

Then Paul quotes Isaiah, and the quotation is one of the most beautiful moves in the letter: Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than those of the one who has a husband.

That is Isaiah 54:1, and where it sits matters enormously. It is the verse immediately after Isaiah 53 — the very next thing said after the suffering servant is pierced for our transgressions and makes many to be accounted righteous. The barren woman is told to sing because of what the servant has just done. Her fruitfulness is purchased. That is the logic of the whole gospel in the order of two chapters, and Paul knew exactly what he was picking up.

In its own setting the barren one is Zion in exile — a city stripped, emptied of its children, with nothing to show. God tells her to start singing before there is anything visible to sing about, because the children are coming and there will be more of them than the woman who never lost anything ever had. Paul applies it to Sarah, who spent decades with an empty tent while Hagar had a son, and then to the church: this small, unimpressive, mostly Gentile movement will out-populate the establishment that despises it.

And a word for a particular reader, because this verse will find her. Some woman reading Galatians 4 is literally barren, and has been told to rejoice by people who meant well, and it landed like a stone. The text is not asking her to pretend. Isaiah’s command to sing is addressed to a woman whose grief is real and whose situation has not yet changed — that is the whole point of the verse — and it is grounded not in optimism but in what God has promised to do. Scripture never asks anyone to feel that a loss is not a loss. It does say, here, that God’s way of filling a house has never depended on the ordinary mechanisms, that the desolate one ends the story with more, and that the emptiness he leaves in a life for a while is not a verdict on it.

Look at how God has always worked. Sarah barren, Rebekah barren, Rachel barren, Hannah barren, Elizabeth barren and old — and the line of promise runs straight through every one of them, so that when the child finally comes nobody can mistake where he came from. He does not build his family out of human capacity. He never has. He waits until there is nothing left to explain it, and then he fills the tent. (cf. Isa. 54:1; 1 Sam. 2:5)

verseByVerse.quote: Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. But just as at that time he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also it is now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. Before the hard verse comes, the assurance. Paul tells them who they are, and he does it in the plainest terms: not candidates, not applicants, not probationers — Isaac. The miracle child. The one nobody could have produced.

But a reader will not simply accept the compliment, and he is right not to. The obvious question at verse 28 is: how do I know which son I am? Both were Abraham’s. Both lived in the same tent. Ishmael was circumcised and Isaac was circumcised, and for the first thirteen years of Ishmael’s life nobody watching that household could have told you which boy the promise was attached to.

Paul has already given the test, twice, and it is not a matter of intensity. Ishmael was not less sincere than Isaac and probably worked harder. The difference is where each son came from. So ask what you are actually resting on when you are honest, and the answer usually surfaces fastest at the two extremes. After a good stretch — prayer flowing, temper holding, a real usefulness to somebody — does your confidence before God quietly rise? And after a bad one, does it fall? If it moves with your performance, you have been measuring the wrong thing, whatever you believe on paper; that confidence is Hagar’s, because it was produced by you.

And notice what the test is not. It is not have I enough faith, which sends a man back inside himself to look for a quality he will never be able to weigh. Isaac did not qualify by being a better baby. He was born, and the birth was a gift, and the gift was announced before he existed. If you have come to the end of what you can contribute and are resting on what Christ has done, you are not being told to work up more assurance. You are being told your name.

Then verse 29, and it explains something the Galatians were living through and could not account for. Just as at that time he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also it is now.

The reference is to Genesis 21:9. On the day Isaac was weaned Abraham threw a feast, and Sarah saw Ishmael laughing — and the Hebrew word is a play on Isaac’s own name, Yitzchaq, he laughs. Ishmael was Isaac-ing. Mocking the child by turning his name into a joke, at the party held in his honour. It looks small in Genesis, and Paul calls it persecution, which tells you how he read it: the older brother, produced by human arrangement, could not bear the existence of the child who was pure gift.

And that is the pattern he says is repeating. The people persecuting the Galatian churches were not pagans. They were religious men with a claim to Abraham, and what they could not tolerate was a family they had not qualified for.

It helps to understand why grace provokes rage rather than indifference. A man who has spent his life earning his standing has an enormous investment, and the doctrine of free grace does not merely disagree with him; it writes off the investment. If the Gentile farmer who believed last month is as accepted as the Pharisee who has kept the calendar for forty years, then the forty years bought nothing. Nobody hears that calmly. The elder brother in the parable is furious at exactly this, and he never once says an untrue thing about himself (Lk. 15:29–30).

Two things follow for the reader. The first is a comfort for anyone bruised by opposition that came from inside the church rather than outside it. Paul says so also it is now, as a settled expectation. Hostility from religious people is not evidence that you have gone wrong; it has a long pedigree, and it begins at a child’s birthday party in Genesis.

The second is a warning, and it is the more useful one, because most of us are likelier to be Ishmael than Isaac on any given Tuesday. Watch what rises in you when someone is blessed without having earned it — the convert with the disgraceful history who is radiant, the newcomer given the opportunity you waited eleven years for, the brother whose prayers appear to be answered while yours are not. That flicker is not a small sin of the temperament. It is the flesh recognising the child of promise and hating him for it.

verseByVerse.quote: But what does the Scripture say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.” So, brothers, we are not children of the slave but of the free woman.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But what does the Scripture say? Paul has been arguing; now he stops and lets the text pronounce, and the sentence he chooses is the hardest in the chapter. Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.

It is Genesis 21:10, and in Genesis it is Sarah who says it, in a temper, and Abraham is very displeased because it is his son (Gen. 21:11). What makes it Scripture rather than a domestic quarrel is verse 12, where God tells Abraham to do as Sarah says — for a reason that is not about Sarah’s feelings at all: through Isaac shall your offspring be named. The line of promise must not be confused with the line of human arrangement, and you cannot keep both in the same house pretending they are the same thing.

So what is Paul telling the Galatians to cast out? Read what he does with it. He is not issuing instructions about persons; he applies it to the two covenants he has been contrasting for ten verses. The thing that cannot stay is the system — law-keeping as the ground of acceptance, sitting alongside the gospel as a supplementary option. The Galatians were trying to keep both mothers in the house. Paul says the arrangement is impossible, and not because grace is intolerant. Because the two produce different children, and one of them has no share in the estate.

This is where the letter is at its least accommodating and most necessary. There is no version of Christianity in which grace and merit are balanced. Add merit to grace and you do not get a moderate position; you get merit, because the moment my performance is part of the ground, the whole weight has shifted onto it. A little law as the basis of standing is like a little water in petrol. It is not a mixture. It is a failure.

Two guards, because this verse gets misused. It is not a licence for cruelty to people. Paul casts out a doctrine; he spends the surrounding verses in labour pains for the people who hold it, calls them his little children, and wishes he could soften his voice. Anyone who quotes verse 30 to justify being hard with a person has read the sentence and missed the chapter. And notice how Genesis itself handles Ishmael: God hears the boy crying in the desert, promises to make him a nation, and is with him as he grows (Gen. 21:17–20). The one cast out of the inheritance is not cast out of God’s care. Scripture is more tender than our use of it.

So, brothers, we are not children of the slave but of the free woman. The chapter lands on an identity, not a warning, and the pronoun has changed — not you now, but we. Paul puts himself in the sentence with them. Everything that follows in chapter 5 about standing firm and not submitting again to a yoke is built on this one line: he is not telling them to become free. He is telling them what they are.

And it is worth stopping to consider how it was done. The son of the free woman is the one who inherits — and the only Son who ever had that standing by right laid it down, was counted with the slaves, took the outsider’s place, and was cast out beyond the camp so that the children of Hagar could be brought into the house as heirs. Sarah’s son kept the inheritance because Ishmael was sent away. Ours was kept because the true Son was.
