5.title: For Freedom Christ Has Set Us Free: The Spirit and the Flesh
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is the hinge on which the entire letter turns from theology to life. The freedom Paul has argued for throughout — freedom from the law as a system of justification, freedom from the curse, freedom from the elementary principles of the old age — must now be shown to produce not moral chaos but something far better than law-keeping ever could. The chapter answers two questions that the letter’s argument raises: What does this freedom look like in practice? And what is its alternative to the law as the shaping force of Christian behavior?

The answer to the first question is given negatively and positively. Negatively: freedom is not license (“do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh”). The Judaizers’ accusation — that a gospel without law-requirements would produce moral anarchy — is not left unanswered. But the answer is not to reinstate the law; the answer is to walk in the Spirit. Positively: the whole law is fulfilled in one word — “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (v. 14). Those who walk by the Spirit do not need the law to produce love, because the Spirit is the Spirit of the God who is love, and his fruit in the believer is love. The Judaizers’ program produced biting and devouring; the Spirit produces love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.

The heart of the chapter is the contrast between the works of the flesh (vv. 19–21) and the fruit of the Spirit (vv. 22–23). The language itself is instructive: works (plural, produced by human striving) versus fruit (singular, the organic product of the Spirit’s life within). The flesh produces a catalogue of self-serving, community-destroying behaviors; the Spirit produces a coherent, integrated character that is nothing less than the character of Christ. The goal of the Christian life is not the avoidance of the flesh’s works by rule-keeping but the cultivation of the Spirit’s life by staying close to the one who gives it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1 compresses four chapters into a line: for freedom Christ has set us free. The apparent tautology is the point — freedom is the destination, not a stage on the way to a stricter religion. Stand firm is a military verb, because freedom is not a resting state; slavery is restful in a way liberty is not, since a slave always knows where he stands. The yoke of slavery is Peter’s own phrase for the law at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:10), and it sits against the yoke Jesus offers in Matthew 11:29–30. Nobody goes without a yoke; the question is whose.

Verses 2–3 are the warning. If a man accepts circumcision as what completes his standing, Christ is of no advantage to him — not less, none, because he has changed systems into one that has no column for what somebody else has done. Verse 3 closes the escape route: he is obligated to keep the whole law, not the one item he was sold. Verse 4 states the result in two phrases that describe a change of position rather than of behaviour: severed from Christ, fallen out of the sphere of grace. Verse 5 draws the line with an emphatic we ourselves, and adds the note of waiting; v. 6 says neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts, but faith working through love.

Then the appeal. Verse 7 uses a technical word for cutting in on a runner — somebody stepped into their lane. Verse 8 says quietly that this persuasion is not from him who calls them. Verse 9 warns that a little leaven changes the whole loaf, invisibly, while it is happening. Verse 10 is the surprise: Paul is confident about them, in the Lord, and leaves the troubler to God. Verse 11 shows what was being said about him and names the offence of the cross, and v. 12 aims a deliberately shocking wish at teachers who make the knife the mechanism.
verseByVerse.theology:
Freedom as the Goal of Redemption, and What Falling from Grace Means

The Reformed tradition has always held that gospel freedom is more than freedom from sin’s penalty; it is freedom from performance-based religion — liberty to live as sons rather than as slaves calculating wages. This is not antinomianism. The law’s moral demands are fulfilled from within by those who walk in the Spirit rather than imposed from without on those who must earn a standing. Luther’s paradox holds both: a Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none, and a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all.

Verse 4 must be read for what it says. Both its clauses describe position, not conduct: the people addressed have become more religious, not less, and Paul identifies them in the same breath as those who would be justified by the law. To fall from grace here is to step off the ground of grace onto the ground of law, where Christ’s work is inoperative — not to have disgraced oneself, which is the phrase’s modern and quite different meaning. That Paul writes v. 10 six sentences later, expressing confidence about the very same people, settles how v. 4 is functioning: it is the warning that prevents the thing it describes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Circumcision was offered to the Galatians as an upgrade — a fuller belonging. Verses 2–3 show it is not an upgrade but an exchange, and v. 3 reads them the rest of the contract nobody mentioned. Verse 11 reveals that Paul was being quoted against himself, probably on the strength of Timothy (Acts 16:3); his answer is his scars. Verse 12 would have landed with local force, since the shrine of the mother goddess at Pessinus in Galatia was served by priests who castrated themselves.

Now: Verse 1 asks what standing firm looks like on a Wednesday, and the answer is refusing to answer one question the way instinct wants to. Where do I stand with God today? reaches for the last few days; standing firm declines to answer it that way. Verse 4 belongs to the reader who has just gone cold reading it — and the test is simple: the verse describes a man at peace with being justified by his own record. Fear that your record will not carry you is the opposite of the condition described. Verse 8 gives a usable test for any new teaching: does it come to you the way the God who called you came to you? He came with a gift, and the effect was relief.

verseByVerse.quote: For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything Paul has argued for four chapters is now compressed into one line, and it is the line the letter is remembered by. For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.

The first clause looks like a stammer. For freedom he has set us free — why say it twice? Because Paul is answering a question nobody had thought to ask: what is the freedom for? And his answer is that it is not for anything. It is not a stage on the way to a stricter and more mature religion, not a probationary liberty granted so that you can demonstrate you deserve something better. Freedom is the destination. Christ did not release his people so that they could be transferred to a superior master; he released them because he wanted them free.

That needs saying, because a great many Christians treat grace as the doorway and law as the corridor beyond it. They will tell you cheerfully that they were saved by grace, and then describe a daily life in which everything depends on their performance. Paul says the door and the corridor are made of the same thing.

Stand firm. The verb is stēkete, and it is a military word — hold the position, do not give ground. Which tells you something about freedom that nobody expects: it is not a resting state. Left alone, a free man drifts back toward slavery, because slavery is restful in a way that liberty is not. A slave is told what to do and knows exactly where he stands. Freedom requires you to live without a scoreboard, and a great many people find that harder than obedience.

A yoke of slavery. The image is a wooden beam laid across the shoulders of an animal, and it is a deliberate quotation. Peter used exactly this phrase at the Jerusalem council about the law — a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear (Acts 15:10). And it sits against another use of the word that every reader should hear beside it, because Jesus also offers a yoke: take my yoke upon you… for my yoke is easy and my burden is light (Matt. 11:29–30). So the question is never whether a man will wear a yoke. It is whose.

Do not submit again. The verb is passive, and that is worth noticing: do not let yourselves be subjected. Nobody was going to force the Galatians. They were going to agree to it, for reasons that felt like devotion. And again is the sharpest word in the sentence — these were Gentiles who had never been under Moses in their lives. Paul means that a return to law-keeping would land them back where their paganism had them: performing, appeasing, never sure.

So what does standing firm actually look like on a Wednesday? Mostly it looks like refusing to answer one question the way your instincts want to answer it. The question is where do I stand with God today?, and the instinctive answer reaches for the last few days — how you prayed, how you spoke to your wife, whether you did the thing you promised yourself you would stop doing. Standing firm is declining to answer it that way. Not because the week does not matter; it matters a great deal. But it is not the ground you are standing on, and the day you let it become the ground, the yoke is back on your shoulders and nobody had to put it there.

verseByVerse.quote: Look: I, Paul, say to you that if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you. I testify again to every man who accepts circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look: I, Paul, say to you. He stops the argument and puts his name in the sentence. The whole weight of his apostleship, defended at length in chapters 1 and 2, is being set down on what comes next, and what comes next is the most alarming sentence in the letter.

If you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you. Not less advantage. None. And that is startling, because on the face of it circumcision is a small thing — a rite God himself commanded, which Paul elsewhere says counts for nothing either way (v. 6), and which he had personally arranged for Timothy (Acts 16:3).

So the act is not the issue. The issue is what it is being asked to do. If a man accepts circumcision as the thing that completes his standing with God, he has not added a little security to Christ. He has changed systems. And in the system he has entered, Christ is not an asset, because that system does not deal in gifts. It deals in obligations, and it has no column for what somebody else has done.

This is also where a reader who knows his New Testament raises an entirely fair objection, and it should be answered rather than dodged, because Paul’s opponents were evidently raising it too (see v. 11). Paul circumcised Timothy. He refused to let Titus be circumcised (2:3). How is that not simple inconsistency?

Because the two cases are opposite in everything that matters. Titus was a test case: the demand was made in Jerusalem, as a condition, to prove that a Gentile could not be fully accepted otherwise. Paul refused, and says he did not yield even for a moment, because the gospel itself was on the table. Timothy was a different situation entirely. His mother was Jewish, so in the eyes of every synagogue in the region he was a Jew who had been left uncircumcised, and that fact would have shut the door of every building Paul wanted to preach in. Nobody was claiming it justified him. It was a matter of access, not of standing.

So the same physical act meant two irreconcilable things, and Paul’s judgement in each case was governed by one question: is anyone claiming this is necessary? When nobody is, it is a matter of freedom and he is flexible to the point of inconvenience. The moment somebody says you must, he will not move an inch. That principle is worth carrying well beyond circumcision. There are a hundred secondary practices in church life, and the same believer may rightly take them up in one setting and refuse them in another, and be entirely consistent both times.

Then verse 3, and it closes the escape route. Every man who accepts circumcision is obligated to keep the whole law. The Judaizers were selling one item. Paul says there is no such thing as one item. The law is a single garment, and a man who takes hold of a corner of it has taken hold of all of it — every clause, every festival, every sacrifice, for life, without a single failure. Nobody was offering that in the sales pitch. Paul reads them the whole contract.

verseByVerse.quote: You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace.

This is the verse in Galatians that frightens people, and it should be handled with care, because the reader most likely to be holding it is not a Judaizer. He is a Christian who has had a bad year, or a bad decade, and who has just read fallen away from grace and gone cold.

So begin with what the sentence actually says, because the popular use of the phrase has almost nothing to do with it. In ordinary speech, to have fallen from grace means to have disgraced yourself — a scandal, a moral collapse, a public fall. Paul is not describing that at all. The people he is addressing have not fallen into sin. They have become more religious, not less. They are keeping a calendar and considering a rite, and they are doing it in order to please God more thoroughly.

Look at the two halves of the sentence and the meaning is plain. Both describe a change of position, not a change of behaviour. Severed from Christ renders a verb meaning to be rendered inoperative, disconnected from any benefit — and Paul says who it applies to in the same breath: you who would be justified by the law. And fallen away from grace is, in the Greek, falling out of grace as out of a place: you have stepped off the ground of grace onto the ground of law, and grace is where Christ does his work.

Think of a man in a lifeboat who decides to swim alongside it, still holding the rope. He has not stopped believing in the boat. He has simply stopped being in it, and the boat is doing nothing for him while he is out there. That is Paul’s point. He is not telling the Galatians that God has thrown them out. He is telling them what law-standing does: it does not add to Christ’s work, it replaces it, and there is no arrangement in which a man is partly justified by each.

And now hold this verse beside verse 10, six sentences later, written to the same people in the same breath: I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view. The man who has just written verse 4 is confident about them. Which tells you exactly what verse 4 is for. It is not a verdict passed on the Galatians; it is the warning that will keep them from the thing described — and the warning works by being heard.

Which is where the frightened reader can be answered directly. Ask what the verse actually describes: a person who is seeking to be justified by his own law-keeping and is at peace with that arrangement. Now ask whether that is you. If you are afraid because you know your record will not carry you, that fear is not the condition Paul is describing — it is the exact opposite of it. Nobody standing on his own performance is troubled by the news that performance will not do. A warning against a cliff is not a report that you have gone over it, and the people who read it most anxiously are almost always the ones furthest from the edge.

What the verse does require is a change of footing, and that is simple enough to do today. Not more effort. Less. Stop asking whether you have done enough to be received, and look at what was done for you, and stand there. That is all grace has ever asked of anybody. (cf. Rom. 11:6; Phil. 3:9)

verseByVerse.quote: For through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having said what the law-standing does, Paul says what the other position looks like, and the first word is emphatic in a way most English readers miss. For through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness.

He has just said you to the ones seeking justification by law. Now he says we ourselves — the pronoun is doubled in the Greek for emphasis, drawing a line down the middle of the room. There are two positions here, and Paul is telling the Galatians which side of the line he stands on and inviting them back over it.

And notice how much of the sentence is about waiting. Eagerly wait is apekdechometha — to expect something with the neck stretched out, watching for a thing that is certainly coming and is not here yet. That is a striking word to use of righteousness, when Paul has spent three chapters insisting the believer is justified already.

Both are true and holding them together is the whole balance of the Christian life. The verdict has been passed: you are righteous in Christ now, today, with nothing outstanding. What is not yet delivered is the state that matches it — the day when you are finally and actually like him, when the man you want to be and the man you are have at last become the same man. Every believer lives in the gap between those two, and the gap is uncomfortable, and it is not a sign that anything has gone wrong.

Which is exactly why a legalist cannot wait. Waiting requires that the outcome be secure without your involvement, and a man whose standing depends on his own progress cannot afford to wait for anything; he has to be getting somewhere, visibly, or the whole structure wobbles. The gospel produces patient people because it has already settled the question they would otherwise spend their lives trying to answer.

Then verse 6, and it is one of the great summarising sentences of the New Testament. In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love.

The first half is remarkable coming from Paul in this letter. He has fought circumcision for five chapters; you might expect him to say that being uncircumcised is what counts. He says neither does. The moment you make your uncircumcision a badge, you are playing the same game with the pieces reversed — and every generation of the church finds a way to do it, taking pride in the tradition it has rejected as thoroughly as its neighbours take pride in keeping it.

Faith working through love. Five words, and they have been fought over for centuries, so it is worth being exact. Does love make faith able to justify — is it faith plus love that saves? No, and the grammar is against it: love is not what qualifies faith, it is what faith does. The verb is one of energy and operation; faith is the living thing, and love is faith at work. A faith that produces no love is not a faith that needs supplementing. It is a report of something that was never there.

So the test is neither have I done enough nor do I believe the right things in the abstract. It is whether the trust you have placed in Christ is doing anything — and the place to look is not your religious activity but the person nearest you who is difficult to love. That is where faith shows whether it is alive, and it is a far more searching examination than any of the ones the Judaizers were offering. (cf. Jas. 2:17–18; 1 Cor. 13:2)

verseByVerse.quote: You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth? This persuasion is not from him who calls you. A little leaven leavens the whole lump.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You were running well. The metaphor is the stadium, and Paul uses it warmly. He is not sneering at them. He is a coach watching a runner who had a good rhythm, a good line, and was going to finish — and something happened.

Who hindered you from obeying the truth? The verb enekopsen is a technical one: to cut in on a runner, to break into his lane and check his stride. In the ancient games it was a foul. So Paul is not describing a runner who got tired or lost heart. Somebody stepped in front of him.

That is a more useful diagnosis than it first appears, because Christians who have gone backwards usually blame themselves for a failure of stamina, and it is often not that at all. Somebody cut in. A teacher, a book, a friend with strong opinions, a season under a ministry that made the gospel conditional. The question Paul asks is worth asking honestly of any cooled faith: not why did I run out of energy, but who got in front of me, and when? Very often there is a date.

Then verse 8, and it is a quiet, devastating sentence. This persuasion is not from him who calls you.

He does not say the teaching is unhelpful, or unbalanced, or that its advocates mean well. He says God is not behind it. And notice how he identifies God: as him who calls you — the one who summoned them in the first place, present tense, still calling. The argument is: you know the voice that called you, because you have heard it. This is not that voice.

Which gives a test that ordinary believers can actually use, and it is more reliable than assessing arguments. Does this teaching sound like the God who called you? Not is it strict — God is often strict. But does it come to you the way he came to you? He came with a gift, to someone with nothing to offer, and the effect was relief. When a teaching arrives and its effect is that you feel measured, watched, and slightly behind, you may not be able to refute it. You can still recognise that it is not the voice that called you.

Then verse 9, a proverb: A little leaven leavens the whole lump. Everyone in that world had watched it happen. A pinch of sour dough goes into a large batch, and nothing appears to happen for hours, and then the whole mass has changed and there is no part of it that has not.

Two things follow. First, quantity is irrelevant. The Judaizers were asking for one concession, and Paul’s point is that a gospel with a small condition attached is not mostly the gospel; given time, it is a different loaf entirely. Second, the change is invisible while it is happening. Nobody in a church that is losing the gospel can feel it going. The sermons remain biblical, the meetings continue, the language is unchanged, and what alters first is only the atmosphere — the quiet arrival of measurement into a room that used to be full of relief. That is why Paul is writing at this volume about what looks, to everyone in Galatia, like a modest adjustment.

verseByVerse.quote: I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view, and the one who is troubling you will bear the penalty, whoever he is. But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been removed. I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves!
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the leaven, a surprise. I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view.

Nothing in the letter prepares you for that sentence. He has called them foolish, bewitched, severed from Christ, and now he says he is confident about them — and where that confidence rests is stated with precision: in the Lord. Not in their good sense, of which he has seen little, nor in the strength of his own arguments. He is confident in the Lord, about them.

That is how a Christian holds on to somebody who is drifting, and it is worth learning, because the alternatives are both bad. You can be confident in the person, which is not faith but optimism, and it collapses on contact with facts. Or you can write them off, which is tidier and feels like realism. Paul does neither. He tells them the worst honestly and then declares his expectation that God will keep them — which is the only ground on which anyone has ever been kept, including him.

Then the other half: the one who is troubling you will bear the penalty, whoever he is. The singular is interesting — a particular man, evidently, whose name Paul may not know. And notice what he does with him. He does not organise a campaign against him; he hands him over to God’s judgement and leaves him there. Whoever he is has a shrug in it: he will answer, and Paul does not need to know his name to be sure of it.

Verse 11 lets slip what was being said about Paul. If I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? Somebody in Galatia had been claiming that Paul himself taught circumcision when it suited him — the Timothy business would have served nicely — and therefore that the Galatians were only being asked to do what the apostle really wanted. Paul’s answer is not a denial but a piece of evidence: look at my life. Nobody stones a man for preaching what everybody already accepts. The scars are the argument.

And then the phrase that explains everything: the offense of the cross. The word is skandalon, the trigger of a trap, the stone that trips a man. What offends is not the suffering — the world has always admired a martyr. It is what the cross says about the person looking at it: that he could not be saved by any other means, that his religion and his decency contributed nothing, that he had to be rescued like a criminal. Add circumcision, or any other requirement, and the offence drains away instantly, because now there is something for the man to do, and a religion you can contribute to is a religion the world will tolerate. Paul says the persecution is the proof that the offence is still in his preaching. A gospel nobody is annoyed by has usually been adjusted.

Then verse 12, and it is startling: I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves! It reads as a crude outburst until you know where the letter is going. In Galatia, at Pessinus, stood the great shrine of the mother goddess, whose priests castrated themselves in ecstatic worship. Every reader of this letter had grown up with those men in the region. So Paul is not merely being coarse. He is saying: you want to cut flesh to be accepted by God? Then you already know what that religion looks like, because it is on your own doorstep — and if the knife is the mechanism, why stop where Moses stopped? Take it to the shrine and finish the job. It is the most cutting sentence he ever wrote, and it is aimed at showing the Galatians that the road they are on ends somewhere they have already seen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 13 faces the objection every preacher of grace hears: if people are genuinely free, what stops them doing as they like? Paul does not dodge it. Freedom must not become an aphormē for the flesh — a military word for a base of operations, the staging ground from which an assault is launched. The danger is real, and the flesh’s reasoning is always theologically impeccable: I am not under law, God has forgiven this already, grace is greater than my sin. All three are true, and all three have been used to wreck a family.

But watch what Paul refuses to do. Having diagnosed the problem, he does not reintroduce law as a fence. His answer to the flesh is love, and the verb in v. 13 is deliberately shocking — douleuete, be slaves to one another. He has spent five chapters removing a yoke, and the first thing he tells them to do with their liberty is to put themselves at each other’s disposal. The slavery he fought was bondage to a system in order to be accepted; this is bondage to a person because you already are.

Verse 14 grounds it: the whole law is fulfilled — not merely summarised — in loving your neighbour as yourself. Every commandment was always describing what love looks like in a particular situation, which is why the standard is higher and not lower: a code can be completed, and as yourself cannot. Verse 15 then shows the alternative in three escalating animal verbs — bite, devour, consumed — and Paul’s warning is that everyone loses. The congregation being perfected by law-observance was eating itself.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Fulfilment of the Law

The relation of law and love in Reformed ethics is exact. The law’s moral demands are not abolished for the believer; they are fulfilled, but from a different source and in a different direction. The law compels from outside and leaves the sinner exposed; love, produced by the Spirit, constrains from within and overflows. This is what the older divines meant by the law written on the heart (Jer. 31:33) — not a different law, but the same law internalised by the Spirit of adoption and obeyed as the expression of a heart that loves the God who gave everything, rather than as the price of his favour.

Verse 13 also settles the charge of antinomianism that has followed the doctrine of free grace since the first century. Paul concedes the danger frankly and then refuses the remedy his opponents wanted. That refusal is the test of whether a man has understood the gospel he preaches: it is easy to answer licence with law, and it undoes everything. And v. 15 exposes the mechanism by which a doctrine of performance destroys a congregation — once standing is earned, every other believer becomes a measurement, and the resulting suspicion has a righteous vocabulary to conduct itself in.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians were living out v. 15 while arguing about how to be holy, which is not an irony but a mechanism. The very community the Judaizers claimed to be perfecting by law-observance was tearing itself apart, and vv. 13–14 name the only thing that binds a church in the way rules never can.

Now: A church that makes the Christian life primarily about observable markers will always produce the same social weather: pride in those who meet the standard, shame in those who do not, comparison, and division. Verse 15 offers a test for a disagreement you are currently inside — ask what you want to be true about the other person. If you would be disappointed to find he was right, or that his motives were good, then whatever the merits of the case you are biting; the verse does not ask whether your position is correct. And the cure is in v. 13 rather than in a new rule: serve him, concretely, while you still disagree. It is very hard to keep eating a man you are carrying something for.

verseByVerse.quote: For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you were called to freedom, brothers. Paul returns to where the chapter began, and now he faces the objection that has been waiting since verse 1 and that every preacher of grace has had put to him: if people are genuinely free, what is to stop them doing as they like?

He does not dodge it. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. The word aphormē is military — a base of operations, the staging ground from which an assault is launched. So the danger is real, and Paul names it plainly: your liberty can be occupied. The flesh will move into the space grace has cleared and use it as a forward position, and the reasoning it offers is always theologically impeccable. I am not under law. God has forgiven this already. Grace is greater than my sin. Every one of those sentences is true, and all three have been used to excuse things that wrecked a family.

But watch what Paul does not do next. He has just diagnosed antinomianism, and the obvious remedy is a fence — some law, reintroduced at the end of the letter, to keep freedom in bounds. He refuses. Having spent five chapters demolishing law as the ground of standing, he will not smuggle it back as the ground of behaviour. His answer to the flesh is not restriction. It is love.

But through love serve one another. And the verb is deliberately shocking: douleuete, from doulos, a slave. Be slaves to one another. Paul has spent the whole letter tearing the yoke off their shoulders, and the first thing he tells them to do with their freedom is to put themselves at each other’s disposal.

That is the paradox at the centre of Christian liberty, and Luther put it exactly: a Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none, and a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all. The two are not in tension, because the slavery Paul has been fighting is slavery to a system in order to be accepted, and this is bondage to a person because you already are. One is how you get standing. The other is what standing does.

Then verse 14: the whole law is fulfilled in one word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. A reader is entitled to be puzzled. Paul has said the believer is not under the law — and here he quotes Leviticus 19:18 as though it settles everything.

The resolution is in the verb. He does not say the law is summarised in love, as if love were a convenient abridgement. He says it is fulfilled, and the tense is a perfect: filled full, brought to its intended completion. The law was never an arbitrary list; every commandment in it was describing what love looks like when it meets a particular situation. Do not steal is love meeting your neighbour’s property. Do not bear false witness is love meeting his reputation. So a man who genuinely loves is not evading the law. He is doing the thing the law was written to produce, and he no longer needs the list, in the way that a man who loves his wife does not need a rule against reading her letters.

Which is why the standard is higher and not lower. A code can be satisfied; you can reach the end of a list. As yourself has no end to reach. Nobody has ever gone to bed having loved his neighbour as much as he instinctively looks after himself.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.

The three verbs are all taken from animals, and they escalate. Bite is what a cornered creature does — a snap, a wound, not fatal. Devour is eating, taking a part of the other. Consumed is the end of the process: nothing left. Paul is describing a sequence, and he is describing it in a church.

Which tells us something about the situation on the ground that the doctrinal argument alone would not. This was not a seminar. The Galatian congregations were tearing each other apart, and the argument they were tearing each other apart over was an argument about how to be holy. That combination is not an irony. It is a mechanism, and it is worth understanding, because it is still the commonest way a good church destroys itself.

Here is how it works. Once standing before God is tied to performance, every other believer in the room becomes a measurement. If he keeps more than I do, he is a threat, and I must find the flaw that explains him. If he keeps less, he is a reassurance, and I need him to stay where he is. Neither of those is love, and both feel like discernment. Add a genuine doctrinal disagreement, and the whole thing has a righteous vocabulary to conduct itself in, so that people who are defending their own standing believe they are contending for the truth.

And notice Paul’s warning. He does not say the strong will eat the weak. He says you are not consumed by one another — everyone loses. Church conflicts of this kind have no winner. The party that prevails is left holding a smaller, colder, more suspicious congregation than the one it was fighting for.

Two practical things follow. The first is a test for a disagreement you are currently inside: ask what you want to be true about the other person. If you find you would be disappointed to discover he was right, or that his motives were good, then whatever the merits of your case, you are biting. The verse does not ask whether your position is correct. Paul obviously thought his was.

The second is the direction of the cure, and it is in the verse before. Paul does not answer biting with a rule against biting; he has just said through love serve one another. The specific antidote to devouring a brother is serving him — deliberately, in some concrete way, while you still disagree with him. It is very hard to keep eating a man you are carrying something for. (cf. Prov. 30:33; Jas. 4:1–2)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–26 — The Flesh and the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 16 gives Paul’s whole answer to Christian behaviour, and it is neither a law nor a technique: walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. The order is the strategy — he does not say stop gratifying the flesh and then you will be able to walk. Sin is displaced more often than it is defeated head-on. Verse 17 is honest about the cost: a settled war, which young believers often mistake for evidence that something went wrong at their conversion, when in fact before conversion there was no war at all. Its last clause is genuinely difficult and the grammar allows either direction. Verse 18 sets the alternative: led by the Spirit, and therefore not under law — a person to be followed rather than a code to be kept.

Verses 19–21 catalogue the works of the flesh, and the word works deliberately echoes works of the law. Sexual sin comes first (v. 19), then corrupted religion in v. 20 with idolatry and pharmakeia — but eight of the fifteen items, from enmity through envy in vv. 20–21, are sins of the church meeting rather than the tavern. That is not an accident in a letter to people who are biting one another. Verse 21 closes with a warning whose verb is a present participle: those who go on doing such things, whose lives are characterised by them.

Verses 22–23 answer with fruit rather than works — singular, one character with nine facets, which is finally the character of Christ — and end in dry understatement: against such things there is no law. Verse 24 states as accomplished fact that those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh, and the crucifixion image explains why something already condemned is still audible. Verse 25 changes the verb from walking to keeping rank, and v. 26 brings the whole argument down onto how a believer feels about the Christian three seats away.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mortification and Vivification, and Why the Fight Is Evidence of Life

Reformed theology has always described the Christian life as two complementary movements: mortification, the putting to death of the flesh, which v. 24 states as something already done to every believer; and vivification, the coming alive to God, which v. 25 calls keeping in step with the Spirit. Neither is self-powered. The mortification is the application to daily life of what happened to the old self in Christ’s death (2:20); the vivification is the fruit of the Spirit’s indwelling. The believer does not produce either. He participates in both by faith.

The tension between v. 17 and v. 24 is resolved by the image itself. Crucifixion was chosen by Rome precisely because it was slow: a man nailed to a beam was mortally wounded, fixed, going nowhere — and still perfectly capable of shouting. That is the flesh in a believer. Its authority is broken and its outcome settled, and it will go on being audible until the body dies. Verse 21 must be read with the same care. Scripture never confuses a man who falls into a ditch with a man who lives in it, and the ache that makes a tender conscience afraid of that verse is itself the evidence the verse is not describing him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians needed to see that law and moral chaos were not the only two options, and vv. 16–18 give the third. Verse 20 would have been the most uncomfortable line in the letter read aloud in those congregations, since the middle of Paul’s list of fleshly works is a description of what was happening in the room. Verse 25 carries a piece of quiet artistry: stoichōmen, keep in step, is built on the same root as the stoicheia that had them in bondage in 4:3 and 4:9. Paul does not tell them to stop marching. He tells them who sets the pace now.

Now: Verse 16 deserves a concrete answer rather than fog. Walking by the Spirit is asking before the difficult conversation rather than after it, going where he speaks often enough to know his voice, obeying the small prompt you would rather not have noticed. In vv. 22–23, three things should be said to the believer who finds almost none of the fruit in himself: it is slow and seasonal, he is the worst-placed person to assess it, and the list is called the fruit of the Spirit and not of the diligent Christian. Verse 25 names the two ordinary failures — marching ahead on your own energy and calling the exhaustion faithfulness, or agreeing with the small thing you should do until agreeing has replaced doing. And v. 26 has a test anyone can run: what happens in you when good news is announced about the believer whose life is flourishing most visibly?

verseByVerse.quote: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. Here is Paul’s whole answer to the problem of Christian behaviour, and it is neither a law nor a technique.

Walk is peripateite, a present imperative — go on walking, the ordinary word for how a man conducts his daily life. Not soar, not fight, not achieve. Walk. The Christian life at this point is being described in the plainest verb available.

And the reader is entitled to ask what that actually means, because it is easy to say and most explanations of it are fog. Paul is not describing a mystical state or a special sensitivity that some believers have and others lack. To walk by the Spirit is to conduct today in dependence on the Spirit rather than on yourself — and in practice it has recognisable parts. It is asking, before the difficult conversation rather than after it. It is going where he speaks, which is the Scriptures, often enough that you know his voice. It is obeying the small prompt you would rather not have noticed. It is doing the next right thing in the strength of somebody else. None of that is exotic. It is what dependence looks like when it is spread across an ordinary week.

Then the promise, and it is a promise and not a command: you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. The Greek carries a strong negative. Paul is not saying the desires will stop; he is saying they will not be carried out. And notice the order, which is the whole strategy of Christian holiness. He does not say stop gratifying the flesh and then you will be able to walk by the Spirit. He says walk, and the other will follow. Sin is displaced far more often than it is defeated by direct assault, because a man staring at his temptation and gritting his teeth is still looking at it.

Verse 17 is honest about the cost. The desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other. This is a settled state of war inside every believer, and it should be said plainly, because young Christians often assume the conflict is evidence that something went wrong at their conversion. It is the reverse. Before conversion there was no war; the flesh had the field. The fight itself is a sign of life — there is now something in you that wants what God wants, and it will not be quiet.

The last clause of verse 17 is genuinely difficult: to keep you from doing the things you want to do. Read one way it means the flesh frustrates the good you intend; read the other, the Spirit blocks the evil you intend. Both are true of the Christian and the grammar allows either, and Paul may well mean the situation as a whole: you are no longer a single, simple will that can do as it pleases. That is the price of having been rescued, and it will last as long as this life does.

Then verse 18 puts the alternative to the law where the chapter has been heading all along: if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law. Note the passive — led. The Judaizers offered a code to be kept; Paul offers a person to be followed. And a code, however holy, can only stand outside you and tell you what to do. The Spirit is inside, and he does not merely require the life. He produces it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the works of the flesh are evident: sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality, idolatry, sorcery, enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the works of the flesh are evident. Before the list begins, one word is worth weighing: works, erga. It is the same word Paul has used all through the letter for works of the law, and the echo is deliberate. Law-keeping and licence look like opposites, and Paul files them under the same heading, because both are things a man produces out of his own resources. Only the products differ.

The list has fifteen items and falls into groups. Sexual sin comes first: sexual immorality (porneia, the broad word for anything outside marriage), impurity, and sensuality — the last being not merely indulgence but indulgence that has stopped caring who sees.

Then religion goes wrong: idolatry and sorcery. The second word is pharmakeia, from which we get pharmacy — the ancient trade of potions, spells and drugs used to bend outcomes. Both belong on a list of fleshly works because both are attempts to manage the divine: an idol is a god you can locate, and a spell is a result you can arrange.

And then the long middle, which is where the reader should slow down. Enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy — eight items, more than half the catalogue, and every one of them is a sin of the church meeting rather than the tavern. This is not an accident. The Galatians were biting and devouring one another, and Paul has put the sins of the religious right at the centre of his list of the works of the flesh. A congregation that would be horrified by verse 19 will often carry verse 20 as its ordinary weather.

Then drunkenness and orgies, and finally and things like these — Paul is not writing a legal code. It is a portrait, not a schedule, and nobody can plead that his particular version is not itemised.

Then the warning, and it is one of the passages in the New Testament that most disturbs tender consciences: those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. A believer reads the list, finds himself somewhere in it — and most honest Christians will find themselves in the middle section within the last month — and concludes that the door has closed.

So read the verb carefully, because everything turns on it. Those who do such things is a present participle describing the settled practice of a life — those who go on doing them, whose lives are characterised by them, who have made their peace with them. It is not a description of the sin you fought and lost this week and hated yourself for. There is a world of difference between a man who falls into a ditch and a man who lives in it, and Scripture never confuses them.

Here is the test, and it is one anyone can run. What do you do the morning after? Not whether you sinned — you did, and so did everyone reading this. Whether the sin still grieves you, and whether you take it anywhere. A man in whom the Spirit lives cannot sin comfortably. The very ache that makes you afraid of this verse is the evidence the verse is not about you. Nobody who has stopped inheriting the kingdom is troubled by the thought of losing it.

verseByVerse.quote: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the fruit of the Spirit. Note the change of word before anything else. The flesh has works; the Spirit has fruit. Works are manufactured — you decide, you exert, you produce. Fruit is grown, and it is grown by something the branch does not do. No apple was ever produced by an apple tree straining.

And note the singular. Not fruits, nine of them, to be collected like badges. One fruit with nine facets — a single character, which is finally the character of Christ himself, being formed in a person. You do not choose patience this year and gentleness next. They come together because they are one life.

Love heads the list, as it must, since verse 14 has just said the whole law is fulfilled in it. Joy — and the New Testament’s joy is not the same thing as cheerfulness of temperament; it survives circumstances that ruin cheerfulness, because its ground is outside them. Peace — first with God, and then, as a consequence, the inward quiet of a man who has stopped negotiating his standing.

Then three that turn outward. Patience is makrothymia, literally long-tempered — a long fuse, specifically with people; it is the word used of God’s forbearance with us. Kindness is not politeness but active usefulness to somebody. Goodness is moral substance, the quality of a man who is the same when nobody is checking.

Then three that hold the rest together. Faithfulness — reliability, being where you said you would be. Gentleness is prautēs, and it is not weakness; in Greek it was used of a powerful horse that had been broken to the bridle, so it is strength under control. And self-control, last, which is a striking thing to find on a list of things the Spirit produces, since it is the one every self-help programme in the world sells. Paul says it is a fruit. You do not generate it. You receive it, and then you use it.

Against such things there is no law. A dry piece of understatement, and it lands the whole argument of the chapter. The Judaizers were afraid that grace would produce lawlessness. Paul says: look at what the Spirit actually produces, and then find me the legislature that would want to prohibit any of it. There is no statute against being patient. The law was always aiming at this, and the Spirit is producing it without the law’s help.

Now the pastoral matter, because this list is used to wound. A believer reads nine words, recognises almost none of them in himself, and concludes he has no Spirit. Three things should be said to him. First, fruit is slow, and it is seasonal, and nobody digs up a tree in March to check. Second, you are the worst-placed person in the world to assess it — ask the people who live with you, who will almost always report growth the man himself cannot see. And third, notice what the sentence does not say. It does not say the fruit of the diligent Christian. It says the fruit of the Spirit, and he is not slow, and he is not uncertain of the outcome, and the growing was never your department.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.

The tense is the thing to notice: have crucified, a past action, complete. Paul is not issuing an instruction here. He is stating what happened to every Christian, and stating it as a fact about them before it is a duty for them.

Which raises the obvious difficulty, and it is worth putting bluntly. Seven verses earlier Paul described a war going on inside the believer that keeps him from doing what he wants. Now he says the flesh has been crucified. If it is dead, what exactly has been fighting?

The answer is in the image itself, and it is one of the most useful things in the chapter. Crucifixion was not a quick death. That was the point of it: Rome chose the method precisely because a man nailed to a beam could take days to die, and for the whole of that time he was mortally wounded, fixed in place, going nowhere — and still perfectly capable of shouting at people. He was finished. He was not yet silent.

That is the exact condition of the flesh in a believer, and it explains something that otherwise makes Christians despair. The old life has received a wound it will not survive; its authority is broken and its outcome is settled. But it is still audible, and it will go on being audible until the day the body dies. So the voice you hear on a bad Thursday is real, and it is loud, and it is not evidence that nothing happened to you. It is the noise of something that has been executed and has not yet stopped.

When did this happen? Paul has already told us: I have been crucified with Christ (2:20). It happened at the cross, and it became yours when you were united to him. Which is why the sentence begins where it does — those who belong to Christ Jesus. This is not an achievement of unusually consecrated believers. It is a description of everyone who is his.

And there is real practical relief in that order. If crucifying the flesh were your project, every failure would mean the work was not done and would have to be started again, and the Christian life would be a series of restarts. Because it is Christ’s finished work applied to you, your failures are the noise of a dying man rather than the recovery of a victorious one. You are not trying to kill the flesh. You are refusing to take orders from something that is already condemned.

Which is worth a moment of sheer wonder. He was nailed to a beam so that the thing that had owned us could be nailed there with him. Everything in us that was in love with its own ruin was fastened to that wood in his body, and the sentence carried out on him was carried out on it, and it will never get down. (cf. Rom. 6:6; Col. 3:5)

verseByVerse.quote: If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.

The if is not a doubt. In the Greek it assumes the thing is true — since we live by the Spirit, and we do. Paul is arguing from a fact to its consequence, and the shape of the argument is the shape of all New Testament ethics: this is what you are, therefore be it. He never asks a Christian to become something in order to qualify. He tells him what he is and then asks him to live like it.

Then a change of verb that is easy to miss but is the whole point. In verse 16 the word was walk, the ordinary word for daily conduct. Here Paul uses a different one: stoichōmen, a military term for keeping rank — marching in line, holding formation, matching the step of the man beside you.

And here is the thing that makes the sentence remarkable, and it is a piece of quiet artistry that runs right back through the letter. That verb is built on the same root as stoicheia, the word Paul used twice in chapter 4 for the elementary principles that had the Galatians in bondage (4:3, 4:9). He takes the word for the thing that enslaved them and turns it into the word for walking free with the Spirit. The Galatians had been in ranks before; they had marched to a calendar and a code. Paul does not tell them to stop marching. He tells them who sets the pace now.

So Christian freedom is not the absence of order. It is a different formation, and the two distinctions that matter are these. Under the law you kept step with a system that could not help you keep it; now you keep step with a person who is himself the power to do it. And under the law the marching was how you got your standing; now it is what your standing produces.

The practical force of keep in step is that it names two ways of getting it wrong, and most Christians are prone to one or the other. You can march ahead of him — running on your own energy, taking initiatives you were never given, driving a ministry or a decision at a pace nothing has been given to sustain, and calling the exhaustion faithfulness. Or you can lag behind — hearing the small thing you should do, agreeing with it, and not doing it, until the agreeing has quietly become a substitute for the doing.

Neither is dramatic, and neither looks like rebellion. Both are simply being out of step, and the correction in each case is the same and is not complicated: find where he actually is, and be there. He is not marching away from you. He sets the pace at something a real person can sustain over a whole life, which is exactly what the law never did.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.

It is a small verse, and it is doing a large job. It stands between the fruit of the Spirit and chapter 6’s instructions about restoring a brother caught in sin, and it is the hinge between them: here is what walking in step actually looks like in a room full of other people. Paul brings the whole soaring argument of the chapter down onto how you feel about the Christian sitting three seats away.

The root is named first. Conceited translates a word meaning empty-glory — kenodoxoi, glory with nothing inside it. Not glory that is deserved, and not glory that is even real; a reputation held up by air. And the moment a man’s significance depends on something that hollow, he cannot leave other people alone, because the only way to maintain a comparative standing is comparatively.

So the two symptoms follow, and Paul pairs them because they are the same disease at different altitudes. Provoking is what the man ahead does: challenging, needling, making sure the gap is felt. Envying is what the man behind does: resenting, watching, quietly hoping for a stumble. They look like opposites and they are identical — both are a person whose eyes are fixed on another believer rather than on Christ, and whose sense of himself is being calculated from the difference.

This is also exactly what a religion of performance manufactures, which is why the verse sits where it does. If standing before God is earned, then every other Christian is either a rival or a reassurance, and there is no third option. It is only when a man knows he was received with empty hands that another man’s gifts stop being a threat.

Here is the test, and it is uncomfortably easy to run. Think of the believer whose ministry, family or reputation is flourishing most visibly in your circle. What happens in you when good news about him is announced? A flicker of something before the congratulation catches up is not a trivial fault of temperament. It is verse 26 with your name on it, and Paul puts it directly after nine words about the fruit of the Spirit for that reason: envy is the one thing that cannot coexist with love, joy and peace, because it needs somebody else to have less.

And the cure is not to try harder to be pleased. It is to look somewhere else. Empty glory is only attractive while it is the best glory in view. Set beside the real thing — the Son of God who had glory in full, laid it down, took the form of a slave and was executed for people who were arguing about rank — the competition in the third row loses its grip, not because you have condemned it but because you have stopped finding it interesting. (cf. Phil. 2:3–7; Jn. 3:30)
