6.title: Boasting Only in the Cross: The New Creation and the Community of Grace
6.overview:
The letter’s final chapter moves from the Spirit’s inner work to its outward expression in the community of faith. The freedom of the gospel, Paul has shown, is not moral permissiveness; it is the freedom that produces love, and love expresses itself in the concrete practices of the community. Chapter 6 describes what the community shaped by the gospel looks like: it bears burdens, restores the fallen gently, gives generously, sows to the Spirit, and refuses to grow weary in doing good.

The chapter reaches its climax in Paul’s autographic conclusion (vv. 11–18), where he returns one final time to the contrast that has driven the entire letter. The Judaizers boast in their circumcision program; they want to make a good showing in the flesh, to avoid persecution for the cross. Paul boasts in nothing except the cross of the Lord Jesus Christ — the event that crucified the world to him and him to the world. And this cross has created something radically new: not merely reformed Judaism, not a hybrid of law and grace, but a new creation. In the new creation, “neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.” The old categories — the categories by which the Judaizers were demanding conformity — have been abolished. What remains is the new creation in Christ, the Israel of God, the community of those who walk by the rule of the cross.

The letter ends as it began: with the gospel. Paul opened with grace and peace; he closes with “grace be with your spirit, brothers.” He opened with astonishment that they were deserting grace; he closes with the reminder that grace is still there, still sufficient, still the only ground on which any person, anywhere, stands before God. Galatians is, from first to last, a letter about grace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul takes six chapters of doctrine and puts them to work on the hardest situation in ordinary church life. Verse 1 concerns a brother caught in a transgression — the passive verb suggests a man ambushed rather than one who planned his rebellion, which does not make the sin smaller but does change the posture you approach him in. Restore is katartizete, the word for mending a torn net and for setting a broken bone: get close, know what you are doing, cause only the pain the job needs, and aim at a limb that works again. The gentleness required is prautēs, the fruit named eleven verses earlier at 5:23. And the safeguard turns suddenly singular — keep watch on yourself — because the danger in a restoration is rarely committing the same sin. It is enjoying the position.

Verse 2 puts the two commands together as one activity: bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ. The word is barē, a crushing weight, and dealing with a brother’s sin is not an alternative to carrying it but a form of it. The law of Christ is not a replacement code; Paul has already defined it as love (5:14), and the Lord gave it as love one another, just as I have loved you (Jn. 13:34). His name is on it because he is the one who bore what nobody else could lift (Isa. 53:4).

Verses 3–5 explain why restoration goes wrong, and the problem is self-assessment rather than technique. Verse 3 describes the one sin that blinds you specifically to itself: the man who thinks he is something deceives himself. Verse 4 gives the remedy — assay your own work, not your neighbour’s — because a verdict reached by comparison changes whenever the neighbour changes. And v. 5 resolves the apparent contradiction with v. 2: the word there is phortion, a soldier’s pack proportioned to its carrier, and the tense is future, looking to the day each of us gives his own account.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as a Community of Restoration

The Reformed tradition has never regarded the church as merely a preaching station but as a communion of saints — a body committed to mutual care, discipline and restoration. Verse 1 is the practical expression of the justification theology of the whole letter. We deal gently with a failing brother because we know we stand only by grace; the man who forgets his own proneness to sin will always be a prosecutor, and the man who remembers it will be a restorer. Gentleness without truth produces sentimentality, and truth without gentleness produces further fracture. Both are failures of the same verse.

Verses 2 and 5 together give the balance that keeps a church healthy, and both errors are recognisable. What is crushing a man, others are commanded to help carry; what is properly his own — his obedience, his repentance, his answer at the last day — nobody can carry for him, and pretending otherwise is not kindness. There is the Christian who will not let anyone near a weight that is breaking him and calls it strength, and the Christian who has quietly transferred his own pack to his church or his spouse and calls it fellowship.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatian congregations were biting and devouring one another (5:15). Freedom had evidently been taken by some as licence, and the response of others was condemnation rather than restoration. Verse 1 corrects both errors at once, and v. 3 names what was fuelling the second: men who thought they were something. Verse 4 answers the comparison culture that ends chapter 5 in provoking and envying.

Now: Verse 1 has a practical shape. Go, rather than discuss him. Go having asked whether you would want the conversation conducted on you the way you are about to conduct it. Say the true thing plainly, since gentleness that will not name the sin is cowardice wearing its coat. Verse 2 puts a specific question that a warm and orthodox church can still fail: whose weight are you actually under? Not who you pray for, which costs very little and can be done in your own house — whose burden has cost you a Saturday, or money you had other plans for. And v. 4 is uncomfortably clarifying: when you last felt good about your Christian life, was that a judgement about your work or about somebody else’s?

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has spent five chapters on doctrine, and the first thing he does with it is put it to work on the hardest situation in ordinary church life: what to do about a Christian who has fallen.

If anyone is caught in any transgression. The verb is passive — prolēmphthē, overtaken, caught out, surprised by it. The picture is not of a man who sat down and planned his rebellion but of one who was walking along and was ambushed. That does not make the sin smaller; Paul calls it a transgression, a stepping over the line. It does change the posture you approach him in. You are looking at a casualty, not a defector.

You who are spiritual should restore him. Who qualifies? Not an elite tier of believers — Paul has just spent a chapter saying every Christian lives by the Spirit and should keep in step with him (5:25). The spiritual are simply those actually walking in step today. But there is an edge in it, because the Galatians were full of people who thought themselves advanced, and Paul is quietly saying: if you are so spiritual, here is the job.

Restore is katartizete, and it is a lovely word. It is used of mending torn nets (Matt. 4:21) and, in medical writing, of setting a broken bone. Both pictures teach the same thing. Nobody sets a bone carelessly, and nobody sets one by shouting at it. It requires that you get close, that you know what you are doing, that you cause pain deliberately and only as much as the job needs — and that the entire object is a limb that works again. A surgeon who enjoyed the pain would be struck off.

In a spirit of gentleness. The word is prautēs, and it appeared eleven verses ago in the fruit of the Spirit (5:23). That is not an accident. Paul has said what the Spirit produces, and now he shows you the room where it is needed most. Gentleness is not softness about the sin; it is strength under control, the broken horse rather than the tame one.

Then the safeguard, and the grammar shifts to make it land: keep watch on yourself — singular, suddenly, in a sentence full of plurals. Paul turns from the church to the individual doing the restoring and speaks to him alone. Lest you too be tempted.

Which is worth taking seriously, because the danger is real and it is not the obvious one. The temptation in a restoration is rarely to commit the same sin. It is to enjoy the position — to find that being the one who is well is unexpectedly pleasant, to relay the details as a prayer request, to feel a quiet firmness of ground under you that you did not have last week. That is a worse condition than the one you came to mend, and it is invisible to the man in it.

So here is the practical shape of it. Go, rather than discuss him. Go having asked honestly whether you would want this conversation conducted on you the way you are about to conduct it. Say the true thing plainly, because gentleness that will not name the sin is not gentleness but cowardice wearing its coat. And go knowing that the only thing separating you from him is grace you did not generate. A man who has really grasped the first five chapters of this letter cannot be a prosecutor. He has read the charge sheet with his own name on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.

Bear is bastazete, a present imperative — go on carrying, as a habit. And the noun is barē: a weight, something heavy, the word for a load that presses a man down. Paul is not talking about minor inconveniences. He means the things that are genuinely too much for one person: a marriage that is failing, a diagnosis, a son who has stopped speaking to them, the particular sin from the verse before that a man cannot get free of on his own.

And notice how the two verses sit together. Verse 1 says restore the fallen; verse 2 says carry each other’s weight. Paul evidently thinks these are the same activity. Dealing with somebody’s sin is not an alternative to bearing his burden. It is bearing his burden, if it is done as verse 1 describes it.

Then the phrase that startles: and so fulfill the law of Christ. Paul has spent five chapters saying that the believer is not under law — and here, at the end, he uses the word positively and attaches Christ’s name to it.

He is not smuggling the old system back in through the last door. The law of Christ is not a replacement code with new clauses; he has already said what it is. The whole law is fulfilled in loving your neighbour as yourself (5:14), and the Lord himself gave it as a new commandment: love one another; just as I have loved you (Jn. 13:34). So the law of Christ is the law of love, defined not by a list but by a life — and the standard is not as you love yourself any more, but as I have loved you, which is a good deal more expensive.

And there is a deeper reason his name is on it, which turns the whole verse from an instruction into something better. Christ did not merely legislate burden-bearing. He is the one who bore the burden nobody else could lift — surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows (Isa. 53:4). When a Christian takes the weight of another man’s failure onto his own shoulders, he is not obeying a rule. He is doing, in miniature and at infinite distance, the thing that was done for him at Calvary.

Which makes the practical question quite specific, and it is worth answering rather than admiring. Whose weight are you actually under at the moment? Not who do you pray for — praying costs a Christian very little and can be done entirely in his own house. Whose burden has cost you a Saturday, or money you had other plans for, or a friendship that got harder because you told the truth inside it? A church can be doctrinally immaculate, warm on a Sunday, and carrying nothing at all, because burden-bearing is invisible and voluntary and nobody ever notices its absence.

And it will not be reciprocal, which is the last thing to say. Paul writes one another’s, and in a healthy church it evens out over years. But it does not even out on any given Tuesday, and the man who keeps accounts will not last. You carry, and sometimes you are carried, and the ledger between you was closed at the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: For if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each one test his own work, and then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor. For each will have to bear his own load.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three verses that look like scattered proverbs and are in fact a single argument about why restoration goes wrong. The problem is not technique. It is self-assessment.

If anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself. Paul is describing the exact frame of mind that makes a man unfit for verse 1. Note that he does not say such a man deceives his neighbour, although he probably does. He deceives himself — the verb is one of leading your own mind astray. This is the peculiar quality of spiritual pride: it is the one sin that blinds you specifically to itself. A man knows when he has lost his temper. Nobody has ever thought, this morning I am inflated.

When he is nothing. That sounds crushing until you remember what the letter has established. Paul is not saying you are worthless; he has spent two chapters telling these people they are sons and heirs of God. He means you are nothing on your own account. Everything you have that is worth having came in as a gift, and a man who forgets that has mistaken a delivery for an achievement.

Then the remedy, in verse 4: let each one test his own work. The word is dokimazetō, the term for assaying metal — putting it in the fire to find what it actually is rather than what it looks like. And notice the object: his own work. That is the whole point. The Galatians were measuring themselves against one another, which is why the chapter before ends with provoking and envying (5:26).

The result is stated oddly and repays attention: then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor. Paul is not endorsing self-congratulation. He is making a point about where the measurement comes from. A man who has assayed his own work has a real, if modest, sense of what God has actually given him to do and whether he is doing it. A man who has measured himself against his neighbour has nothing at all — because his verdict depends entirely on who happens to be standing next to him, and it will change when the neighbour changes.

Run the test and it is uncomfortably clarifying. When you last felt reasonably good about your Christian life, was that a judgement about your work, or about somebody else’s? And when you last felt like a failure, the same question. Almost all of both feelings, for most people, most of the time, is arithmetic performed on other people.

Then verse 5, and the reader stops, because it looks like a flat contradiction of verse 2. Bear one another’s burdens, and now each will have to bear his own load. Which is it?

Two things resolve it. First, the words are different. Verse 2 is barē, a crushing weight, the thing a man cannot carry alone. Verse 5 is phortion, which is the word for a soldier’s pack or a ship’s cargo — an assignment, a load properly proportioned to the one carrying it. It is the very word the Lord uses when he says my burden is light (Matt. 11:30).

Second, the tense. Verse 2 is a present imperative about now; verse 5 is a future indicative — will have to bear. Paul is looking ahead to the day when each of us gives his own account, and no one else can stand in the queue for us.

So the two verses are not in tension at all; they divide the world sensibly. What is crushing you, others are commanded to help carry. What is properly yours — your own obedience, your own repentance, your own answer at the last day — nobody can carry, and it is not a kindness to pretend otherwise. Both errors are common and both are recognisable. There is the Christian who will not let anyone near a weight that is breaking him, and calls it strength. And there is the Christian who has quietly transferred his own pack to his church, his counsellor or his spouse, and calls it fellowship.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 6 arrives without preliminaries and it is about money: let the one taught share all good things with the one who teaches. The verb is koinōneitō, from the word for fellowship, which tells you Paul did not regard the subject as a lower order of thing. Note also who is instructed — congregations to give, not teachers to raise support. The reversal has done real damage, because a man who must ask for his own living finds it very hard to say the unwelcome thing, and this letter exists because somebody said one.

Verse 7 hardens the tone. God is not mocked uses a verb built on the word for the nose: nobody sneers at God and gets away with it. The farming principle that follows carries three certainties every agricultural town understood — you reap what you sowed, more than you sowed, and later than you sowed. It is the third that deceives people, because the gap is long enough to make the connection look unreal. Verse 8 names the two fields, and corruption is phthoran, decay: the flesh pays out not usually in catastrophe but in decomposition. The promise of eternal life to those who sow to the Spirit is not wages — six chapters forbid that — but the full growth of a life that was given.

Verse 9 assumes weariness rather than forbidding it, and Paul includes himself in the us. The one condition attached to the harvest is not achievement but persistence: if we do not give up. Verse 10 turns the weariness outward. As we have opportunity uses the same word as the season in v. 9, so the sowing season is now — which disposes of the commonest evasion, since it means while there is time, not when it is convenient. Doing good to everyone forbids the church turned inward; especially to the household of faith forbids a general benevolence that never reaches the believer two streets away.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Harvest as the Motive of Present Faithfulness

Reformed ethics has always read present obedience in the light of a future harvest, and vv. 7–9 are where Paul states it most plainly. The believer does not do good in order to earn the harvest; the harvest is secured by grace, and this letter has spent six chapters proving that nothing a man sows can purchase eternal life. But the harvest is real and the reaping is certain, and the knowledge of it sustains present faithfulness. That is the farmer’s wisdom applied to the Christian life, not works-righteousness.

Verse 8 must be read in the terms already set, or it will contradict the letter. What it describes is a direction of life: the seed a man scatters shows which field he believes he lives in, and a person indwelt by the Spirit sows to the Spirit for the same reason a living tree puts out leaves. And v. 6 grounds the support of gospel ministry in something older than church order — the Levites had no land and Israel ate with them, and Paul states the principle elsewhere as the labourer deserving his wages (1 Cor. 9:11; 1 Tim. 5:17–18), which is the Lord’s own saying.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians were weary — theologically confused, socially fragmented, and without Paul. The Judaizers’ programme was more structured and far more socially comfortable, and drifting toward it would have ended the trouble. Verse 9 is aimed exactly there: the harvest is coming, do not walk off the field. And v. 6 was not incidental either, since nothing in a congregation's life is a more exact readout of what its people actually believe than what happens to their money.

Now: Verse 8 becomes usable rather than frightening once you see the scale of sowing. This morning’s twenty minutes with the Bible open, the apology made instead of the point you were entitled to make, the money that went quietly — none of it felt like anything, which is what seed is like in the hand. Christians so rarely connect their dullness to anything because they are looking for a cause the size of the effect. Verse 9 belongs to named people: the mother who has prayed twenty-two years and stopped expecting the phone to ring, the man teaching eight children in a back room, the wife gentle with a hard husband for a decade with nothing to show. Paul does not offer them encouragement about their prospects. He offers a fact about the universe.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the one who is taught the word share all good things with the one who teaches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the one who is taught the word share all good things with the one who teaches. After the burdens and the boasting, money — and it arrives without any preliminaries at all.

The word for share is koinōneitō, from the family of koinōnia, fellowship. That is the term the New Testament uses for the deepest communion of the church, and Paul uses it here of paying the teacher, which tells you he did not regard the subject as a lower order of thing. Money is fellowship in its most testable form. And all good things is broad: not only cash but food, hospitality, the ordinary provisions a household can share.

Notice also who is instructed. Paul does not tell teachers to raise support; he tells congregations to give it. That is the healthy direction, and the reversal of it has done a great deal of damage. A man who must ask for his own living will find it very hard to say the unwelcome thing, and this letter exists because somebody said an extremely unwelcome thing.

The principle is stated more fully elsewhere: if we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you? (1 Cor. 9:11), and the laborer deserves his wages (1 Tim. 5:17–18), which is Paul quoting the Lord. So the teaching is consistent across his letters and it is not novel; the Levites had no land, and Israel ate with them.

But why here, in this letter, at this point? Because it is the first thing Paul thinks of after burden-bearing, and because of what comes next. Verse 7 begins do not be deceived: God is not mocked — and the sowing and reaping that follows is not first about morals in general. Its immediate subject is what a congregation does with its money. Nothing in church life is a more exact readout of what people actually believe.

And a word to the man for whom this is not an abstract question. Paul did not always take money; he made tents in Corinth rather than be a burden and boasted of preaching free of charge (1 Cor. 9:15–18). So this is not a rule that a paid ministry is the only faithful shape. It is an instruction to the congregation, and the congregation is not permitted to use the apostle’s freedom as an excuse. He chose to go without. He never once said the teacher was not owed.

Then the searching part, which is what makes this more than church administration. Ask what your giving is actually being decided by. Most Christians give from what is left, which means the teaching of the word is funded by the residue of a lifestyle that was designed without reference to it. Paul’s word is share — not tip, not subsidise, not fund from surplus. It assumes a common life in which what one has is available to the other, and that is a considerably more disturbing idea than a percentage.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap. For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. The tone hardens without warning. And the verb is worth seeing: mykterizetai comes from the word for the nose, and it means to turn your nose up at someone — to sneer. Paul says God does not get sneered at, and the sense is not that he takes offence but that nobody gets away with it. You may treat him as a system to be worked around; the treatment simply does not succeed.

Whatever one sows, that will he also reap. The picture is a farmer, and it carries three certainties that everyone in an agricultural town understood without being told.

You reap what you sow — the field returns the kind of thing that went into it, and no farmer has ever been surprised by the species of his own crop. You reap more than you sow, which is the entire point of farming and cuts both ways: a handful of seed returns a sheaf, and so does a handful of the other thing. And you reap later than you sow, which is the certainty that deceives people, because the gap between the sowing and the harvest is long enough to make a man think the connection is not real.

That gap is what verse 7 is aimed at. Nobody sneers at God while the harvest is coming in. The sneer happens in month four, when nothing has visibly followed and the whole warning seems overwrought. Paul’s answer is not that judgement is coming quickly. It is that the ground is keeping the account whether or not anyone is watching it.

Then verse 8 names the two fields. The one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. The word is phthoran — decay, the process by which a thing rots. That is a precise description rather than a threat. The flesh does not pay out in catastrophe so much as in decomposition: a marriage that goes quietly hollow, an appetite that needs more each year to do the same work, a conscience that stops registering, a man in his sixties who cannot say what he built. Nothing dramatic ever happened. It simply went off.

But the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life. And here a guard is needed, because the sentence can be read as wages for services rendered, which would contradict the entire letter. Read it in the terms Paul has already set. Eternal life is not a crop you grow; it is the gift of God in Christ Jesus, and this letter has spent six chapters proving that nothing you sow can purchase it. What verse 8 describes is a direction of life. The seed a man scatters shows which field he thinks he lives in, and a person indwelt by the Spirit sows to the Spirit for the same reason a living tree puts out leaves. The harvest is not his wages. It is the full growth of a life that was given to him.

Which turns the verse into something usable rather than frightening. Sowing is small, repeated and unremarkable, and nobody has ever sown a field in one afternoon. This morning’s twenty minutes with the Bible open, the apology you made instead of the point you were entitled to make, the money that went quietly, the conversation you had with the difficult person at church — none of it felt like anything. That is what seed is like in the hand. The reason Christians so seldom connect their spiritual dullness to anything is that they are looking for a cause the size of the effect, and there never is one. There is a field, and there is what has been going into it for eleven years.

verseByVerse.quote: And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up. So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And let us not grow weary of doing good. The us matters. Paul has been saying you for five chapters and he now puts himself inside the exhortation, which means the apostle knew what it was to be tired of doing good.

And notice that he does not tell them to stop being weary. He assumes it. The verb enkakōmen carries the sense of losing heart, going slack, running out of the will to continue — and it is not a warning against wickedness but against a very ordinary exhaustion. That is a mercy in itself. A Christian who is worn out from carrying burdens, restoring the fallen and giving away money is not in a state Paul finds surprising. He is in the state this verse was written for.

For in due season we will reap. The phrase is kairō idiō — at its own proper time, the season that belongs to that harvest. No farmer resents June for not being September. He works a field that shows him nothing for months, because the timetable was never his to set and he knows the difference between nothing is happening and nothing is visible.

If we do not give up. The one condition, and it is not achievement. Paul does not say we shall reap if we sow enough, or well, or with the right motives. He says we shall reap if we do not stop. The whole risk in the Christian life at this point is not failure but abandonment — walking off the field in the eleventh year, three weeks before something comes up.

So this verse belongs to particular people, and they should be named, because they are the ones most likely to be reading it at the end of their strength. The mother who has prayed for a son for twenty-two years and has stopped expecting the phone to ring. The man who teaches eight children in a back room while the church around him talks about growth. The wife who has been gentle with a hard husband for a decade with nothing whatever to show for it. The pastor in a small town who has buried more people than he has baptised. Paul’s answer to every one of them is not encouragement about their prospects. It is a fact about the universe: sowing is followed by reaping, and the season is God’s.

Then verse 10 turns the weariness outward rather than inward: as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone.Opportunity is kairon again — the same word as the season in verse 9. The harvest has its kairos and so does the sowing, and the sowing season is now. Which quietly disposes of the commonest evasion, since as we have opportunity does not mean when it is convenient. It means while there is still time.

To everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith. Both halves are needed and each corrects a different failure. Everyone forbids the church that has turned inward and does its good only where it will be appreciated by people who share its views. Especially forbids the sentimentality that regards a general benevolence toward mankind as an adequate substitute for helping the specific believer two streets away whose boiler has failed. It is family first, which is not the same as family only — and the word household is chosen with care, because a family does not run an application process. The claim on you is not that the person deserves it. It is that he is kin.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — The Cross and the New Creation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
In v. 11 Paul takes the pen from his secretary and writes the closing paragraph himself, in large letters — the ancient equivalent of underlining hard enough to score the page. What he writes large is not doctrine but motive. Verse 12 says the men forcing circumcision want to make a good showing in the flesh and to avoid persecution for the cross, which had a concrete meaning in that century: Judaism was a recognised religion under Rome, and circumcised converts made the whole problem disappear for everyone. Verse 13 exposes the second motive, converts as trophies, and adds the detail that collapses the programme — the men selling the law do not keep it themselves, which 5:3 said it obligates them to.

Verse 14 answers with the sharpest contrast in the letter. They boast in flesh; Paul boasts in a gallows, and far be it from me is his most violent negative. The cross was not yet jewellery: it was Rome’s method for killing slaves in public, and for a Pharisee it carried the curse of Deuteronomy 21:23 that Paul quoted at 3:13. The double crucifixion he describes runs both ways — the world's offers have lost their force on him, and he has lost his standing in its eyes, which is the harder half and precisely what the Judaizers were avoiding.

Verse 15 gives the verdict: neither circumcision nor uncircumcision, but a new creation — kainē ktisis, new in kind, the age to come arriving early in a person, not a renovation of the old. Verse 16 pronounces peace and mercy on all who walk by that rule, and on the Israel of God, the most argued-over phrase in the letter. Verse 17 closes the case not with an argument but with scars — stigmata, the brand of ownership — and v. 18 ends where 1:3 began, with grace, and with the word brothers standing last in the Greek sentence before the Amen.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cross as the Permanent Centre, and the Israel of God

Paul’s boast in v. 14 is the summary of everything the letter has argued. The cross is where the law’s curse was absorbed, where the old creation died and the new was born, and Reformed theology has always insisted it is not merely the entrance to the Christian life but its permanent centre — the ground the believer stands on at every moment from conversion to glory. This is Luther’s theology of the cross against a theology of glory: God’s ways are read from below, through shame and suffering, not from above through human notions of power and success.

On v. 16 everything turns on the small word kai, which can mean and or even. Read as even the Israel of God, the phrase caps the sentence: those who walk by this rule, Jew and Gentile together, are the Israel of God, which is the standard Reformed reading and is supported by 3:29 and 4:26. Read as simply and, a second group is in view, most naturally believing Jews. This commentary takes the first, and says so openly; the second is held by serious readers who love this book, including many who expect a future for ethnic Israel on the strength of Romans 11. On what actually matters here nobody disagrees: whoever they are, the rule they walk by is the cross and the new creation, and no one enters that number by ancestry or by a mark.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers wanted social safety, and vv. 12–13 name it without charity. Jewish nationalist feeling was rising through those decades, and Jewish Christians seen to be dissolving the boundary paid for it at home; circumcising the Gentiles satisfied the synagogue and left Rome uninterested. It was a solution any reasonable committee might reach. Verse 17 answers it with the marks Paul carried from the stoning at Lystra, in Galatia itself, which some of the men hearing this letter read aloud had watched happen.

Now: Verse 13 puts a question to anyone who has softened a conviction and given a theological reason for it. The test is not whether the reason is defensible — the Judaizers had excellent reasons, one of which was avoiding a beating. The test is what the adjustment costs you, and the flesh has never once recommended a course of action that would get its owner persecuted.

Verse 14 can be tested directly: ask what would happen if the reputation you have built quietly collapsed, not through sin but through being overlooked. If you would lose something painful but survivable, the crucifixion has been done. If you would not know who you were, the world is very much alive. And v. 17 belongs to anyone whose faithfulness has cost them something unglamorous — a career that went nowhere, a body worn out in a small work nobody counted. Paul filed his scars under the same heading as the wounds of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand. It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised, and only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ. For even those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the law, but they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand. Paul takes the pen off his secretary. Letters in that world were normally dictated, with the author adding a line at the end in his own hand as a signature (cf. 2 Thess. 3:17); here he takes over for the whole closing paragraph, and he writes big. Possibly his eyes were poor, which would fit 4:15. Chiefly it is emphasis — the ancient equivalent of underlining hard enough to score the page. What follows is the whole letter compressed, in his own handwriting, and he does not want it missed.

And what he writes large is not doctrine. It is motive. It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised.

The phrase is literally to present a fine face — to look well in public. And then Paul names what they are actually buying with the Galatians’ foreskins: only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ.

That is worth setting in its own century, because it turns an insult into a diagnosis. Judaism was a recognised religion under Rome, with legal protection and exemptions that other cults did not enjoy. A movement of circumcised Jews who followed a Messiah could shelter under that. A movement of uncircumcised Gentiles worshipping a crucified Jew could not, and it looked to the synagogues like apostasy and to Rome like a new and unlicensed sect. Meanwhile Jewish nationalist feeling was rising through those decades, and Jewish Christians who were seen to be dissolving the boundary paid for it at home.

So the Judaizers were not primarily theologians. They were men under pressure, doing something explicable. Get the Gentiles circumcised and the whole problem goes away: the synagogue is satisfied, Rome is uninterested, and nobody has to be beaten. It is a solution any reasonable committee might reach.

Then verse 13 exposes the second motive, and it is uglier: they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh. Converts as trophies. Something done to another man’s body that can be counted and reported. Every generation of ministry has its version of this — the number, the testimony repeated at conferences, the person who has become a credential.

And Paul adds the detail that collapses the whole programme: even those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the law. He had told them in 5:3 that circumcision obligates a man to the entire code. Here he observes that the men selling it are not keeping it either. So this was never a serious attempt at law-righteousness. It was a way of belonging safely, dressed in Scripture.

Which puts a question to anyone who has ever softened a Christian conviction and given a theological reason for it. The test is not whether your reason is defensible; the Judaizers had excellent reasons and one of them was avoiding a beating. The test is what the adjustment costs you. Every change these men proposed made their lives easier, and there is no recorded instance of the flesh recommending a course of action that would get its owner persecuted. Paul’s alternative is in the next verse, and it is a cross — which is exactly what the whole manoeuvre was designed to avoid.

verseByVerse.quote: But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.

They boast in flesh; Paul boasts in a gallows. And the opening phrase is mē genoito, the same violent negative he used at 2:17 and 3:21 — God forbid, may it never be. He is not saying he has other grounds for boasting and modestly declines them. He is saying the thought is unthinkable.

Feel how strange the sentence would have sounded. The cross was not yet jewellery. It was the Roman state’s instrument for killing slaves and rebels in public, deliberately obscene, so shameful that polite Roman writers avoided the word. Cicero said the very name of it should be far from the body of a Roman citizen. And a Pharisee had the additional certainty of Deuteronomy 21:23, which Paul quoted back in 3:13: a hanged man is cursed by God. To boast in a crucifixion was, in Jewish terms, blasphemy, and in Roman terms, disgusting.

That is the object Paul says is the only thing in the universe he will glory in. Not his conversion, which was spectacular. Not his missionary record, which was unmatched. Not his learning, his visions, or his suffering. One thing, and it is something done to him rather than by him.

Then he says what the cross accomplished in him personally, and it is a double death: by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.

Take the two directions separately, because they are different operations and most Christians have only had one of them done. The world has been crucified to me: its offers have lost their force. What it holds out — standing, security, the approval of the people whose approval you were raised to want — is not evil, and Paul is not saying he despises it. He is saying it is dead to him. It cannot buy him any more, because he has seen the one thing it had no answer for.

And I to the world: he has lost his standing in its eyes too. This is the harder half, and it is the one the Judaizers were desperate to avoid. A man dead to the world is a man the world has finished assessing. He is not being ranked, because he is not a candidate. Which is precisely why he was free to write this letter and they were not.

What does that look like in an ordinary life with a mortgage and a family? Not withdrawal. Paul had trades and travelled and cared enormously about money for the poor. It looks like this: the world can still take things from you and can no longer take anything that matters from you, and it can no longer set your price. Ask what would happen if the reputation you have built quietly collapsed — not through sin, just through being overlooked or misunderstood. If the answer is that you would lose something painful but survivable, the crucifixion has been done. If the answer is that you would not know who you were, the world is still very much alive.

And stand back and look at what Paul is glorying in. The Son of God, hanging on a beam outside a city, stripped, mocked, numbered with criminals, bearing a curse that belonged to other people — and there is not a throne in the history of the world that has ever been so completely a throne as that. The universe has one boast in it, and it is a man on a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. And as for all who walk by this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. The verdict that ends the argument, and it is worth pairing with the two other places Paul finishes the same sentence differently. In 5:6 what counts is faith working through love; in 1 Corinthians 7:19 it is keeping the commandments of God; here, a new creation. Three answers, one thing: the question is never the mark on the body but whether God has done something.

A new creation is kainē ktisis, and kainos means new in kind, not merely recent. Paul is reaching for Genesis 1 and for Isaiah’s promise of new heavens and a new earth. What the gospel produces is not a reformed version of the old thing — not a better man, a tidied-up religion, a Judaism with the difficult parts adjusted. It is the age to come, arriving early, in a person. If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation (2 Cor. 5:17).

Which is why the Judaizing offer was so hopeless. They were proposing an alteration to somebody who had already been raised. It is the difference between renovating a house and being born.

And as for all who walk by this rule — kanoni, a measuring rod, a straight edge. The rule is what he has just said: not circumcision, not uncircumcision, new creation. Peace and mercy be upon them, and notice the order, which is not the order of Paul’s greetings anywhere else. He normally writes grace and peace. Here mercy comes second, after peace, as though at the end of a letter this severe he wants the last word on the Galatians to be that they will be dealt with kindly.

And upon the Israel of God. This is the most argued-over phrase in the letter, and honesty is better than false confidence. Everything turns on the small word kai, which can mean and or even.

Read it as even the Israel of God, and the phrase caps the sentence: those who walk by this rule — Jew and Gentile together in Christ — are the Israel of God. That is the standard Reformed reading, and the letter’s whole argument supports it, since Paul has already said that those who are Christ’s are Abraham’s offspring and heirs according to promise (3:29), and that the Jerusalem above is our mother (4:26). Read it as simply and, and a second group is in view — most naturally Jewish believers, the believing remnant, singled out for a particular blessing at the end of a letter that has been hard on their nation’s badge.

This commentary takes the first reading, for the reason given: it is what six chapters have been arguing. But the second is held by serious readers who love this book and read it carefully, including many who expect a future for ethnic Israel on the strength of Romans 11 and who honour the Scriptures as fully as anyone who differs from them. It is worth saying plainly that on the point that actually matters here, nobody disagrees: whoever the Israel of God is, they are those on whom peace and mercy rest, and the rule they walk by is the cross and the new creation. A man does not get into that number by ancestry or by a mark, and never has.

And there is comfort in the phrase however it is parsed. The Galatians had been told for months that they were outsiders to the people of God, provincial latecomers who would always be second-tier. Paul’s final blessing lays peace and mercy on everyone walking by this rule, and does not check anybody’s papers on the way past.

verseByVerse.quote: From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus. It sounds abrupt, almost weary, and the reason is in the word he chooses. The marks are stigmata, and in that world a stigma was a brand: burned or cut into the skin of a slave to show whose he was, into a soldier to show whose army, into a temple servant to show whose god.

Now put that against the argument of the whole letter. The Judaizers wanted a mark cut into Gentile flesh to prove ownership and belonging. Paul says: I have marks. I did not choose them and I cannot show them without embarrassment, and they were put there by people trying to stop me. The lash at Philippi. The stones at Lystra, in Galatia itself, where some of the men reading this letter had watched him dragged out of their own town and left for dead. Those are his credentials, and they are on the same page of the ledger as circumcision and settle the question of whose he is far more conclusively.

There is a quiet finality in from now on. The case is closed. He has argued covenants, chronology, Abraham, Hagar and the Spirit for six chapters, and at the end he simply shows the scars.

Which is worth pausing on for anyone whose faithfulness has cost them something visible and unglamorous — a career that went nowhere because of a conviction, a family that cooled, a body worn out in a small work nobody counted. Those marks are not evidence of a failure to manage life well. Paul filed his under the same heading as the wounds of Christ, and expected them to be honoured.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.

And look at what the last word is. Not foolish Galatians, which is how the argument started; not a final warning; not the name of an opponent. In the Greek the sentence ends, just before the Amen, with brothers. The man who wrote an anathema in the first chapter signs off calling them family.

He began with grace (1:3) and he ends with grace, and everything between the two is an argument that nothing may be added to it. Not circumcision, not a calendar, not the endorsement of Jerusalem, not the record of the man reading this. The letter closes exactly where it opened, because there is nowhere else for a Christian to stand.

So the last thing Galatians does is hold up its subject one more time. A Son sent in the fullness of time, born of a woman and under the law; who kept every clause of it and then went out to a tree and was made a curse, so that the blessing sworn to Abraham could reach a farmer in Lystra with no ancestry and no merit and nothing to bring; who bought slaves out of the market, cancelled the debt, gave them his own name, put his Spirit in their hearts and taught them to say Father. Nothing was cheapened to do it. Everything was paid. And the whole of it, from first to last, was grace — which is why the letter can end with the word it began with, and there is nothing left to add. Amen.
